The Chase Air Canada Aeroplan® Credit Card is one of the most compelling co-branded airline credit cards out there. I’m a huge fan of the Air Canada Aeroplan program — even if you have no connection to Air Canada or Aeroplan, the program is fantastic for partner redemptions, and this card is worth being aware of. And if you do fly Air Canada with any frequency, the perks for travel on the airline are strong.

So this post is my in-depth Air Canada Aeroplan Card review. Let’s go over all the details, and discuss if the card is worth it.

Link: Learn more about the Chase Air Canada Aeroplan® Credit Card

Before I review the Air Canada Aeroplan Card benefits in detail, here’s a high-level look at everything you need to know about the card:

Here are my thoughts on the Air Canada Aeroplan Card’s biggest pros and cons:

If you’re thinking about applying for the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card, you’re probably most interested in the welcome bonus it’s currently offering, along with its annual fee and general eligibility rules for getting the card. So let’s get into those details.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card currently has the following welcome bonus: Limited Time Offer: Earn up to 80,000 bonus points. Earn 60,000 bonus points after you spend $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months your account is open. Plus, up to 20,000 more bonus points by earning 50% more bonus points per $1 spent on purchases that normally earn 1 bonus point in the first 2 months from account opening..

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Aeroplan points to be worth 1.4 cents each. That means the 80,000 points are worth $1,120 to me. However, even if you have a different valuation of these points than I do, you can at least use the “Pay Yourself Back” feature to redeem these points for 1.25 cents each toward a travel purchase, so that’s a pretty high “cash out” value.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card is issued by Chase, and has pretty standard application restrictions:

While Chase doesn’t have a public credit score requirement for the Air Canada Aeroplan Card, you’ll have the best chances of approval if your score is in the good range or higher. That roughly translates to a minimum score of 670. However, people have been approved with lower scores and rejected with higher scores, as it’s one of only many factors that determine card eligibility.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card has a $195 annual fee. There’s no cost to add authorized users to the card, and their spending will count toward your points balance and any spending thresholds.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s a great card to use globally, and possibly even earn bonus rewards on your spending depending on what you’re using the card for.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Card has a well rounded rewards structure, among the most interesting you’ll find on any airline credit cards. This isn’t just about the number of points that you earn, but also about the additional rewards for spending. Specifically, the Aeroplan Card offers the following:

Those are some excellent bonus categories. For what it’s worth, the card offers 1x Aeroplan points on all other purchases, so there are better cards for everyday spending.

There’s a lot to love about Air Canada Aeroplan points, even if you don’t usually fly Air Canada or travel to Canada. Among other things:

I redeem miles through Aeroplan all the time, and consistently get great value. Booking award flights on Air Canada itself rather than other partners isn’t always the best deal, though, especially if you’re booking during a peak travel time, since Air Canada awards use dynamic pricing.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Card gives cardmembers plenty of opportunities to earn elite status with Air Canada Aeroplan. You get some status outright just for being a cardmember, and you can earn further status with spending.

Those who are approved for the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card receive Aeroplan 25K status. This is valid for as long as your account is open. Aeroplan Elite 25K is Air Canada’s entry level status, and includes travel perks with Air Canada, including:

Each year, those with the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card also receive 5,000 Status Qualifying Credits (SQCs) to help work toward the next level of Aeroplan status. This is automatic, but as I’ll cover below, you can stack additional credits on top through hitting certain spending thresholds in the calendar year.

For those curious, below are the Aeroplan elite requirements.

Beyond the automatic 5,000 SQCs you’ll receive each calendar year just for having the Air Canada Aeroplan Card, you can earn up to 20,000 additional credits by hitting spending thresholds. Here’s how that breaks down:

So you can earn a total of 25,000 SQCs each calendar year through the Air Canada Aeroplan Card.

Whether or not that’s worth it really depends on how much you fly Air Canada, and what the opportunity cost of your credit card spending is.

Those with the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card can get a one-tier status upgrade to Aeroplan 35K status when they spend $75,000 on the card in a calendar year. You’ll get status for the remainder of the calendar year you qualify and the entire following calendar year.

If you ask me, the value here is really for someone who is actually loyal to Air Canada. Aeroplan 35K status gets you three complimentary checked bags on Air Canada flights (vs. just one with Aeroplan 25K), 10 eUpgrade credits, and a 3x elite points multiplier on eligible Air Canada or Star Alliance flight bookings, among other things.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers a variety of valuable benefits and credits, beyond the elite status perks covered above. Some of these benefits are offered just for being a cardmember, while others can be earned with spending. The perks are pretty comprehensive, and you’ll find almost everything you could want short of lounge access. So let’s go over those.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers up to $100 in Air Canada statement credits when you make qualifying Air Canada purchases. The credits apply to paid airfare, taxes and fees on award flights, and inflight food and drinks, though onboard Wi-Fi is excluded.

This breaks down as two credits of up to $50 each, one from January 1 through June 30 and one from July 1 through December 31. If you book cash fares on Air Canada twice a year, this is an easy way to put $100 back in your pocket, and this benefit alone can cover about half of the card’s annual fee.

As an Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card holder, you can receive a 15% discount on the Aeroplan points required to book an award flight on Air Canada, Air Canada Express, or Air Canada Rouge. In practice, this also seems to work on partner award flights, as long as at least one segment is on Air Canada. The upside here can be absolutely huge, and it’s a great reason to have this card.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers a free first checked bag on Air Canada flights for the primary cardmember and up to eight others traveling on the same itinerary. This applies to itineraries with Air Canada, Air Canada Rouge, or Air Canada Express. The value of that could add up pretty quickly. There’s no need to actually pay for the ticket with the card, as long as you’re the primary cardmember and have your Aeroplan number linked to the reservation.

Once every four years, the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers a credit that’s valid toward a membership with Global Entry, TSA PreCheck, or NEXUS, worth up to $120. These are all programs that can save travelers time at the airport, and potentially even at the border.

I specifically love that the card also offers a NEXUS credit, since that’s historically something we haven’t seen card issuers offer. NEXUS is arguably the best of the three programs, since it gets you access to Global Entry, TSA PreCheck, and expedited immigration in Canada.

Admittedly this is probably more interesting in theory than in practice, but I still like where Aeroplan is going with this. Those with the Air Canada Aeroplan Card will automatically have carbon offsets purchased for their flights when redeeming Aeroplan points for an Air Canada flight.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card is a World Elite Mastercard, which comes with certain perks, including a concierge service and presale tickets for eligible events.

While you’ll want to consult the cardmember agreement for full details, the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers a variety of travel protection when paying with the card, including the following:

There’s another feature that you’ll find on the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card, which isn’t available on any other airline card. Specifically, the Aeroplan Credit Card offers a Pay Yourself Back feature, whereby cardmembers can apply their Aeroplan points toward travel purchases on any airline, hotel, or rental car, at the rate of 1.25 cents per point, up to 200,000 points per year.

This is an incredibly innovative concept, and something that cardmembers may find to be valuable. So whether you want to redeem your points for a stay at a Four Seasons or a flight on JetBlue, the possibilities are endless. It’s also a reason to potentially think of the welcome bonus differently — the bonus points earned with the welcome offer can over time be redeemed toward any recent purchase or even toward the card’s annual fee.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card also offers the ability to earn priority reward vouchers. Each can be used to get 50% off an eligible Aeroplan award ticket, and is valid for travel on Air Canada or a partner airline.

You earn these vouchers at the following four annual spending thresholds:

These can each be used in the same way, and the value depends on your status:

As you can tell, the value here will depend on your status and travel patterns, but there’s potentially quite a bit of value to be had.

While this is something that most people won’t be able to achieve, I love the concept behind this, and for some it might just be the best deal in travel. The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers what I’d consider to be the world’s most valuable companion certificate, for those who spend a million dollars per year on the card.

If you reach that threshold, you’ll receive an award redemption companion voucher that’s valid globally:

We’ve never seen a credit card offer a perk quite this valuable before. Obviously, the spending requirement is massive here, and this would only make sense if you were planning a lot of travel in a particular year. For a certain type of consumer, though, this is an incredible opportunity.

A few Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card benefits are set to expire on December 31, 2026, so they won’t be around for too much longer. Here’s a quick look:

If you already have the card, now is your last chance to take advantage of these perks. Especially with the 10% transfer bonus, it’s worth seeing if an Aeroplan award flight makes sense with your upcoming travel plans so you can get some extra value for your rewards before this perk retires.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card is an innovative product with a big welcome bonus, great return on spending, and valuable perks. That’s just about all that I look for in a credit card.

Airline co-brand credit cards are extremely popular given the allegiance many people have to a particular airline. Admittedly Aeroplan is at a disadvantage in the US market, since not as many people in the US are loyal to Air Canada as they are to American, Delta, or United, for example.

That being said, I think the thoughtful value proposition of this card more than makes up for it for Air Canada loyalists. If you like to redeem points for international premium cabin awards, it could be worth applying for this card. Similarly, the card can be worth it for the Pay Yourself Back feature, whereby you can redeem your Aeroplan points however you’d like toward a travel purchase.

Hopefully most people find value beyond just the bonus, given the excellent rewards structure.

Arguably the biggest challenge with the Aeroplan Credit Card is how easy Aeroplan points are to earn with other cards that provide more flexibility. Aeroplan is transfer partners with several bank currencies, including Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Chase Ultimate Rewards, and all those currencies can be converted at a 1:1 ratio.

That means the points are pretty easy to come by, and in many cases there are compelling value propositions on those cards as well.

If you’re under 5/24, consider these two cards from Chase:

If you’re over 5/24, these are some other top Aeroplan Card alternatives to consider:

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card is phenomenal, and easily the most innovative co-branded airline credit card we’ve seen. The card offers a nice welcome bonus, a lucrative rewards structure with a variety of incentives for spending, and comes with great perks, like elite status.

The Aeroplan program is rewarding in general, but if you don’t fly Air Canada or book award flights through Aeroplan more than once or twice a year, you might want to consider earning flexible points that transfer to this program instead.

Booked a discounted UA short-haul economy flight for my son and me, using miles from P2's (UA CC holder) UA account. Since she isn't on the same reservation and I have 25k status through the Aeroplan CC, I used my Aeroplan member number in the hope that we can get a free checked bag each.

#6114. How Many Lockheed C-5 Galaxies Are Left In 2026?

The Lockheed C-5M Super Galaxy is the largest military transport aircraft built for the United States Air Force and the third largest in the world (after the now-destroyed Antonov An-225 and the An-124). A total of 52 Super Galaxies remain active, with the rest in storage, scrapped, written off, or cannibalized for parts. Most flying C-5Ms are upgraded C-5Bs, although there are also some upgraded C-5As.

The US Air Force is the only C-5M operator, and it now plans to keep the type flying far longer than it once expected. Its Fiscal Year 2027 budget request moves the fleet's retirement to FY2050, five years later than the previous plan, even though only about 37% of the jets were mission capable in FY2025. Here is how many C-5s were built, what happened to them, and how many still exist.

The C-5 Galaxy traces its roots back to 1961, when the US Air Force started looking for a heavy jet-powered aircraft to replace its Douglas C-133 Cargomasters, while also complementing its Lockheed C-141 Starlifters. The US Army also wanted the Air Force to procure a strategic airlifter larger than the Starlifter, able to carry outsized loads. By 1964, the project had led to the 'Heavy Logistics System' program and received proposals from the US's then-existing airplane makers.

The companies in question were Boeing, Douglas, General Dynamics, Lockheed, and Martin Marietta, and their proposals came with engine options provided by General Electric, Curtiss-Wright, and Pratt & Whitney. The Air Force selected the Lockheed design with General Electric's TF39 engines (the first high-bypass turbofan to enter service). The USAF liked the Boeing design but rejected it, and Boeing took elements of it to develop the Boeing 747-100 with Pratt & Whitney engines.

A total of 131 Lockheed C-5 Galaxies were produced, of which 81 were C-5As. In the 1970s, these were found to have cracks in the wings, forcing the Air Force to drastically reduce allowed payloads until new strengthened wings were installed on 77 remaining C-5As between 1981 and 1987.

The Lockheed C-5 Galaxy has been a pivotal air mobility asset for the United States Air Force for decades. It is responsible for the rapid deployment of combat forces to any point in the world at short notice. First delivered in 1970, the Air Force explains that, "the C-5 has seen extensive use in every major global contingency since the Southeast Asia War."

The massive airlifter provides range and cargo capacity that greatly exceed the capabilities of the airlifters that came before it. Not only do these aircraft transport soldiers, smaller aircraft, helicopters (including three CH-47 Chinooks), armored vehicles, munitions, and supplies, but they can also accommodate two Minuteman Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles. A standard crew is seven: two pilots, two flight engineers, and three loadmasters (see how many crew members it takes to fly a C-5 Galaxy).

Lockheed C-5M Super Galaxy specifications (per the US Air Force)

4,800 nautical miles with 120,000 pounds of cargo (7,000 nautical miles with no cargo)

One notable operation for the Galaxies came on October 14, 1973. On that day, the C-5s flew the first Operation Nickel Grass mission to resupply Israeli forces during the Yom Kippur War. Operation Nickel Grass saw the United States supply Israel with 22,325 tons of supplies, including tanks, artillery, and ammunition, using C-141 Starlifters and C-5 Galaxies.

As stated, Lockheed delivered a total of 81 C-5A variant aircraft, as well as producing the improved C-5B variant. Two C-5As were upgraded to the C-5C standard to carry larger cargo, like satellites. Lockheed proposed the improved re-engined C-5D in the 1990s as an alternative to the McDonnell Douglas C-17 Globemaster III strategic airlifter, and, while this didn't happen, design elements of the C-5D were later used for the C-5M Super Galaxy program.

Lockheed planned to produce a civilian variant of the Galaxy, called the L-500. The company developed a design for both passenger and cargo versions of the aircraft, with the passenger aircraft being able to carry up to 1,000 passengers (far more than an Airbus A380). While the designs attracted some interest, in the end, no airlines purchased the aircraft, and it wasn't produced.

In the late 1990s, it was found that 80% of the Galaxy's airframe service life was still remaining, so the USAF embarked on upgrading 52 examples with GE CF6 (General Electric F138-GE-100) engines, the same family of engines that power the Boeing 767. These produced 22% more thrust, provided a 30% shorter takeoff roll, and other improvements. Other aspects, like avionics, were also upgraded. The Air Force received its first upgraded C-5M in 2008, with work concluding in 2018.

Of the 131 Galaxies produced, Planespotters.net lists six as having been written off. One (66-8303) was damaged beyond repair after a ground fire during maintenance in one of its 12 fuel cells, and another (67-0172) was destroyed by a fire that broke out in the cargo compartment while taxiing. 68-0218 crashed while attempting an emergency landing amid 'Operation Babylift,' where it would have taken Vietnamese orphans to the US as South Vietnam collapsed and the Fall of Saigon neared.

Planespotters.net lists 15 C-5s as scrapped, with another example listed as 'partially scrapped.' These are all older C-5A models built from 1969 to 1972. A further 37 are stored, mostly at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Arizona, while one is listed as 'preserved.' That airframe (69-0014) is on display at the Air Mobility Command Museum at Dover Air Force Base. 70-0451 was meant to be displayed at the Travis Air Force Base Heritage Center, but was scrapped after space couldn't be found.

Multiple sources confirm that a total of 52 C-5 Galaxies are listed as active. All of these have been upgraded to the C-5M Super Galaxy standard and are newer airframes, with most of them having been built between 1985 and 1989 and originally delivered as examples of the C-5B Galaxy model. The Air Force now plans to keep them in service until FY2050.

The Air Force's FY2027 budget request pushes the C-5M's retirement back to FY2050, The War Zone reported. Earlier plans had the fleet bowing out around 2045. The jets are also getting harder to keep serviceable: about 37% of the fleet was mission capable in FY2025, down from 49% the year before.

Their replacement is still more than a decade away. The Air Force expects the first aircraft from its Next-Generation Airlift (NGAL) program around 2038, according to Air & Space Forces Magazine, and each NGAL aircraft is set to replace one C-5M until the last Super Galaxy retires. The same program is expected to succeed the C-17 eventually, which is why the Air Force believes one aircraft can replace both.

According to AMARC Experience, the boneyard at Davis–Monthan Air Force Base has a total of 57 Lockheed C-5A Galaxies in storage, well above the 37 stored airframes Planespotters.net lists. While these airframes exist, it is unclear how many have been mothballed in a condition where they could feasibly be reactivated and returned to service, and how many are just being cannibalized for spare parts. The 309th Aerospace Maintenance and Regeneration Group has different 'Type' categories for its aircraft stored at the boneyard.

Type 1000 aircraft are placed in long-term storage and are maintained until recalled to active service. These are aircraft that have a high potential to return to flying status, and parts are not permitted to be removed from them. They are 're-preserved' every four years. Meanwhile, Type 1500 includes aircraft that were previously fully preserved, and Type 2000 includes aircraft whose parts are available for reclamation. These are cannibalized.

Type 3000 includes aircraft on 'flying hold,' where aircraft are kept in flyable condition in short-term, temporary storage as they are transferred elsewhere. Type 4000 aircraft are in excess of US military needs and may be broken down for scrap, recycled, or have their usable parts reclaimed. It is unclear how the Galaxies at the boneyard are classified, but it is possible that some are Type 2000 and others are Type 1000.

Production of the C-5 Galaxy ended in 1989, while production of the C-17 Globemaster III ended in 2015, and there is now no discussion of putting the C-5 back into production. However, there is chatter at Boeing (which absorbed McDonnell Douglas) to restart production of the comparatively diminutive C-17. The chances of the Globemaster going back into production are unlikely, but if it does, it would likely be for export orders.

Few strategic military transports remain in production today. None are in production in the United States, while the smaller Airbus A400M Atlas strategic/tactical airlifter is being produced in Europe, and Russia is producing the Ilyushin Il-76 airlifter in low numbers. The Il-76 is sized between the A400M and the Globemaster. China has also put its Xi'an Y-20 airlifter, which resembles the C-17, into production.

With no new C-5s coming, 52 remain in service. Add the stored airframes and the preserved example at Dover, and somewhere between 90 and 110 C-5s still exist, depending on whether you take Planespotters.net's storage count (37) or AMARC Experience's (57). The C-5M is still the Air Force's largest airlifter, although large aircraft are increasingly seen as vulnerable, and the Air Force is looking for more roles to be taken over by smaller S/VTOL aircraft where possible.

The cruise world welcomed another giant on Wednesday as MSC Cruises took delivery of one of its largest ships ever, the 216,638-ton MSC World Asia.

Built at the massive Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France, the 20-deck-high, Asia-themed vessel is the third in the line's new World Class series of ships — by far the biggest ships that MSC Cruises has ever built.

Perhaps more notably, it is the tenth largest cruise ship ever built by any line, smaller only than Royal Caribbean's three Icon Class ships and six Oasis Class ships.

"Our ambition is simple: To give every guest the best holiday ever," MSC Group executive chairman Pierfrancesco Vago said Wednesday during a dockside ceremony at the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard to mark the vessel's official handover to MSC Cruises.

MSC Group is the parent company of MSC Cruises and sister brand Explora Journeys, a luxury line.

"We invested in rethinking spaces, developing new concepts and reshaping the experience," Vago added during remarks from a stage set up just in front of the MSC World Asia's bow.

Vago noted that 60% of the spaces on MSC World Asia are either new or significantly redesigned as compared to the two World Class ships already sailing, MSC World Europa and MSC World America.

Like those two vessels, MSC World Asia has nearly 2,600 rooms and is capable of holding a whopping 6,758 passengers with every berth filled — more than almost any other passenger vessel afloat.

It also has similarly massive dimensions with a length of 1,093 feet — the equivalent of nearly four football fields stacked end-to-end — and a width of 154 feet.

But many of its interior and exterior venues, including a sprawling decktop water park with multiple waterslides and a record-setting dry slide that drops 11 decks, are different from what you'll find on the earlier World Class ships in ways big and small.

Related: The terrifying, record-breaking slide on MSC World Asia

Among the most significant changes is the addition of new dining and food concepts, including MSC Cruises' first pan-Asian restaurant and a Venchi chocolate and gelato venue.

Like the earlier World Class vessels, the ship also offers a sushi bar, teppanyaki restaurant, American-style steakhouse and a branch of the Italian chain Eataly (currently found only on MSC World America), among 20 dining options in all.

In addition to the water park and dry slide, MSC World Asia's top decks offer multiple pool areas; a suspended-over-the-ocean swing ride called The Cliffhangar; and a ropes course.

Notable interior features include a three-deck-high dining and entertainment zone called the World Galleria, which is covered by one of the largest LED-lit ceilings at sea. An outdoor extension of this area, called the World Promenade, features more dining and entertainment, plus a new suspended, illuminated Dragon sculpture — part of the ship's Asia theming.

Related: MSC Cruises cabins and suites guide

The arrival of MSC World Asia marks the latest milestone in MSC Cruises' rapid expansion.

With the addition of MSC World Asia, the brand now operates 24 ships, up from just 13 vessels as recently as 2017. It has nine more on order.

The ships on the way include five more World Class vessels scheduled for delivery by 2031. Also coming is a new class of four somewhat smaller, 180,000-ton vessels that will be known as the Frontier Class.

Wednesday's delivery ceremony included a ceremonial lowering of the Chantiers de l'Atlantique and French flags in front of attendees and the raising of the MSC Cruises flag as well as the flag of Malta, where the vessel is registered.

MSC Group chief financial officer Alexa Aponte Vago, who is married to MSC Group executive chairman Pierfrancesco Vago, served as the traditional "godmother" for the event, which included the smashing of a bottle of Champagne against the ship's hull.

Joining her husband on stage, Alexa Aponte Vago cut a ceremonial blue ribbon to release the bottle of Champagne against the side of the vessel right on the letter C in its name.

While it included a bottle smash, Wednesday's event was not the vessel's official naming. That will take place Saturday in Le Havre, France, at a much larger event.

MSC World Asia will then head to the Mediterranean, where it will begin its first cruises with paying passengers on Dec. 4 with a voyage out of Barcelona.

The ship initially will operate seven-night Mediterranean voyages that include stops in France, Italy, Malta and Spain.

In November 2027, it will reposition to the Southern Caribbean for seven- to 14-night sailings. The itineraries will include stops in Saint Lucia, Grenada, St. Maarten, Antigua and Barbuda, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.

Founded in 1861, the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in St. Nazaire is one of the world's most famous shipyards, known for building many of the world's largest cruise ships as well as naval vessels and wind-powered commercial ships. Notable vessels built at the shipyard include the SS Normandie, SS France, Cunard's Queen Mary 2 and several of Royal Caribbean's Oasis Class ships.

The shipyard has built 20 vessels for MSC Cruises over the past 25 years.

It is located at the mouth of the Loire River on the West coast of France.

#6112. KLM Offloaded A Passenger Rather Than Use The Blocked Seat We Offered

I recently flew KLM from Amsterdam to Barcelona, and a passenger was taken off our full flight even though my wife and I offered him the empty seat between us. The crew followed a rule exactly, and as far as I can tell, nobody got anything out of it.

Business class inside Europe is basically a regular economy seat with the middle seat blocked. On some planes the middle seat is physically blocked with a small table. On this flight it was just empty, blocked online so nobody could book it, but technically a regular seat anyone could sit in.

I was on KL1519 on 2 September, in row 2 with my wife, with that empty middle seat between us.

After the doors closed, it turned out that two passengers had boarding passes for the same seat. Whoever got there first sat down. The other one was a fairly young guy, and now he had nowhere to sit. The flight was completely full, there wasn’t a single free seat in economy.

I heard the crew apologizing to him and saying they would have to take him off the plane and put him on the next flight.

I knew this would take a while, because the doors were already closed and he had boarded. Getting him off meant opening the doors again, and maybe taking his bag off too. Once on another flight someone got off and everyone had to hold up their bags.

And I felt sorry for the guy. Maybe he was in a hurry to get somewhere, and none of this was his fault. The airline gave two people boarding passes for one seat, and he was already on board.

So I asked my wife if she minded giving up the empty seat between us. The flight is only about two hours. She was fine with it, so I went to the crew and offered it.

The crew was very grateful, but said seating someone there was against the rules and they couldn’t decide it themselves, they had to check with someone.

That took about 10 minutes. Then they came back, thanked me again, and said that unfortunately it wasn’t possible under the rules.

So they opened the doors and offloaded the guy, I hope they rebooked him on the next one. In the end we pushed back about 40 minutes late and landed in Barcelona about half an hour late. After landing I think even the captain came over, shook my hand and thanked me.

As I understand it, the middle seat is blocked to give the business class passengers more space. In this case that was us, and we were the ones offering to give that space up.

We didn’t need the space, and we’d have put up with one more person in the row for two hours.

On a completely full KLM flight, two passengers got boarding passes for the same seat. My wife and I offered the empty blocked seat between us in business, so he wouldn’t have to get off. The crew checked with someone, the answer was no, and he was offloaded anyway, and we left about 40 minutes late.

I get that the crew couldn’t make this call themselves. Still, we didn’t need that seat at all.

Is there a good reason for this rule that I’m missing?

#6111. Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

That bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an important part of it.”

“I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” said Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”

The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

“They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very company that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”

A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

“We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson said. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”

Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

She also said that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

“Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”

The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

#6110. Why Flight Attendants Sit Facing Backward During Takeoff & Landing

Have you ever noticed that flight attendants sit facing backward during take-off and landing? While most passenger seats are forward-facing, some business-class configurations have rearward-facing seats, which some passengers dislike; therefore, backward-facing seats are rarely used for passengers.

The jumpseat is a very important part of an aircraft's safety equipment and is designed to protect the crew members during taxiing, takeoff, and landing, which are critical phases of flight when accidents are more likely to occur. It is important that the crew are protected at these times so that they can evacuate the aircraft if necessary.

Flight attendants face backward in their jump seats during takeoff and landing primarily for safety. During a sudden stop or impact, a rear-facing seat backrest absorbs the force across the back, shoulders, and head instead of concentrating it on a strap across the chest, as in a car. The seatback supports the head, neck, and torso during sudden forward deceleration, reducing strain on the spine and neck and improving force distribution.

Rearward-facing seats are safer for the upper torso and reduce the impact on the body in landings or emergencies. Crew seats facing backward are designed to allow brace positions during normal or abnormal takeoff and landing and help protect against debris. That is why infants are encouraged to stay in backward-facing car seats for as long as possible. During sudden deceleration, your body naturally wants to keep moving forward.

The jumpseat protects the crew from severe injury and helps them stay conscious and mobile in an accident, so that they can direct an evacuation and assist passengers in an emergency. They are always positioned near the emergency exits so that they can respond quickly. In the event of an accident, cabin crew are better protected than passengers in forward-facing seats. The crew member needs to be conscious and uninjured in an emergency for a fast, efficient evacuation and to potentially save lives.

Cabin crew jumpseats are almost always facing rearwards. While most face backward toward the tail, some jumpseats face forward or sideways depending on the aircraft type, cabin layout, and door position. They can be single or double jumpseats. Double jumpseats are usually found in the aircraft galleys at the main doors, while single jumpseats are often next to emergency exits throughout the cabin. On private jets, jumpseats are commonly forward- or side-facing depending on type, although they differ from those on commercial jets and may have a different harness and no safety equipment underneath.

Forward- or sideways-facing seats still meet certification rules and use multipoint harnesses and brace positions to protect the crew. The seat base flips up when the crew member stands, so it doesn’t block the exit during an evacuation. The seats are heavily padded around the back and head area and are next to or inside the galley and adjacent to exit doors. A four-point safety harness secures the crew member firmly during take-off and landing. The lap belt must sit low and tight across the pelvis (not the stomach), with shoulder straps snug and free of twists. It has a single release point.

Below each standard crew jumpseat, there is a container that holds the life vest, a torch, and a manual release tool for the oxygen system. An interphone is attached to every seat or double seat for communication with the crew and flight deck. Around the seat and above the seat, there will be a smoke hood, fire gloves, and a fire extinguisher. During the emergency equipment check, crew must ensure the harness is fully functional and fitted correctly.

Experts have analyzed whether seats such as the exit row, the aisle, the middle, and the window have higher survivability rates.

Facing into the cabin allows crew members to observe the passengers and spot hazards during critical phases of flight. It also ensures passengers follow safety instructions and are seated when the seat belt sign is on. They can typically be used only by airline crew, depending on the airline's policy. There are more jumpseats than the minimum working crew onboard. There are also jumpseats in the flight deck, but there are very strict rules on who can use them.

These seats are strategically located so that the flight attendants have visibility over different areas of the cabin on take-off, landing and whilst taxiing. There is also the potential to spot unruly passengers or if someone is sick and needs help. They also need to prepare for the silent review in case of evacuation and observe outside conditions through the windows to prepare as needed.

However, in the rear or aft galley, this would not be the case as the passengers cannot be seen clearly if the cabin crew are in their harnesses. On some aircraft types, such as the Airbus A320, one cabin crew seat in the aft is stored flat but maneuvered to face forward, and an extra crew member can observe the rear cabin from there if carried.

While rear-facing seats offer strong impact protection, airlines generally keep passenger seats forward-facing due to passenger preference, motion sickness concerns, and structural or weight factors. Aircraft burn more fuel due to heavy rear-facing seats, making them less popular with airlines.

There is also some psychology behind them. Passengers don’t want someone facing opposite them as a rule, as it makes them feel uncomfortable. Some people don't like the sensation of flying backwards, and it could cause motion sickness in some people. It could also be an issue in an evacuation knowing which way to go, as passengers tend to head in the same direction as the door where they entered the aircraft.

Although backward-facing seats are more commonly found in military aircraft, some airlines offer seats that face backward. If you do want to try out a rear-facing airplane seat, opt for business class seats with airlines like American Airlines, United Airlines, Qatar Airways, and British Airways. The brace position for passengers in rearward-facing seats is different from that of the standard brace position.

Finding the best seat in the house can be tricky.

The cabin crew brace position is specifically designed to prevent the body flailing, protect limbs needed for opening emergency exits, and minimize head and neck injuries during an impact. When facing the back of the aircraft, impact forces push the body backward into the seat. The back and head should be firmly against the seatback and headrest to prevent whiplash. Knees are together, and feet are placed flat forward or back depending on the airline and whether facing forward or rearward.

Hands should be placed under the thighs with palms facing up or down, depending on airline procedures, or may be placed on the knees and elbows tucked in to avoid fractures. If facing forward, the chin should be placed down towards the chest and feet slightly forward. In an abnormal landing, the brace position is the same apart from placing hands one on top of the other behind the head with elbows brought together in front of the face and not covering ears, so commands can still be heard. This may differ at different airlines.

Where there is a side-facing jumpseat, feet should be flat on the floor, hands should be tucked under thighs or placed on the knees. However, extra support is needed, and the head and body should lean against the adjacent bulkhead or headrest on the side toward the direction of impact, securing the shoulder harness tightly.

Crew adopt a "semi-brace" or standard brace posture during every normal takeoff and landing. This is often paired with a "silent review" of emergency exit procedures, so they are protected against sudden runway excursions or aborted takeoffs and prepared for any incident or accident. They secure themselves in their jumpseats on the flight crew's command: "Cabin crew seats for take-off" or "Cabin crew seats for landing."

On most narrowbody aircraft, both the forward double jumpseat and rear double jumpseat face rearward, apart from the Airbus A320, which has another seat at the rear that faces forward into the cabin. On widebody aircraft, seats can be single at some exits, and the double seats in the rear galley may face forward depending on aircraft type.

In the United States, 14 CFR 25.785(h) says a flight attendant seat must be “near a required floor-level emergency exit”, that one must sit adjacent to each Type A or Type B exit, and that the rest must be “evenly distributed among the required floor-level emergency exits to the extent feasible”. The rule requires a flight attendant seat to be forward- or rearward-facing with an energy-absorbing rest supporting the arms, shoulders, head and spine, and to sit near a floor-level emergency exit. The brace position differs depending on which way the seat faces and the airline's safety procedures.

#6109. Malaysia Airlines Orders Up To 16 Boeing 787-10s, Deliveries Start 2032

Malaysia Airlines has just placed a new aircraft order, as the airline will be adding a new wide body aircraft type to its fleet. This seems logical enough, even if the carrier’s long haul fleet seems rather diversified at this point.

Malaysia Airlines has placed its first-ever Dreamliner order, as the airline will be taking delivery of up to 16 Boeing 787-10s. This includes a firm order for 10 jets, plus options for six more, with deliveries expected between 2032 and 2035.

For context, the 787-10 is the largest variant of the Dreamliner. While it has the least range of any 787 variant, the per-seat economics are great, given how it’s “stretched.” While some airlines have started to use the 787-10 for high capacity regional routes, Malaysia Airlines is taking a different approach.

The oneworld carrier intends to use these planes to support its long haul fleet modernization and international expansion, including routes to Europe, along with destinations throughout Asia-Pacific. The airline points out how long haul demand to and from Southeast Asia has increased by more than 50% over the past decade.

Here’s how Malaysia Airlines Group CEO Nasaruddin Bakar describes this:

“The acquisition of the 787 Dreamliner represents a strategic investment in the future of Malaysia Aviation Group. As we look ahead to the next phase of growth, these aircraft will strengthen our ability to serve key international markets with greater capacity, efficiency and flexibility, while delivering the elevated travel experience our customers expect. Beyond fleet renewal, this investment reinforces our commitment to maintaining a modern, competitive airline that supports Malaysia’s connectivity and global aspirations.”

For context, Malaysia Airlines currently has a fleet of just over 90 aircraft, with another 75 aircraft on firm order. As it stands, Malaysia Airlines has:

Now the airline has the following planes on firm order:

A few things stand out here. First of all, it’s cool to see Malaysia Airlines growing again, after a rather rough… what, nearly 15 years? At this point the airline has enough planes on order to both replace its previous generation fleet, and expand. I’d expect the 16 A330ceos will be retired at some point in the coming years, and more than replaced by the A330neos that remain on order. Furthermore, the 737-800s will all be replaced by the 737 MAXs.

The 787-10 is an incredible plane in terms of economics, especially as Boeing has been able to make incremental range improvements, turning it into a true long haul aircraft.

At the same time, I can’t help but feel like it’s unusual how the airline has just seven A350s, with no more on order, and is now switching to the 787 for fleet renewal. Admittedly the A350 was ordered back in the day under a completely different management team, which also at one point thought the A380 was a good fit for the airline.

So I am curious how the carrier’s fleet evolves. Will the seven A350s stick around, or will they eventually just be replaced by 787-10s? Even with airspace restrictions and headwinds, it seems like all of Malaysia Airlines’ routes should be within range for the 787-10, though admittedly London (LHR) might be on the cusp, depending on how airspace closures evolve, how dense of a configuration the airline selects, etc.

The big challenge with the airline industry is that it’s never static, and decisions aren’t made in a vacuum. One management team makes one decision, and then a management team later on can’t just undo what the other management team did, without it being costly. So I get that they’re doing what they can…

Malaysia Airlines is the newest customer for the Boeing 787, as the airline has ordered up to 16 787-10s, including 10 firm orders and six options. The airline plans to use this for a long haul expansion to Europe, as well as for flights in Asia-Pacific.

It’s cool to see Malaysia Airlines continuing to grow, as the carrier has quite the order book at this point. I am curious if the airline keeps around the seven A350s in the long run, or how the airline manages its three wide body aircraft types.

What do you make of Malaysia Airlines’ Boeing 787-10 order?

There's no doubt about it: The airport lounge wars are heating up with credit card issuers like American Express, Capital One and Chase launching new outposts at a blistering pace.

American Express maintains the largest footprint with its Global Lounge Collection, while Capital One has been expanding its map of Capital One airport lounges.

However, it's Chase in particular that has turned up the heat, expanding its U.S. lounge collection since 2023, with more on the way, including a location at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

Here’s everything you need to know about the family of Chase Sapphire Lounges by The Club, their amenities and how to access them.

Apply for the : Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening (see ).

Chase’s lounge collection includes nine Sapphire Lounge locations. The JFK location is temporarily closed.

Additional lounges are planned at the following airports:

Chase has partnered with Airport Dimensions to build out its lounges. Airport Dimensions currently operates dozens of lounges worldwide, most of which are branded as “The Club” or “Club Aspire” and are largely accessible via Priority Pass membership.

Related: Is a Priority Pass lounge membership actually worth it?

This location was the first branded Chase lounge to open in the U.S.

It's located in the Terminal B-to-C connector near gates B39 and B40 and is accessible post-security from Terminals B, C and E. Passengers departing from Terminal A will need to clear security again when returning to their departure terminal.

The lounge has an expansive footprint, at over 11,000 square feet with seating for over 200 guests, though lines to get in can certainly form at busy times, with waits topping an hour. It is open from 5 a.m. until 11 p.m. daily.

In addition to a variety of restaurant- and living room-style seating areas, there is a self-serve buffet at one end. Guests can also order a la carte dishes created by Boston-area chef Douglass Williams as well as specialty cocktails and Massachusetts-brewed beers from table-mounted QR codes.

The lounge also has wellness rooms with massage chairs and comfortable loungers for relaxation and products from Brooklyn-based fragrance brand Apotheke.

The newest Chase Sapphire Lounge opened at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in July 2026. Located post-security near gate D25 in Terminal D, the 18,000-square-foot lounge is one of the largest in the Sapphire network. It is open from 5 a.m. until 10 p.m. daily.

In addition to Chase's signature made-to-order dining (with dishes like blue corn butterscotch pancakes from favorite local restaurant Encina), an all-day buffet and full-service bar, the DFW location introduces several features unique to the network. Travelers can visit the first dedicated Sapphire whiskey lounge featuring guided tastings of Texas whiskeys (and a specialty honey pecan Old Fashioned cocktail), book a complimentary 30-minute Face Haus treatment, freshen up in a shower suite or relax in dedicated rest areas.

Families will also appreciate the children's play area and private nursing room, while travelers in a hurry can take advantage of a grab-and-go food station — a feature Chase is currently testing at this location.

Chase and Airport Dimensions revamped The Etihad Lounge at Dulles, located in Concourse A near gate A14.

The space is small, at just over 5,000 square feet, but features two levels with various seating areas, including a library-themed space, gender-neutral restrooms, shower suites, a reflection room for quiet meditation and a family room.

As with the other lounge locations, this one features locally-inspired food and cocktails plus locally-brewed java from Commonwealth Joe Coffee Roasters.

The lounge is currently open from 6 a.m. until 10 p.m. daily.

Chase's lounge at LAS is located past security in Terminal 1, Concourse C, between gates 23 and 24. It opened in December 2025, spans two stories, covers 4,590 square feet and has seating for up to 87 people. It is open from 4:30 a.m. until 11 p.m. daily.

Though compact compared to the other Chase Sapphire lounges, this one packs a punch in terms of ambience. The space features colorful artwork and a lively atmosphere, not to mention a rather glamorous "Champagne parlor" plus a menu of cocktails inspired by Sin City and a wine list curated by New York retailer Parcelle.

Food options include bites like pork buns and a spicy cucumber salad from Momofuku.

There are no showers, spa services or meditation rooms here, though.

The issuer is bringing a lounge to LAX on an unconfirmed date. It will be adjacent to gate 148 near the connector to the west gates at Tom Bradley International Terminal.

Now that all terminals at LAX are connected airside (post-security), any traveler with access could theoretically visit this lounge, although it is a bit of a hike from other terminals.

The new lounge will measure around 9,000 square feet, which is on the smaller side — especially for an airport the size of LAX — so expect some long wait times once it opens, much as you'll find at the nearby Centurion Lounge.

The Chase Sapphire Lounge by The Club at JFK is located in Terminal 4 near gate A2, not far from the security checkpoint and up one level.

Like the location at IAD, this space is a redesigned Etihad Lounge rather than one Chase created from scratch, and it's rather limited in size at just 7,600 square feet.

It is usually open from 4:30 a.m. until 9 p.m. daily, but at the time of publication, it is temporarily closed due to plumbing issues. There are grab-and-go food options, though.

Typically, you can find a buffet of small plates, plus seasonal items (but always the famous burger) available for order via QR code. This lounge also has three shower suites.

The LaGuardia Sapphire Lounge is the largest of the collection, at 21,000 square feet spanning two floors. It is located in Terminal B and is open from 4:30 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. daily.

The lounge houses plenty of spacious seating areas, including a restaurant-style section and more casual vignettes. There are also family-oriented areas, including a children's playroom and arcade.

The lounge offers a buffet and a seasonal menu featuring select dishes from Sailor, a restaurant in Fort Greene, Brooklyn, plus locally inspired cocktails by Apotheke and wines chosen by Parcelle.

There's also a wellness area where guests can enjoy Face Haus facial treatments, guided meditations from podcaster Devi Brown and private rest pods.

Uniquely, the lounge features Reserve Suites, Chase’s lounge-within-a-lounge concept, which you can reserve for $2,200-$3,000 for a three-hour private retreat.

This 20,000-square-foot Chase lounge opened in February 2025 in the connector between Terminal D (home of Air Canada, Delta Air Lines, Spirit Airlines, Alaska Airlines and United Airlines) and Terminal E (where gates for Frontier Airlines, JetBlue, Alaska Airlines, Southwest Airlines and Spirit Airlines can be found).

If you go through the Terminal D Transportation Security Administration checkpoint, it is upstairs and is open from 5 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily.

It offers a similar layout to other Chase lounges, but with some unique features including a wellness center with two treatment rooms for facials, two shower suites, a game room, Elixr Coffee drinks and a bar with Philadelphia Eagles-themed cocktails, plus a beer garden and local dishes courtesy of Fishtown eatery Middle Child Clubhouse.

The Sapphire Lounge at PHX opened in November 2024 and is located at the new eight-gate facility in Terminal 4 near gate D11.

This lounge began accepting reservations in June 2025. Sapphire Reserve cardmembers departing from Phoenix can reserve their visit from 14 days up to 24 hours before arriving at the lounge, so you don't have to be physically present to make your reservation. That's because this is the smallest lounge, at just 3,500 square feet.

The lounge is open from 4:30 a.m. to 10:30 p.m. daily, though its site notes that hours may vary.

There are a few different seating areas, with the tables around the central cocktail bar being in high demand. There's also an indoor terrace separated from the terminal, where a retrofitted Airstream food truck serves specialties from Gallo Blanco. Guests will also find Arizona-based Press Coffee drinks on hand, craft cocktails and a Parcelle-selected list of wines.

Located in San Diego's Terminal 2, this 11,000-square-foot Chase lounge opened in December 2024 with plenty of surfer-themed art and floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the tarmac.

The lounge is open from 5 a.m. until 10 p.m. daily and has a swanky wraparound cocktail bar, a small buffet area (plus à la carte dishes by Oscars Mexican Seafood on offer via QR code) and plenty of distinct seating areas.

There's also a wellness area with four relaxation pods and Face Haus treatments, a family room, showers and a nursing room.

Chase is planning a new 16,000-square-foot Sapphire Lounge in Concourse A at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. The Port of Seattle approved the project in October 2026, with a planned $70 million investment covering the initial build-out and a future refurbishment. An opening date has not yet been announced.

Cardholders can access the lounges up to three hours before departure (or up to five hours before a connecting flight) and can also bring up to two guests per visit for free. If you're a cardholder and wish to bring more than two guests, you'll be charged a fee. Children under 2 can enter for free.

While Priority Pass members previously got to access a Chase Lounge once per calendar year, this benefit has been discontinued.

Select Etihad travelers (the airline’s Gold and Platinum elite members and those flying in business or first class on Etihad-operated flights) can visit the IAD and JFK locations before their flights.

For years, Amex's network of Centurion Lounges was the major player in the card-run lounge space, but in recent years, Chase has quickly caught up, opening a series of lounges around the country in record time, with more on the way. With the airport lounge competition intensifying among major credit card issuers, the real winners are cardholders, though.

That said, these lounges feel like they're getting more crowded by the day, so when you get to an airport with one, make a beeline to the entrance and put your name on the list for access just in case there's a wait. After all, you wouldn't want to miss out on their many amenities.

#6107. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”

Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

For his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

“I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”

Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

“This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”

He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

“I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”

Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”

The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

Bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6106. Why 97% Of Boeing 777 Pilots Continue An Unstable Approach Instead Of Going Around

Boeing 777 pilots, like their counterparts on the vast majority of aircraft at most airlines, have set-in-stone parameters they should work within prior to carrying out landings. These ensure what is known as a stable approach and give pilots a clear set of rules to stick to when committing to a landing. If they are not met, the decision should be easy: go around and try again.

But most of the time, flight crews push on with a landing even if the criteria for a stable approach are not met. Thankfully, this does not mean the majority of landings are made in such conditions. However, it leaves a huge disparity between what should be done and what is actually done when it comes to almost all unstable approaches. Why? Well, psychology and the human factor play a huge part in what is really a very short space of time relative to an overall flight.

Whether an approach is stable or not is essentially based on the carriers’ own standard operating procedures (SOPs) being met before a minimum height is reached during descent. That is according to the Flight Safety Foundation (FSF), which coined the term “stabilized approach” in its Approach and Landing Accident Reduction (ALAR) toolkit back in 1998. In this, the organization recommended a minimum height of either 1,000 feet (305 meters) or 500 feet (152 meters) above airport elevation in instrument or visual meteorological conditions (IMC or VMC), respectively.

The FSF’s recommendations stretched to specific criteria behind a stable approach. Simply put, these suggested the correct flight path, speed, landing configuration, and rate of descent by 500 feet (152 meters) in good weather, leaving only small control tweaks needed. Some leeway was granted, namely around speed and sink rate. Overall, though, there was a clear-as-day checklist there for airlines and flight crew alike.

FSF stabilized approach criteria in VMC, from Sky Library

The aircraft is on the correct flight path

The airspeed is not more than the reference landing speed (VREF) plus 20 knots (23 mph / 37 kmh) indicated speed, and not less than VREF

The aircraft is in the correct landing configuration

Sink rate is no greater than 1,000 feet (305 meters) per minute

Power setting is appropriate for the aircraft configuration and is not below the minimum power for the approach as defined by the operating manual

All briefings and checklists have been conducted

All of this aimed to further ensure safety at what is realistically the most dangerous part of a flight. Indeed, the FSF’s toolkit came after its own research found that unstabilized approaches were a causal factor in 66% of 76 accidents and serious incidents during the final stages of those flights between 1984 and 1997. Through the guidance, the organization sought to aid airlines and pilots in preventing aircraft from arriving at runway thresholds too high, too fast, out of alignment, incorrectly configured, or otherwise unprepared for landing.

The issue is that the recommendations appeared not to give the industry the overwhelming push the FSF would have desired. Almost two decades after the organization published the toolkit, it cited evidence that showed almost all unstable approaches were still resulting in aircraft touching down in another report.

Some 95% to 97% of flight crews whose aircraft were in an unstable state continued to touch down, its 2017 report into go-around decision-making stated. This problem of go-around policy non-compliance, the FSF went on to conclude, was “real” and “arguably the largest threat to flight safety” currently. Improving compliance would be “significant,” it added.

Among a string of findings that the report laid out, it noted the industry had “predominantly” turned to reducing unstable approaches, rather than incorporating go-arounds as standard practice, to avoid accidents in the final stages of flights. But clearly, entirely eradicating unstable approaches was always going to be impossible. When it came to why pilots still pressed on despite finding themselves in such situations, the reasons were plentiful.

Excellent Boeing engineering, good engines, and sustained investment all played a key role.

It is easy to pass judgment from the outside. Pilots are tasked with safely delivering passengers, and so what seems an overwhelming disregard of parameters put in place to minimize the risk of incidents raises some pretty serious questions. It is important to consider the realities in cockpits, though, in order to paint a picture of why unstable approaches may be ignored. Among the most blatant factors is timing.

Take the 777 from Boeing, which is among the bestselling widebody series ever produced. If traveling long-haul frequently, there is a good chance you will have stepped foot aboard a 777 variant at some point. Pilots behind the controls of a 777 have well under a minute of decision-making time after reaching the vital 500 feet (305 meter) threshold at which an approach should be stable. At an appropriate landing speed of 132 knots (152 mph or 244 km/h), a typical 777 will touch down 35 to 42 seconds after hitting this point.

Boeing itself recommends approach speeds for different 777 variants of between 139 knots (160 mph or 257 km/h) and 150 knots (172 mph or 278 km/h), so this could vary. Either way, the point stands: A pilot might have little over half a minute, while in the thick of bringing an aircraft down safely, to process whether a go-around is required, make that call, and then carry it out. That is not to try and justify landings made following unstable approaches, but the timing factor does offer some useful context.

It is really in the context of timing that the human factors behind landings made after unstable approaches start to make sense. The FSF said in 2017: non-compliance with go-around policies was the “industry norm”; awareness of risks among pilots and management was “low”; policy itself was viewed as “unrealistic”; and the practice of going around came with its own complexities and caveats. All of this meant pilots could well have had such thoughts racing through their minds when deciding what to do with an unstable approach.

Pilot James Albright provided an insight into the decision-making process in such circumstances previously. “If 95% to 97% of flight crews are failing to go around when their SOPs tell them to, we have a problem with the crews, the SOPs, or both,” he wrote. “Too many of us find ourselves in unstable approaches and believe, ‘I can save this.’ The fact that we almost always do reinforces our decision to deviate from our stable approach rules.”

But there could be other factors at play, Albright noted in the particular account of a landing made despite questions surrounding the stability of the approach. Among them was the fear that other crew members may not be supportive of a decision to go around, passengers might complain, or questions might be asked by employers. Naturally, that lingering thought of what a delay might entail is worth bearing in mind.

Modern airliners are incredibly automated, but pilots remain fully responsible for every decision during a flight. What do they actually do?

Arguably, the key reason most unstable approaches result in landings is down to how go-arounds are viewed. Whether it be fears that the maneuver is riskier than a landing, lack of training, or the belief that go-arounds are only for exceptional cases, potential misconceptions frequently pop up as reasons why they might be avoided.

Guidance from the International Air Transport Association (IATA) stated in 2026: “It is the responsibility of operators to develop and promulgate a clear policy on go-arounds.” Such policy, the trade body said, should state that a go-around was “a normal flight maneuver” and something “to be initiated whenever a continued approach would not be safe” or, notably, “when the approach does not meet the stabilized approach criteria”.

But the body went a step further, noting operators should clarify that there would be “no punitive response from management to a go-around” and any failure to do so “when appropriate” would be followed up. All of that goes to say, questions looked to still be there among pilots over when to go around, and how that decision may be received.

While perhaps somewhat alarming to those unfamiliar with being behind the controls of an aircraft, the important thing to remember is that most landings do indeed follow stable approaches. As the Flight Safety Foundation reported previously, 95% to 97% of all unstable approaches were continued to landing. However, just 3.5% to 4% of all approaches were unstable. So, before vowing never to set foot on a plane again, rest assured that the majority of landings are carried out following approaches that meet SOPs.

What these figures do mean is that there is room for improvement across the industry. Whatever the psychological factors preventing pilots from going around in most cases, the practice is yet to be normalized. With that, fears around the likes of causing delays, judgment from colleagues, or carrying out a go-around need to be addressed. As the FSF wrote in 2017: “No other single decision can have such an impact in the reduction of aviation accidents as the decision to go around.”

#6105. SkyWest Pilots Do The Right Thing At SFO, Then Get Snapped At By ATC

With the number of close calls we see at airports nowadays, it’s great to see when pilots or air traffic controllers go above and beyond to be observant, and exhibit good situational awareness. So along those lines, here’s a case of a pilot paying close attention to ensure everyone’s safety, and then an air traffic controller being frustrated by that…

YouTube channel You can see ATC has the air traffic control audio and a visualization of an interaction that happened shortly before noon on November 21, 2026, at San Francisco International Airport (SFO).

In this interaction, a SkyWest Embraer E175 operating on behalf of American Eagle had just landed on runway 28L, after flying from Los Angeles (LAX). The pilots were switched to the ground frequency, and that’s when things quickly went downhill:

The SkyWest pilots then continued their taxi, and when they got to the gate, the conversation continued:

When you screw up, I suppose it’s human nature to get a bit defensive, and I think that’s exactly what happened here.

Credit to the SkyWest pilots for their situational awareness here. They were instructed to taxi in front of another plane, and another plane was instructed to give way to them, but never read back those instructions. The air traffic controller absolutely should have caught that, and as a pilot, they 100% did the correct thing by noticing the lack of a read back, and erring on the side of caution.

This isn’t just some theoretical risk, but ground collisions are the most common kinds of accidents involving commercial aircraft. Could the SkyWest pilots have said “we’re holding short because the other plane didn’t read back instructions?” Sure, but it seems like the time gap here was a matter of seconds, and they didn’t want to step on the radio calls of another pilot, in case they were going to read back.

What I think is really unprofessional is how the air traffic controller then responded to this:

The pilots of a SkyWest flight decided to hold short of a taxiway after they observed the plane that was supposed to give way to them not reading back the correct instructions. That was absolutely the right move, and the air traffic controller should’ve caught that.

When the pilots explained why they held short, the air traffic controller didn’t respond particularly well. Then when they asked for a phone number, she said the pilots would be talking to someone else, and she clearly wasn’t having it. But then she was also mad when the pilot explained very briefly what was going on, saying the conversation should happen off frequency… a conversation she wasn’t willing to have!

This is a clear situation where you have two very professional pilots, and one very unprofessional air traffic controller.

What do you make of this SFO ATC interaction?
