#6103. Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”

“And fortunately, I think that will fail.”

Several senators leaving the meeting said the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

“No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”

“Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”

Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

“They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday said at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”

“We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

“I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”

Several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

That included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”

Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

“Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”

“The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

“I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

“They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

“We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”

“That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”

Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”

Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

#6102. Why JetBlue Is My Favorite Way To Fly Economy Across The Atlantic

I’ve flown back and forth across the Atlantic dozens of times in all cabins, including many times in economy. JetBlue definitely stands out as being my favorite, and dare I say it, the most premium of all the transatlantic economy flights I’ve experienced.

My most recent trip was from Europe to Boston (BOS) for the opening of JetBlue’s newest BlueHouse location. The airline covered my flights for the event, but had no input in this article. I’d like to share some of the reasons that JetBlue’s transatlantic experience impressed me so much.

Economy class meals can seem like quite the downgrade should one be accustomed to the elevated fare at the pointy end of the plane.

JetBlue currently partners with NYC-based Dig Inn for its transatlantic economy-class meals, and they’re far better than average. They also offer products from a range of interesting brands, rather than just your classic soda labels.

Here’s an example of the drinks menu on my flight from Amsterdam to Boston.

Meals are served in these stylish, reusable, matte-black sealed containers. I’d love to see more airlines do more to reduce their waste like this.

I was very happy with my choice of chicken pesto pasta salad as the main course, accompanied by sides of beet and carrot slaw and snap peas with feta. The fresh, flavorful, yet cold dishes were far better than many of the reheated slop I’ve been served in economy before.

I was equally impressed by the breakfast I had on the morning departure back from Boston to London Heathrow (LHR). I went for the Bubly sparkling water again, as I avoid coffee on a plane unless it’s served as espresso. The stuff they pour out of those vats is pretty much just glorified dirty water.

As far as pre-landing light meals go, this pizza thing was pretty good, too.

In addition to the main meal and pre-landing light bite, JetBlue keeps a well-stocked pantry at the back of the Airbus A321LR.

JetBlue has been offering fast, free, in-flight Wi-Fi for as long as I can remember. The same cannot be said for some full-service carriers, which still can’t guarantee a reliable, fast, and free connection on their transatlantic flights.

They’ve also added some fun tech features, like the ability to choose the elements for the main meal service via the IFE screen, even in economy. I think it has a more premium feel than being asked “chicken or beef?”

I’m not a frequent JetBlue flyer, so I couldn’t really make the most of the fun personalization features, such as the option to continue watching the movie where you left off on your last flight.

Being given anything more than the standard pillow and blanket in economy is a rare bonus. It had been so long since my last JetBlue flight in economy that I’d forgotten about the complimentary Snooze Kit.

I prefer to use my AirPods to earplugs, but I did make good use of the eye mask for a mid-flight nap.

I’ve flown over my fair share of narrow bodies on long-haul flights, and I genuinely don’t know why such a fuss is made about them being terrible.

JetBlue’s version of the aircraft has comfy seats, with standard Core (economy) seats having 32 inches of pitch. Another common complaint I hear is that there are fewer toilets. For a plane with far fewer passengers (only 114 in economy), fewer toilets kind of makes sense. I didn’t once find myself waiting in line to use the bathroom on either flight.

For what it’s worth, there are two lavatories for 114 economy passengers, so that’s one lavatory per 57 passengers. That’s a little lower than the industry standard, but not by much. For example, American’s standard 787-9s have five lavatories for 255 economy seats, so that’s a ratio of one lavatory per 51 passengers.

If you’ve only got the budget or the points for economy for your next trip to Europe, I couldn’t recommend JetBlue more. They now fly to eight cities in Europe, the planes are comfortable and modern, and the in-flight food and beverage is top of the game for economy.

What do you make of JetBlue’s transatlantic economy offering?

#6101. Why Airline Joint Ventures Are Accused Of Keeping Transatlantic Fares High

Three antitrust-immunized joint ventures now dominate transatlantic aviation: United Airlines with Lufthansa and its Star Alliance partners, Delta Air Lines with Air France-KLM and Virgin Atlantic, and American Airlines with British Airways and Iberia. A Wendover Productions video, as summarized by Pulse, says they control roughly 75% of New York to Europe flights and labels them cartels, a framing that belongs to the video rather than to regulators.

The underlying accusation is more precise: partners who share revenue and set fares together stop competing on the nonstop routes where their networks overlap. Defenders say the same coordination lowers prices for most travelers who connect. Both claims have empirical support, and evidence from the Department of Justice and a study commissioned by the Department of Transportation shows where each holds, where it weakens, and why the argument has persisted for years.

An alliance alone does not permit pricing coordination, since carriers in an arm’s-length codeshare each set their own prices, with the operating airline keeping the revenue and the marketing partner collecting a booking fee. Antitrust immunity changes that arrangement by allowing partners to decide fares, schedules, and other competitively sensitive matters jointly across the routes included in their agreement.

The joint ventures go further by pooling revenue, as partners in a metal-neutral structure share ticket revenue on covered routes under a capacity-based formula, leaving them indifferent about which airline flies a given passenger. A study for the Department of Transportation described the result as carriers behaving like a single airline on the routes in question. American, British Airways, and Iberia argued in 2009 that this removes the incentive to keep a partner’s nonstop flight out of the other carrier’s reach, because a customer choosing it would otherwise transfer revenue away from the selling carrier.

Joint ventures exist partly because ownership rules in the United States and European Union preclude cross-border mergers, making revenue-sharing agreements the closest available substitute for a single airline. DOT approves them under a public interest standard that can weigh foreign policy goals. The video adds that the pooled partners publish matching prices on overlapping flights, citing United and Brussels Airlines selling the same 6:00 PM Brussels departure at the same fare, which it presents as evidence of price fixing.

In a 2011 discussion paper, Antitrust Division economists William Gillespie and Oliver Richard analyzed fares from 2005 to 2010 on 115 routes linking the 20 largest cities in the United States and the European Union. They counted immunized partners serving the same route as a single competitor and found that average one-way fares were $31 higher on routes with one independent nonstop competitor than on routes with two, $62 higher than with three, and $88 higher than with four.

Those gaps equal roughly 7% of the average fare for each competitor lost, and each was statistically significant at the 99% confidence level. The authors read the result as consistent with the ordinary antitrust presumption that reducing competition raises prices, and they observed that nonstop fares averaged 8.3% above connecting fares, yet most economy passengers on the sampled routes still chose nonstop service.

The paper also documents how concentrated the market has become, since three immunized groups, one in each alliance, carried more than 82% of US-EU passenger traffic in the year ending June 2009, and by late 2010 more than half of the sampled routes had a single independent nonstop competitor. Because foreign-carrier fares for itineraries without a US carrier are not public, the economists treated US-carrier fares as representative, a limitation that qualifies any reading of the data. The authors stressed that the paper reflects their own views rather than an official Justice Department position.

Which US airline should you choose when flying across the Atlantic?

Defenders of the structure rely on double marginalization, the idea that when two unaffiliated carriers price their own legs of a connecting trip, each ignores how its markup reduces demand for the other, so the combined fare ends up too high. Partners that share revenue internalize that effect, which should lower fares for itineraries that require both carriers.

A study by economists Jan Brueckner and Ethan Singer, performed under contract to the Department of Transportation and released in 2019, tested the idea on fares from 1997 to 2016. It found that joint venture itineraries were priced about 7.2% below interline tickets, and that their fares were statistically indistinguishable from those of single-carrier trips. On transatlantic routes, the joint venture discount reached roughly 9% across cabins.

The Justice Department paper offered a rebuttal rather than a denial, since its economists agreed that alliances reduce connecting fares relative to interline tickets yet found that within SkyTeam and Star Alliance, immunized itineraries were no cheaper than non-immunized alliance itineraries, implying the pricing benefit does not require immunity. In the 2019 study, alliance partners without immunity priced just 0.7% below interline tickets, compared with 6.4% for immunized partners, which supports the claim that immunity matters. The two bodies of work therefore agree that connecting fares fall under alliances and disagree mainly on whether immunity is what makes them fall. The Justice Department economists added that 68% of US-EU passengers connected in 2009 across all itineraries, which is why the efficiency claim matters even though nonstop routes carry the higher fares.

The same Transportation Department study also found evidence that critics cite, reporting that in the later years of its 1997-2016 sample, granting immunity or joint venture status to two previously unaligned carriers on an overlapping route was equivalent to removing a competitor, with fares rising accordingly. The effect appeared in economy class, where an additional immunized or joint venture pair raised fares by about four to 13% depending on the specification, while business class fares showed no such overlap effect. That finding is notable because most earlier studies had found no nonstop effect, a point the authors flag as unusual.

The authors nonetheless concluded that alliances are beneficial on balance, based on a simulation of removing two joint ventures. On one route, nonstop passengers would save about $2.1 million a quarter while connecting passengers would pay about $3.1 million more; on another route, nonstop passengers would save roughly $469,000, while connecting travelers would pay about $10.8 million more. Brueckner and Singer also noted that the exercise ignores convenience gains such as single check-in and shorter layovers, which would further favor alliances.

Several cautions apply: the simulation covers two unnamed routes, the study pools regions, and the authors call removing a single joint venture unrealistic because it would affect other routes. Studies using structural models, which the authors cite, found no evidence of collusion on nonstop fares, so the literature remains divided on whether partners truly price together.

Could we see the airline finally launch flights to Indianapolis, or will another US city be next on its route map?

Critics argue that the harm persists because new competitors struggle to enter the overlapping routes. Slot scarcity at hubs such as Heathrow, where the video says slots sell for tens of millions, makes an incumbent partnership’s capacity hard to challenge. DOT has sometimes required remedies, including the divestiture of four Heathrow slots by the oneworld applicants, before granting immunity in 2010. The Justice Department economists also noted that applicants offered few specifics on new service, observing that American launched Dallas/Fort Worth to Madrid more than a year before receiving immunity.

Carve-outs, which bar partners from coordinating fares on specific overlapping routes, have a weaker record. DOT excluded routes such as Frankfurt to Chicago from United and Lufthansa’s 1996 grant, yet the exclusions apply only to tickets sold at US points of sale, and the Brueckner and Singer analysis found carve-outs typically had no measurable fare effect. DOT has also said that carve-outs can inhibit the efficiencies of a metal-neutral venture, and it has not required them when partners proposed one.

Immunity can also reshape who competes at all, as a study cited by Brueckner and Singer found that nonaligned carriers’ traffic between alliance hubs and other cities fell as alliances formed, which its authors read as foreclosure, and another found that immunity lowers partners’ costs, making them more formidable and potentially discouraging entry. The video counters that non-immunized partnerships, such as codeshares with Qatar Airways, Emirates, and Riyadh Air, deliver network integration without antitrust waivers.

A federal appeals court recently signaled how much analysis a regulator must show before curtailing an immunized venture. On August 20, 2026, the Eleventh Circuit vacated DOT’s order ending the Delta and Aeromexico joint venture because the agency relied on conditions at a single airport instead of conducting the comprehensive country-pair and city-pair analysis it had always used before. Any future challenge to a transatlantic venture would therefore need route-level fare evidence of the kind the Justice Department economists assembled, and that evidence now looks dated, since the Justice Department paper uses data through 2010 and the Transportation Department study stops at 2016.

The next test is already forming, since on November 4, Lufthansa asked DOT to complete its review of a request to add ITA Airways to the United, Lufthansa, and Air Canada venture. A decision will show whether regulators weigh nonstop harm against connecting benefits when partners expand a venture rather than when they first form one.

The research points toward a narrower remedy than the all-or-nothing debate suggests, because harm concentrates in economy-class nonstop overlaps, business fares show little overlap effect, and connecting passengers gain from integration. Conditions that tie immunity to measurable capacity or slot commitments on specific overlapping routes, with published fare data to verify results, would test the claim that partners deliver benefits unaided competition would not. Until such data exist, both the cartel label and the efficiency defense will remain easier to assert than to prove.

#6100. British Airways Visa Card Review: Is It Worth The $95 Annual Fee?

The British Airways Visa Signature® Card is one of Chase’s co-branded airline credit cards, and British Airways Club is certainly a popular frequent flyer program, given the overall value of the Avios ecosystem, plus the number of destinations in the United States that British Airways serves.

Who should be applying for the British Airways Visa, and under what circumstances is it worth spending money on it? Let’s take a look at what you need to know about this card, and what the best alternatives are.

Link: Learn more about the British Airways Visa Signature® Card

Before jumping into a closer look at every aspect of the British Airways Visa Card, here’s a high-level view of the card’s key features, perks, and fees:

Here are my thoughts on the biggest British Airways Visa Card pros and cons:

If you’re considering the British Airways Visa Signature Card, its welcome bonus, application rules, and annual fee are all probably top of mind. So let’s start by taking a look at these important details.

The British Airways Visa currently offers the following welcome bonus: Earn 75,000 Avios after you spend $5,000 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

Based on my current points and miles valuations, which put Avios at 1.2 cents apiece, this current bonus is worth about $900. That’s a pretty solid welcome bonus, especially for a card with a moderate annual fee.

The British Airways Visa has a $95 annual fee. This is not waived for the first year, and there’s no additional fee to add authorized users.

British Airways’ credit card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s potentially a great card to use for purchases abroad.

The welcome bonus on the British Airways Visa isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have received a new cardmember bonus on the card in the past 24 months. You are eligible for this card if you’ve had the Iberia Visa Signature® Card and/or Aer Lingus Visa Signature® Card, despite the similarities between the cards.

Chase’s other general policies on card approvals apply as well, including the 5/24, whereby you generally won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more credit cards in the last 24 months.

The British Airways Visa Card has no foreign transaction fees, but does the rewards structure warrant putting spending on the card? It might, but only thanks to additional bonuses offered by the card, which incentivize spending.

The British Airways Visa doesn’t have terribly exciting bonus categories. You earn:

There are lots of great credit cards for airfare purchases and hotel purchases. This isn’t a card I would be putting much spending on unless you’re trying to earn a Travel Together Ticket, in which case it could definitely be worth it. More on that below.

British Airways Club is a transfer partner of Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Chase Ultimate Rewards, so it could make sense to put spending on a card earning one of those currencies if you want to earn Avios at an accelerated rate.

There are lots of great uses of British Airways Avios. British Airways Club has roughly distance based award pricing, and the program offers value in situations where other programs might not. Generally speaking, here’s where I see value with Avios:

British Airways is known for adding large taxes and surcharges to some of its own award flights, so this is worth keeping in mind.

Personally I find Avios to be one of the most useful frequent flyer programs for redeeming points, thanks to the number of redemptions this opens up.

Often one of the big challenges people have with points is figuring out how to pool them since you typically need enough points in a single account for a redemption. A cool feature of the British Airways Club program is that you can form household accounts. This allows you to pool the Avios you earn with up to six other people registered at the same address as you.

This is especially awesome in the context of a credit card welcome bonus, since you can pool a ton of Avios in a single account if you have two people get the card in a household, etc.

There are some benefits to the British Airways Visa Card that could alone justify having this card. For some people, it will be worth spending money on the card to unlock some perks, while for others just having the card and not spending money on it offers sufficient benefits. Let’s look at what those benefits are, and how they work.

One of the best benefits of the British Airways Signature Visa is that it offers a 10% discount on British Airways flights starting in the United States. To take advantage of this, just book through ba.com/chase10, and use your card to pay while using promotion code BACHASE10.

If you fly British Airways with any frequency, this could cover the annual fee over and over. See this post for everything you need to know about the British Airways Visa flight discount.

If you have the British Airways Visa Card and redeem Avios for a reward flight, you can receive up to $600 in statement credits annually. You can earn up to three statement credits, as follows:

There are some basic terms to be aware of:

British Airways now also offers Reward Flight Saver from the United States, allowing you to redeem more Avios and pay lower surcharges. Getting a further statement credit of up to $200 on that is pretty great.

One of the potentially great perks of the British Airways Visa is that you can earn a Travel Together Ticket when you spend $30,000 on the card in a calendar year.

This companion ticket will be deposited in your British Airways Club account four to six weeks after you’ve completed the required spending.

With this certificate, you can book a British Airways award ticket at the full cost of Avios (plus taxes, fees, and surcharges), and then for the second passenger you don’t have to pay any Avios, but rather just have to pay all the fees.

This also offers a lot of flexibility — you can also use the voucher as a solo traveler and get 50% off the Avios required for a ticket. Your ticket can originate anywhere in the world, and you can even travel on Aer Lingus or Iberia.

This can represent a fantastic deal for first and business class travel, given how much those tickets would otherwise cost. This isn’t for everyone, though it has the potential to represent a good value, and I know it’s a feature that many value.

See this post for everything you need to know about the British Airways Visa companion voucher.

As a Visa Signature card, the British Airways Visa comes with the following shopping and travel protection benefits:

You’ll want to review the card’s benefits guide for any exclusions and rules that apply.

The British Airways Visa Card has a solid welcome bonus, and that could be a legitimate motivator for picking up this card. However, personally this isn’t a card I would use for everyday spending, since you can earn British Airways Avios at a better rate with other American Express or Chase cards. It also lacks a few benefits that many other airline credit cards offer, including a free checked bag and priority boarding.

That said, I absolutely think this card is worth holding onto if you fly British Airways with any frequency because:

There are several Avios currencies, with three belonging to International Airlines Group (IAG) airlines — there’s British Airways, Aer Lingus, and Iberia. There are also two other US-based credit cards that directly earn Avios from these airlines. Specifically, we’re talking about the Iberia Visa Card (learn more) and Aer Lingus Visa Card (learn more).

Which of these cards should you select? They have a lot in common:

The differences mainly come in the form of the perks associated with just holding onto the cards, and also the perks associated with spending $30,000 on the cards in a calendar year:

The best card to select comes down to which benefits you value most. Also, remember that you’re eligible for all three of these cards, should you be interested, so you don’t necessarily have to choose between them.

See here for a full comparison of cards earning Avios.

If you want to earn British Airways Avios, I’d recommend getting a card that earns either Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, or Chase Ultimate Rewards points. Here’s why:

With that in mind, which cards should you consider? Here are some of my favorite Chase Ultimate Rewards-earning cards:

If you’re over 5/24 or simply prefer Amex points or Capital One miles, here are some top choices:

The British Airways Visa is one of the best co-branded airline credit cards out there, in my opinion. The card offers a solid welcome bonus, and it can be worth spending money on the card to earn a companion ticket.

Beyond that, the card can be worth having for the discounts offered on both paid tickets (up to 10% off) or award tickets (up to $200 in statement credits), which can cover the annual fee over and over. That said, the card would be even stronger if it offered a free checked bag and lounge access as benefits — though I’d expect the annual to increase if those were added, especially the latter perk.

When it comes to earning British Airways Avios long term, personally I’d much rather earn Amex, Bilt, Capital One, and Chase points, and transfer them to British Airways. Not only does this allow you to earn points at a much faster rate, but it also gives you a lot more flexibility.

Few things compare to seeing the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in person on a crisp November morning. Watching massive balloons float down the streets of New York City is an iconic holiday experience on many families’ travel wish lists. Unfortunately, due to severe weather in New York on Nov. 26, 2026, the parade has been postponed to Saturday, Nov. 28.

The last time weather grounded the parade was back in 1971. The parade will now start at 8:30 a.m. on Saturday.

Typically, seeing the parade requires forgoing (or delaying) a traditional Thanksgiving meal at home. However, it will likely be well worth the effort once you see your child giddy with excitement as their favorite cartoon characters float by to the tune of a marching band in full regalia, while giant floats with entertainers glide by at street level.

Note, though, that more than 3.5 million people attend the parade in person each year. It’s important to strategize your visit so you are not far from the curb, struggling to catch a glimpse of the street.

There are several things you’ll want to keep in mind as you plan your day at the parade. Here are our top tips for viewing the 100th annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in 2026.

If you want to get an up-close view of the balloons featured in the annual parade, you won’t want to miss the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Balloon Inflation. Inflation occurs the day before the parade, starting at 1 p.m. on the Upper West Side, at 72nd Street and Columbus Avenue, near the American Museum of Natural History. It runs until 6 p.m., so you have several hours to sneak a peek at what’s to come during the parade. (Tip: The line opens at noon.)

There are 32 balloons that will transform from flat to fully inflated during the course of the afternoon. There are some fun new floats to keep an eye out for this year. To name a few, Bob the Minion riding a giant banana, Sorcerer Mickey, the Geico gecko and Earl the Squirrel, a balloon based on a real-life squirrel who made his home in Universal Orlando's Christmas tree several years ago and has now become the park's official holiday mascot.

Inflating a giant balloon the height of a four-story building takes time. Long lines form as the balloons become fully inflated in the early evening, so you may want to test your luck by arriving closer to 3 p.m., when most of the balloons start taking shape.

To get to the event location via public transportation, allow extra time; the subway station at 72nd Street tends to get very crowded as the afternoon wears on. You can also hail a cab or use a ride-hailing service, though you’ll want to be dropped off a block or two north of the gated-off section to avoid delays. Once you're in the line, you'll progress north and can exit west along any block from West 82nd to West 86th streets.

TPG tip: The closest subway station to the entrance point is the B and C stop at 72nd Street and Central Park West. Consider taking the 1, 2 or 3 train to Broadway and 72nd Street instead. It’s a few blocks west but an easy walk — just follow the crowds.

Related: These are the best New York City hotels for families to check out

Some parade-goers arrive as early as 4 a.m. to snag a coveted front-row spot along the route.

Plan accordingly if you have a particular location in mind. For example, prime seats at covered bus stops start filling up around 4 a.m., while you might be able to get front-row curb seating closer to 6 a.m.

Should you have deeper pockets and want to avoid being outside in the elements, you can pay for a parade brunch with a view along the parade route. Just be sure to make these reservations well in advance, as they tend to fill up quickly. Or, of course, you could book a room with a view directly on the parade route.

For those arriving later in the morning, you can stand in the closed-off side streets leading to the parade. You might be 10-15 people back, but you can still see most of the action.

The parade starts at 8:30 a.m. at Central Park West on 77th Street. Since the route is 2.5 miles long, it can take close to an hour for the lead marchers to reach Macy's. This means you’ll have some idle time before you can start watching the spectacle.

Because you could find yourself waiting several hours for the parade to show up, you’ll want to bring some stuff to stay occupied, like snacks, drinks and games. A backup charger is also a good idea.

You can bring camping chairs, buckets or anything else you may want to sit on to the parade, though these items are not very helpful for the parade itself, since most people stand. Still, at the very least, you’ll probably want to have some hotel towels or blankets to sit on instead of the hard, cold, gum-covered New York City sidewalks.

Don’t forget proper attire, including jackets, hats, gloves and umbrellas if rain is in the forecast, since the weather can turn quickly in late fall.

Like at home, excitement builds as the parade start time nears, and before long, cheers erupt as the parade comes into view. However, what you may not realize from watching at home is how interactive the experience can be. You may get high-fives from clowns and even confetti in your hair.

Not everything you see on TV happens along the parade route, either. Some performances, including those by the Radio City Rockettes and various singing and dance groups, only occur in front of Macy’s Herald Square (where the cameras are). As a result, you’ll want to manage your expectations. Don’t worry about what you’re missing. Instead, focus on all that’s taking place in front of you: the floats, balloons and festivities.

Related: 10 tips for flying during the holidays

The parade covers so much of the city that there isn’t one best hotel for attending the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. While some hotels are physically on the parade route, it’s not as simple as booking a room at one of these properties and watching the festivities from your window.

Sure, some windows at the route-adjacent hotels offer good views — but hotels are savvy, so those rooms are often sold as part of pricier parade packages. As such, you’ll have to pay more and often meet minimum stay requirements to see the parade from your actual hotel room.

If you don’t want to splurge to see all the action from your room, ask if your hotel has a special viewing area for guests. Often, hotels on the parade route have some space outside where patrons can watch the parade as it passes.

A few properties on the parade route include:

Should you have trouble securing a room at a property on the parade route or wish to save a little money, consider staying a block or more off the route at properties like The St. Regis New York and Park Hyatt New York. Both are a very short walk to and from the parade.

Some more points-friendly hotels that are within walking distance of the parade route include:

Related: 10 festive hotels for people who really love the holidays

Since New York City is an incredible place to be for the holidays, there are all kinds of other ways to celebrate the season after kicking it off with the parade. Be sure to see Santa in person at Santaland on the eighth floor of Macy’s on 34th Street (reservations are required). The Big Apple Circus, under the big top in Lincoln Center, is a sure-fire family pleaser. Also, peruse some of the festive holiday markets throughout the city when you’re not busy ice skating at Rockefeller Center or catching a performance of a Christmas classic like “The Nutcracker” or “A Christmas Carol.”

#6098. This Is American Airlines’ Oldest Aircraft Type Flying In 2026

American Airlines touts its flightline as one of the newest in North America, yet dozens of quarter-century-old narrowbodies still fly daily itineraries at its busiest hubs. That largely comes down to the fact that AA acquired all 48 of its older Airbus A320-200 aircraft. Now averaging around 25.7 years old, according to ch-aviation fleet data, the planes arrived via previous mergers with two defunct carriers.

AA plans to retain the 48-aircraft A320 subfleet in service into next year. It even purchased one off lease last year instead of retiring the jets alongside its previous McDonnell Douglas MD-80, Boeing 757-200, and Airbus A330-200.

On June 21, the 27-year-old N107US returned from a three-month retrofit as the testbed for an interior overhaul. On June 23, AA Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden announced that the cabin refresh introduces updated premium seating, expanded overhead bins, and in-seat device power.

It can be described as something like getting on a flying hand-me-down when you board an American A320 today. The earliest aircraft in that group began in Phoenix in 1990 when Edward Beauvais, the founder of America West Airlines, acquired aircraft abandoned by the insolvent Braniff Airlines. AA still operates all 26 of the single-aisle workhorses that America West eventually assembled.

In 1996, US Airways took a desperate risk of its own. US Airways Chairman Stephen Wolf and President Rakesh Gangwal went on an Airbus 'shopping spree' to replace outdated Boeing and Douglas aircraft in an attempt to pull out of a tailspin. "When I came here, it was a very troubled company. People had given up hope of US Airways ever being a force in the marketplace," Gangwal later recalled, according to Wharton Magazine.

US Airways started flying its own batch of 22 A320-200s soon after, setting up an awkward snag for passengers and mechanics alike. America West Airlines took over US Airways before the combined group merged into AA in 2015. All that corporate matchmaking dumped two completely separate Airbus fleets onto the same AA schedule.

For everyday flyers, that merger left behind 48 mismatched A320s with an expensive quirk under the wings. Because America West and US Airways chose rival engine makers, AA must still stock separate spare parts and run different maintenance playbooks for two tiny subfleets. Those upkeep headaches persisted even as AA executives packed tighter seating rows and leaner amenities onto those aging cabins.

Under the 2018 'Project Oasis,' American decided to pack tighter rows onto its A320s. AA opted not to install seatback displays, cut back on galleys, and thinned out seat cushions. Matters were even worse on the 737 and A321s, which saw screens removed and seat pitch reduced. The president of the flight attendants union, Lori Bassani, said the following year, as Fox News reported:

"We find that the seats are not only getting smaller, but there's no padding on them anymore. It is a torture chamber for our customers and for us, that also fly on our own airlines."

Prior to the 2019 Boeing 737 MAX groundings, the pandemic, and chronic plant delays at Boeing and Airbus, AA had intended to retire the cramped A320s sooner. Instead of easing out of service, those older jets kept flying as many as eight short domestic hops a day on flights under two hours. All those daily takeoffs and landings age an airplane much faster than smooth, long-haul cruising.

Keeping all 48 A320s flying through busy hubs in Phoenix, Charlotte, and Philadelphia helped AA keep schedules intact whenever new jet deliveries fell behind. Schedulers leaned on those midsize jets to fill routes too big for regional planes yet too small for larger airliners. Even so, running 1990s jets alongside modern single-aisle planes shows clear limits in seat count, flying range, and fuel efficiency.

Get ready for Simple Flying's latest feature!

Stepping aboard an aging American Airlines Airbus A320-200 can feel surprisingly roomy compared with American Airlines' newer Boeing narrowbodies. While the spec table shows the older Airbus trailing American's Boeing 737-800 and 737 MAX 8 on capacity, range, and fuel burn, the matchup narrows to a window or middle seat.

An A320-200 cabin measures seven inches (18 cm) wider than a 737 cabin, giving flyers in tight 3-3 rows more shoulder room and aisle space. American CEO Robert Isom often spotlights fleet renewal, saying that "over the past decade, we have invested heavily to modernize and simplify our fleet, which is the largest and youngest among US network carriers."

Even with a 14.7-year average fleet age beating Delta Air Lines and United Airlines, AA still flies A320-200s daily. They fly out of Dallas/Fort Worth, Phoenix, Charlotte, and Philadelphia on routes like Dallas/Fort Worth–San Antonio, Boston–Philadelphia, and Cabo San Lucas–Phoenix.

Unrefurbished A320-200 cabins still show their age with worn trim and cramped overhead bins, though American Airlines is closing that gap. According to aeroLOPA, this year's updated A320-200 cabin layout expands first class to 16 seats alongside 134 Main Cabin seats and adds larger Airbus XL overhead storage. Those larger lockers cut down on gate-check scrambles while preserving the A320-200's wider cabin for passengers.

Boeing's newer 737-800 and 737 MAX 8 jets do not automatically deliver a better onboard ride, either. According to View from the Wing, AA's dense 'Oasis' 737 retrofits stripped away seatback screens, packed in extra rows with less room even in first class, and shrank the lavatories. That era without seatback monitors will eventually end for both narrowbody families.

AirlineGeeks reports that American doesn't plan to install new seatback entertainment until 2028. For crews and operators, the A320-200 and 737 force clear trade-offs. Flight attendants get more aisle space on the A320-200 and avoid the tightest retrofitted 737 rear lavatories, while pilots trade Boeing's yoke for an Airbus sidestick and tray table on shorter daily runs.

Why the longest range single-aisle in the Airbus line up is always pointed skyward.

Unlike modern carbon fiber planes such as American Boeing 787-8s, the A320-200 still relies on aluminum for 70% to 80% of its structure. Under the wings, AA's two mismatched engine types also behave differently, burning fuel and wearing out parts on separate schedules. Even the A320's digital controls hit an unexpected snag last November, when Airbus linked an uncommanded midair pitch shift to cosmic activity scrambling onboard software.

Airbus warned in an urgent global bulletin to airlines in November 2025 that "analysis of a recent event involving an A320 Family aircraft has revealed that intense solar radiation may corrupt data critical to the functioning of flight controls." AA's technicians worked overtime across Thanksgiving weekend to install two-hour software fixes across 209 A320 family narrowbodies.

Those emergency patches cleared quickly once crews finished the holiday push. Still, keeping aging Airbus jets flying safely takes far more than quick code updates, as rising airframe repair bills and cabin upgrades push maintenance costs steadily higher.

Understanding the flight profile of the world's longest-range narrowbody jet.

Keeping 1990s A320s flying is pushing American's repair bills steadily higher. Mainline maintenance and parts spending jumped 7.8% through the first nine months of this year after heavier airframe checks drove costs up last year. Worse, because American Airlines leases 36 of its 48 A320-200 aircraft, delivery delays force costly lease extensions.

Even as American Airlines brings Starlink Wi-Fi across its mainline fleet starting early next year, these 48 retiring A320-200s will miss the 2028 seatback screen rollout. Federal airworthiness recalls are catching up with AA's aging A320s which compounds maintenance intensity even further. An August order for Aero Engines V2500 turbofan compressor blades caught the 26 former America West jets flying for AA in its net.

The directive comes alongside other recent recalls and proposals including work on evacuation slides, landing gear doors, and preemptive wing crack checks. Still, A320 family check pilots flew 42 transatlantic training runs last year to prepare line crews for American Airlines' A321-200XLR launch. Retiring all 48 A320-200 jets depends on hundreds of Airbus and Boeing replacements still working through factory backlogs.

Although the Boeing 737 MAX 7 and larger MAX 10 cleared FAA certification in August and October, initial deliveries wait until next year. That timeline keeps American Airlines' oldest single-aisle jets flying toward 2030, bridging the gap until incoming 737 MAX, A321XLR, and future widebody aircraft reshape American Airlines' fleet.

#6097. Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images)

Former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

Prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

"56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot."

In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

#6095. Norse Atlantic Collapses: Airline Cancels Flights, Strands Passengers

Back in August 2026, all-Boeing 787 airline Norse Atlantic Airways announced it was in a rough financial spot, and was pursuing a sale, merger, or other arrangement. Not a whole lot of progress was made in subsequent months, and just this morning, the airline announced that it was in a “critical” financial situation.

Well, it seems that it didn’t take long for things to get much worse, as the airline has seemingly canceled all flights just hours later, leaving travelers stranded.

Earlier today, Norse Atlantic provided an update on its financial situation and ongoing strategic review. There’s no point in paraphrasing this, so here’s the direct statement from the airline:

The Company’s financial situation is critical. It is dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs and to continue its operations. Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover. In parallel, the Board and management have diligently considered other available options, including ACMI contracts. Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution.

To state the obvious, this sounded really, really bad. When the company was publicly stating that its “financial situation is critical” and that it needed to secure financing to meet “short-term liquidity needs,” you knew things weren’t good. I expected we’d see something bad happen in the coming weeks, but it didn’t take that long.

Norse Atlantic has canceled its own scheduled flights effective immediately. On top of that, the airline was leasing two jets to Pakistan International Airlines, and those flights were also canceled with very little notice, “due to an unexpected operational suspension” by Norse Atlantic. Travelers were literally checking in at the airport when they realized the airline was grounded.

Due to an unexpected operational suspension by our wet-lease partner Norse Air without prior notice, tonight’s PK786 (London–Islamabad) & PK710 (Manchester–Lahore) are cancelled.We deeply regret the disruption. Efforts have been made to mitigate the impact, and from tomorrow,…

So while the company hasn’t formally announced that it’s liquidating, it’s clear that operations are at least suspended, and we’ll see how this all plays out.

The airline industry can be a funny business, and there’s no clearer example of that than Norse Atlantic Airways. The airline launched in 2022, with the goal of operating long haul, low cost flights, particularly across the Atlantic.

That wasn’t exactly a unique business model, because this was exactly what Norwegian did, before it discontinued long haul flights in 2021. Not only was the idea sort of copied, but Norse Atlantic had some executives from Norwegian, and even picked up the planes that Norwegian previously flew.

But as is all too common in the airline industry, clearly they thought it would be different this time around… it wasn’t. So in 2024 we saw the airline update its business model, making the focus less about operating regularly scheduled commercial flights, and more about leasing out aircraft, all while reducing its fleet.

The company got a lifeline when IndiGo decided to lease some Norse Atlantic 787s to dabble in long haul flying, ahead of the airline taking delivery of its own Airbus A350s. However, between all the airspace closures, high oil costs, and generally declining performance at IndiGo as the airline increasingly moved away from its core strengths, the airline recently decided to scrap that experiment, and stop leasing planes from Norse Atlantic.

Since then, opportunities for Norse Atlantic have been limited. The airline did manage to lease a couple of Dreamliners to the “new” Pakistan International Airlines, but for an airline with 12 planes, that hardly pays the bills.

Norse Atlantic did still operate some of its own flights, but in a very limited capacity. The airline had some flights from Europe to Thailand, South Africa, and the United States, but most were seasonal, and they were a fraction of what they previously were. Clearly they just didn’t have enough money to “keep the lights on” anymore.

I am curious to see what comes next for Norse Atlantic’s 787s. The airline doesn’t own them, but instead, they’ll presumably return to their leasing companies. I can’t help but point out that Southwest Airlines wants to start long haul flights. The airline had been considering a Boeing 787 order, and was possibly even looking at ways to get planes faster than from a direct order (which requires waiting for years).

Could these dozen Norse Atlantic 787s somehow end up at Southwest? The interiors would just need some updates (assuming the airline wants to offer business class), but talk about a quick way to grow a decent sized fleet.

This morning, Norse Atlantic released a statement admitting that its “financial situation is critical,” and that the company’s future is “dependent on securing financing to meet short-term liquidity needs.” That wasn’t exactly a great sign, but little did we know that the company would collapse just hours later, as the airline has now ceased all flying, including on a wet lease basis.

Financial issues at the company started when… well, it launched. Norse Atlantic was just a direct replica of Norwegian, which had failed. When the airline realized that the long haul, low cost business model doesn’t really work, they tried to pivot to wet leasing. And while there’s some demand for that, it’s also not a 100% consistent business in terms of demand.

I feel horribly for all the frontline employees at Norse Atlantic who put their best foot forward. May they find good opportunities at other airlines.

What do you make of Norse Atlantic’s seeming collapse?

#6094. Not Again: Cargo Jet Overruns Miami Airport Runway (This Time A FedEx MD-11)

Miami International Airport (MIA) is having a bad luck streak when it comes to cargo planes being able to stay on the runway, but at least this time around there were no fatalities. Still, yikes…

At 8:25PM on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, a FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 overran the runway at Miami Airport, leading the airport to be shut down for an extended period of time.

The 34-year-old MD-11 with the registration code N605FE had just performed flight FX910 from Memphis (MEM), and was coming in to land on runway 26R, which is 9,355 feet (2,851 meters) long. That’s a solidly long runway, for what it’s worth.

However, the plane wasn’t able to stop before the end of the runway, and seemed to exit the paved surface at a speed of around 50 knots, and came to a stop around 320 meters (1,000 feet) past the end of the runway, right by the airport perimeter fence.

🚨 USA | FEDEX CARGO PLANE OVERRUNS RUNWAY AT #MIAMI AIRPORT!MD-11 arriving from Memphis skidded into the grass beyond Runway 26R, triggering an FAA ground stop.2 crew members are safe. No deaths or injuries.#FlaPanthers #Survivor51 #ไฟไหม้ pic.twitter.com/kTM48GkeGf

WATCH: FedEx cargo plane in the grass after overshooting runway at Miami International Airport pic.twitter.com/t4DPQwUb0m

Fortunately there were no serious injuries. There’s video footage showing stairs being pulled up to the plane, and the pilots walking off with their bags. There’s always the classic aviation adage that “any landing you can walk away from is a good one,” and if that’s the case, I guess this was a good landing.

Footage showing the FedEx Express MD-11F after it overran the runway at Miami International Airport tonight. As a result of the incident, a ground stop was issued. pic.twitter.com/ldraejGQ4v

This accident ended up causing a ground stop of nearly two hours at the airport. That’s not exactly ideal timing, given what a busy travel day yesterday was, ahead of Thanksgiving. Operations did eventually resume, but with delays averaging over three hours.

🚨 迈阿密国际机场关闭！今晚，一架联邦快递（FedEx）货运飞机在迈阿密国际机场（MIA）冲出跑道，机场目前已实施地面停飞令（Ground Stop）。根据空中交通管制（ATC）的录音，飞机冲出跑道后，管制员通知其他飞行员，机场“刚刚关闭”。这是今年迈阿密国际机场发生的第二起货运飞机冲出跑道事故。…

Of course the concept of a plane overrunning a runway at Miami Airport is fresh on people’s minds, given the September 6 accident we saw with a 21 Air (Amazon Air) Boeing 767-300 that overran runway 30. Tragically that accident claimed five lives, as the plane ran through the perimeter fence, and killed motorists. What we’ve found out about the piloting of that flight since the accident, and just how recklessly the captain was flying the plane, is astounding.

We’ll have to wait for a full investigation to know what happened (the NTSB typically releases a preliminary report within a month), but in terms of circumstances and possible contributing factors, there are a couple of things we know.

First, there’s footage showing the plane’s approach, and it makes it pretty clear that the plane touched down extremely late.

JUST IN: FedEx cargo plane overruns the runway at Miami International Airport. Flights halted pic.twitter.com/PFFH0TNpe1

A recreation of the approach based on flight tracking data shows just how late the plane touched down, and the big question is why the pilots didn’t perform a go around.

🚨 BREAKING: FedEx FDX910, an MD-11F registered N605FE, went off the end of runway 26R landing at Miami International from Memphis at about 8:28 PM local, Nov 25. Tower sent the next arrival around and ground control closed the airport. No injuries reported so far. pic.twitter.com/IhRUGEVR97

It’s also worth pointing out that weather in the region was really bad at the time of the accident. Anna Giaritelli, a reputable aviation journalist with good sources, quotes a Miami air traffic controller, who told her that “this was absolutely the most dangerous operation I’ve seen,” as much of the traffic approaching Miami had run into a “black hole of weather.”

A Miami air traffic controller sent me this chilling text minutes before the FedEx incident in MIA tonight(Controller was not on duty while texting me.) pic.twitter.com/Fvy7vb7xuP

It doesn’t seem like conditions at Miami Airport as such were that awful (compared to reports of severe turbulence in the region), but I imagine the bad weather could’ve contributed to a sense of “get-there-itis” for the pilots.

While this is of course unfortunate, the great news here is the lack of injuries or fatalities. The plane ended up coming to a stop just feet from the airport’s perimeter fence, and if it had crashed through that, the outcome could’ve been completely different, with fatalities among motorists.

It also has to be acknowledged that the pilots seemingly turned the plane a little bit left off the end of the runway, to avoid the localizer antenna. So at least the overrun was handled as well as it could be.

Based on the preliminary information we have so far, DEI does not appear to be a factor in this accident. 😉

A FedEx MD-11 overran the runway at Miami Airport last night, and ended up in the grass just short of the airport perimeter fence. Fortunately there were no major injuries, and the pilots managed to walk off the plane. This had major operational impacts for the airport, as a ground stop was issued, delaying lots of travelers.

Unlike the 21 Air Boeing 767 accident we saw in September, there were no fatalities this time around. Either way, two cargo planes going off Miami runways in under three months is not great.

What do you make of this FedEx MD-11 accident in Miami?

The saga continues between the world's largest operator of the Boeing 737, Southwest Airlines, and the Piquette Family. Earlier this month, Jason Piquette and his family, including twins, had traveled with Southwest to Portland (PDX) in Oregon, and when they arrived, they noticed that their double stroller was badly damaged.

Southwest initially denied that the airline had damaged the stroller, which turned a routine baggage policy complaint into an accusationwhere the carrier told USA Today that they had offered the Piquette family compensation, a claim that has been disputed by the family on TikTok.

On November 7, the Piquette family had flown to Portland to visit family, and on arrival from their Southwest flight, identified that the stroller they had checked into the hold had been delivered with damage sustained, including bent and wobbly wheels, and a damage to the stroller frame.

Piquette challenged the airline, but the airport personnel for Southwest initially denied liability and claimed the airline's limited release of liability policy, which suggests that strollers and car seats travel at the passenger's own risk. This left the Piquette family without a stroller for their visit to Oregon, leading Piquette to take to social media and repeatedly ask the airline for answers.

Simple Flying reached out to Southwest for comment on the matter; however, an airline spokesperson could not immediately be reached.

After Piquette's initial videos on social media were seen by millions, a Southwest executive contacted Piquette, who, according to the traveler, noted that the airline refused to reconsider the limited liability policy. The executive is claimed to have said, 'I'm the highest up person you're gonna get'. On the call, a $200 flight voucher was offered, with an expiry date as offered. Piquette outlined that this voucher would be 'useless', as he and his family had no intention of flying the airline again.

Despite being several weeks after the initial incident, a recent report by USA Today has surfaced, following the Dallas-based airline confirming to the major news outlet that a $500 reimbursement for the stroller, in addition to the $200 flight voucher, was offered. This upset Piquette, which resulted in him posting another video asking for Southwest to explain why they "lied".

Piquette has repeatedly called out to ask why Southwest misled USA Today, suggesting that the airline was trying to 'save face', after confirming that during his call with the airline executive, no $500 reimbursement was offered.

Parent shares shaky footage of damaged stroller and a cold customer service reply that left repairs unaffordable.

According to the US Department of Transportation (DOT) ruling, all major carriers are liable for up to $4,700 for lost, damaged, or delayed domestic checked baggage. However, airlines often require passengers to sign or accept limited release waivers, which apply automatically under the Contract of Carriage that is agreed to when purchasing a ticket. This move exempts the airline from damage claims unless the item is lost completely.

Piquette's use of social media has highlighted his ongoing frustration with Southwest, as the airline has continuously refused to replace or acknowledge the damage to the essential stroller. Through Piqeutte's videos, a number of people have offered donations, and even one viewer lent the family a stroller to borrow during their time in Oregon.

Simple Flying asked Southwest Airlines whether they had any immediate plans to review its limited release of liability policy following the event and following the widespread media attention this incident has created. Families traveling with young children on Southwest are entitled to an additional child item on top of the existing checked baggage allowance; this includes one stroller and one car seat/child restraint per child at no extra cost.

#6090. The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek Will Pay You To Redeem Points Over Peak Dates… But Why?

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is incentivizing people to redeem points at the property for stays over some pretty peak dates, which you don’t often see, as flagged by View from the Wing. This has the potential to be a good deal, but beyond that, I think the more interesting part of this story is the topic of why the hotel would offer something like this, since this is pretty rare.

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is offering 15,000 points back per night when you redeem over some peak dates, for a total of up to 90,000 points back (which you’d get if redeeming for six nights). To cover the basics:

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is a ski-in, ski-out property in Colorado, and it’s one I’ve reviewed before. For what it’s worth, the hotel is currently charging 55,000 World of Hyatt points per night over the dates eligible for this promotion.

Based on my valuation of 1.4 cents per World of Hyatt point, that means a redemption will cost you the equivalent of $770 per night. Meanwhile cash rates are running double as much, and that’s before taxes are factored in.

Understandably, I think a lot of people might be confused as to why the Park Hyatt Beaver Creek would be incentivizing award redemptions in this way. If the hotel wants to fill rooms, why only offer bonus points for points stays, and not for cash stays? That’s especially true when you consider redeeming points is already a good value compared to the cash rate.

The explanation here is probably pretty simple, if you understand the economics at play. I’ve written in the past about how hotels are reimbursed for award stays. Keep in mind that the loyalty program centrally (rather than the individual hotel) sets the cost for redemptions, based on their internal costs associated with redemptions. The way it generally works is as follows:

How does this all factor into the Park Hyatt Beaver Creek’s promotion? I suspect a few factors are at play here:

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is offering 15,000 points per night for award redemption over peak holiday dates. So while the standard rate is 55,000 points per night, you’d end up paying 40,000 points per night, which is quite the deal compared to the cash rate.

Given that some hotels treat points guests as second class guests who are staying for “free,” I think the goal here is pretty clear. Hotels are reimbursed for award stays based on overall occupancy levels, and presumably the hotel hopes that a promotion like this will get it to the occupancy level needed to trigger the highest reimbursement rate.

#6089. Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

“This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.
