#6057. TSA Demanded United Airlines Suspend A Pilot Over Terror Support, Union Accused Of Resisting, Report Says

TSA reportedly told United Airlines to suspend a pilot accused of supporting a terrorist group, after the pilots union resisted action according to a federal government source cited by TV news reporter Mike Wagenheim. The new report says the intervention happened last week. The pilot hasn’t been named. Neither has the terror group he allegedly supported. Mike Wagenheim’s November 24 update on the reported TSA intervention Wagenheim’s earlier report cited two sources saying United knew of up to six additional crew members who’d expressed support for terrorist groups. United’s pilots union spokesman declined to discuss individual cases. He said the Air Line Pilots Association has a professional standards committee and legal team that assess accusations against its ethics code and United’s workplace guidelines. The Pilot Israel Barred Was Already On Leave In October, Israel prohibited flights with Sina Amjadian serving as crew from arriving in the country. Israeli officials confirmed the restriction after receiving allegations that he’d expressed support for Iran’s Revolutionary Guards and Hezbollah. But United said he wasn’t currently flying, having been on leave since 2024. He flew Boeing 737s and wasn’t qualified on long haul aircraft. Apparently there was material showing Iranian leadership imagery and mourning civilians killed in strikes. There are claims of Hezbollah support and that there was a video of him kissing the regime’s emblem. United Pilot Celebrated October 7 Rapes And Murders As ‘Bravery’ I first wrote about Ibrahim Mossallam in November 2023, after his Facebook description of the October 7 attack as “resistance by a brave people.” United removed him from service with pay but he was reported back flying. On October 6, 2026, after the flydubai pilot sought to use his plane as a missile to attack Israel, United told me: We have withheld this pilot from service pending an ongoing review. There were also reports that he returned after just a day, and that two colleagues had given up first class seats to monitor him in the cockpit. United subsequently denied both accounts. A reported claimed the union blocked his firing. TSA Can Order A Pilot Out Of The Cockpit It was striking that the reported order came from TSA. It has authority that extends well beyond passenger checkpoints. Under federal law, a TSA determination that a pilot poses, or is suspected of posing, a terrorism or passenger safety threat requires the Federal Aviation Administration to take action against the pilot’s certificate. TSA can request that the action take effect immediately. It can also issue mandatory security directives to airlines. However, it isn’t clear from the report what legal mechanism is claimed to have been used and doesn’t report an FAA certificate action. It says the pilot’s “TSA credential” was revoked and describes that as Known Crewmember access. TSA can require an airline to remove someone’s access, but losing that privilege doesn’t mean losing a pilot’s license. Flydubai Shows Why The Concern Is Real I don’t need to know a pilot’s politics. But I wouldn’t want someone who celebrates the killing of civilians at the controls of my flight. That calls their judgment into question even without evidence they’ve planned an attack themselves. The September 30 flydubai cockpit attack makes the concern concrete. The co-pilot of that flight planned a suicide attack on the Tel Aviv airport, attacking the captain with an axe to take over the aircraft. He had satisfied the licensing, good conduct and security requirements for the job, and those checks had failed to uncover his extremist intentions. The values of the person in control of an aircraft matter. @Enough – you really don’t seem to know very much about the topic. Stay off social media.

United Airlines carries cargo consistent with its legal obligations and with U.S. foreign policy. There is no demonstrated connection between that cargo and instances of conflict.

Even the U.N. concluded that the October 7 attacks included rape and gang rape, clear evidence of sexual violence and torture of the hostages. https://apnews.com/article/fe1a35767a63666fe4dc1c97e397177e

Hamas uses civilians as human shields, and hides within the civilian population. They used hospitals as military bases. So while every military conflict includes harm to civilians, frequently at a much greater rate than this one, most of that blame can be assigned to Hamas itself. Whenever you hear about lamentable conditions in Gaza, append “because of Hamas” to the end of that sentence.

Calling Israel’s response to Hamas a genocide strips that term of all meaning. Civilian deaths do not, on their own, establish genocide. The legal question is whether prohibited acts were committed with intent to physically destroy a protected group. Even war crimes do not establish that intent.

Obviously, defeating Hamas and recovering hostages are the obvious alternative explanation for Israel’s military campaign in Gaza. Israel targets an armed organization, rather than Palestinians because they are Palestinians (indeed, 21% of Israel’s own population is Arab).

And Israel has taken significant measures in its campaign to protect civilians, which is evidence against an extermination policy. They warn civilians in advance of attacks, and evacuate civilian populations. The argument doesn’t even depend on those efforts being ultimately effective to count against a claim of genocide, which is a claim about intent.

There are statements from some terrible people in Israel’s government that are pretty inflammatory (there are some terrible people in our government, or who run for office, who say inflammatory things as well). Those statements do not express operative government policy. Critics often cite National Security Minister Ben Gvir, but most Americans think that’s a military position. It’s not. It’s like head of the police, but he’s been given a more grandiose-sounding title.

The International Court of Justice has held that genocidal intent must be the only reasonable inference from the pattern of conduct. Evidence compatible with other purposes defeats that inference. https://www.icj-cij.org/node/103223

So no, there is not a genocide in Gaza you ignorant fool.

@Gary – a valiant attempt to speak rationally to the irrational though….In the end, people will believe what they believe and a lot of people believe in all kinds of nonsense. It’s futile. Actions and good deeds are far more important.

#6055. Warning For Families Traveling To California: New Booster Seat Law Covers Kids Through Age 15

I have a California trip coming up with my family. If I hadn’t seen this on Twitter, it wouldn’t have occurred to me that my 8-year-old daughter might need a booster for the ride from the airport. We live in Texas, where she’s aged out of the child seat requirement. Starting January 1, 2027, California will insist on measuring how the belt fits her in the car we actually wind up with from National, Avis or Uber. She could fit the belt in our car at home and need a booster in the SUV we get assigned to, but she’s already aged out of the California law that requires the rental company to have a child seat for her. We might have to bring one with us just in case. New Booster Seat Rules Go Into Effect January 1 Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 435 in October 2025. Through the end of this year, a child 8 or older isn’t required to use a car seat or booster seat. Starting January 1, 2027 the rule becomes that a 15 year old requires a booster seat unless all five of these conditions are met: Their back is all the way against the vehicle seat. Their knees bend over the front edge of the cushion. The shoulder belt sits snugly across the middle of their chest and shoulder, clear of their neck. The lap belt sits as low as it can, touching their thighs. They can keep that position for the whole ride. An 8-year old who meets this can ride with just a belt, while a 15-year old who fails to meet one of these conditions needs a booster. Here’s a demonstration of the fit test: . What Happens At The Rental Counter And The Uber Pickup California’s rental car law requires agencies to have a compliant seat available for rent on request for children under 8. This new law doesn’t change that. I don’t count on rental companies having a car seat for my young son, even where it’s required and I’ve reserved it. If they’re out of seats, or the buckle’s broken in the one they have, my wife or I has to wait at the airport while the other one goes to Target. I wrote about a mother at the Atlanta airport who said the seats Avis rented her for her babies didn’t work. Avis says airport availability can be limited. At participating Hertz locations, the AAA rate includes a child seat with an advance reservation, subject to availability. ‘Availability’ is doing a lot of work here. Meanwhile, this also has a huge effect on rideshare (and taxis). They’re not required to have a booster. And if I don’t have one, I’m responsible for violations and the driver can decline the ride without it. Los Angeles and San Francisco do have Uber Car Seat. You reserve it in advance, pay a $10 surcharge and get one. It tops out at 49 inches and 65 pounds. A 50-inch child is too tall for the seat Uber supplies and can still need a booster for that ride. When a kid scoots forward because their knees don’t bend over a deep seat, the lap belt can ride up over their belly. Typical nonsensical California overregulation. A true nanny state we have here.

Now there’s going to be a teen tourism lobby, e.g. theme parks, in California.

Nonsensical? It really is a safety issue. If a child does not fit the seat properly, they can be seriously injured. It is based on evidence-based recommendations and bioengineering recommendations. There is literature from Washington State (see below) showing a 19% reduction in overall injury rates, and another study showing a 10% absolute reduction in serious injury when boosters are used. Studies on this question are somewhat limited because the research is technically challenging, but what we do have supports a significant benefit.

Car manufacturers state that a child must be able to sit with their knees bent over the front of the seat, their back firmly against the backrest, and the seatbelt across the chest, not the neck. If they can’t, they need a booster. Plenty of kids who are 8 years old are too short or small to be safely restrained by the car’s restraint system, and a booster improves their chances of making it through a collision without serious injury. My own daughter (I live in Texas) was in a booster until she was nearly 12 because of her height.

Other states have similar, albeit with some variation, laws: Colorado, Washington, Louisiana and Minnesota. This law simply ensures people use their cars safely.

While many laws, regardless of jurisdiction, are silly, this one is based on best practices to improve children’s safety.

So, overall, while I know this is inconvenient, it is far from an overreach by a “nanny state.” A big failing of this law, it seems, is that rental car agencies are not required to support their customer’s compliance by providing a booster for older children.

Reading these seating requirements, I realized that I — a petite 5′ 2″ senior citizen — would have ALWAYS required a booster seat because all seat belts rub against my neck when they are worn correctly. I jerryrig seatbelt positions so they do not chafe against my neck. I would imagine everyone who is smaller shares a similar experience.

I think Kevin works for OSHA. Long winded tripe.

California is run by special interests, and sometimes grifters, who want more money in their pockets at the expense of the rest of us. Affordability be dammed, especially while they can still blame Trump.

This is feel good legislation with very little, really zero, science behind it. This from the party of “believe the science”. This is clearly, like a lot of legislation, driven by the lobbyists for the car seat manufacturers.

I don’t know what a car seat costs, but I’m going to risk the ticket if I’m visiting California, vs buying on there, and I’m going to leave the kid with the wife outside the car rental office. Or, in most places I rent anymore, I just go get the car without going in the office.

It’s OK though, in California they have big signs at the rental car agency telling you that renting a car causes cancer. And, I’m serious.

Is there any issue too small for the government not to override our own cost-benefit analysis?

Have you heard about California’s mandate for tires with lower rolling resistance, even though they give you less grip? I prefer better accident avoidance to better gas mileage. Give us the facts and let us make the choice!

15. The age at which one can apply for a learner’s permit in Kalifornia.

“I think Kevin works for OSHA. Long winded tripe.”

Or that Juvenile Products Manufacturers Association.

All your statistics measure age and not height/weight. The point of the regulation is that height/weight are the actually appropriate measurements rather than a rough approximation from age. Most kids aren’t outliers, so the 15 year old won’t be in a booster unless they’re extremely small.

It’s the same reason car seats for babies and toddlers show weights and heights instead of ages for each style and facing of the car seat.

This is a ridiculous law that none of us in CA asked for. My daughter is extremely petite. She’s in her 20s now, but when she was 15 she was still 4’11” – I would have had to keep her in a booster seat halfway through high school. Absurd. I’m 5’5″ and find that in many cars even if I adjust the seatbelt it goes over my throat, not the middle of my chest.

Add in the new ridiculous tire requirements too – that have less grip – last week I had to drive 80 miles each way to an appointment in the rain. I made sure to grab new tires the week before (needed them anyway), before this kicks in too.

And they wonder why there’s a bit of a mass exodus from CA…

Anyone reading this born before 1972? Congratulations you survived childhood without a seat belt.

Sure and have the state doesn’t have insurance. Useless nanny state

Worth knowing for Disneyland and San Diego trips. Rental counters only have to stock seats for under 8s, so for older kids a backless booster from home is the safe bet. They’re light and fit in a carry-on

No self respecting teen is going to use a booster seat when they are in middle school.

this law is going to be DOA in terms of adherence.

Sadly there’s no lack of insipid comments that don’t address the problem.

A reasonable adjustment to the law might be something like requiring this for residents in their own vehicles and giving more leeway to taxis and rideshares to allow for judgement calls for borderline situations.

@Christian, exactly. that would be a reasonable solution, though I would extend the flexibility to visitors getting rental cars. And if the residents do not like it, they have the ability to vote out those who made the law (unlike visitors to the state)

#6054. Senator Grassley Should Heed His Own Warning

Were the longtime Iowa senator to leave office before January, the outgoing governor, Republican Kim Reynolds, would be able to appoint his successor.

Senator Chuck Grassley (R., Iowa) listens as U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem testifies before a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on “Oversight of the Department of Homeland Security” on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., March 3, 2026.

Iowa Senator Chuck Grassley is the oldest member of Congress at age 93, but he remains sharp and focused.

This month, his office announced that he will not be retiring from the Senate, even though a Democrat will take office as governor in January and have the power to appoint someone if any of the state’s two U.S. Senate seats fall vacant.

John Fund is National Review’s national-affairs reporter.

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

As High As 100,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

If you fly American Airlines frequently, one of its cobranded Citi cards could save you money on your trips.

The (see rates and fees) is the only credit card that includes a full Admirals Club membership.

It also offers statement credits, a free first checked bag (on eligible domestic itineraries) and bonuses that can help you reach American Airlines AAdvantage elite status.

The card has a $695 annual fee. Whether it’s worth paying comes down to how often you’ll use the lounges and how much you’d otherwise spend on purchases covered by the card’s credits.

Apply for the : Earn 80,000 bonus miles after spending $8,000 on purchases within the first three months from account opening.

Here’s how the value adds up in your first year and beyond.

New holders can currently earn 80,000 bonus miles after spending $8,000 on purchases within the first three months from account opening.

This bonus is worth about $1,160, based on TPG’s November 2026 valuations. We recommend holding off until at least 100,000 miles are on offer.

A significant portion of the card's overall value comes from its bonus, so earning it and redeeming the miles wisely are crucial to offsetting the card's high annual fee.

Related: The Citi / AAdvantage Executive's new benefits are live: 6 things to do now

Arguably the most valuable ongoing benefit of this card is the complimentary Admirals Club membership you'll receive every year that you hold it. When you have the , all you have to do is walk to the lounge and present a same-day boarding pass for an eligible flight.

American charges $750 a year for a single membership, which covers Admirals Club access for one person. A full membership (with two guests) and partner lounge access costs $1,200 to $1,400 a year (depending on your AAdvantage status). If you’d otherwise pay for a full membership, the card’s $695 annual fee can be worth it for lounge access alone.

With this card, you'll be able to access almost 50 Admirals Clubs and more than 60 partner lounges worldwide when flying American or one of its Oneworld partners. Notably, this includes Alaska Airlines lounges in hubs like Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Oregon's Portland International Airport (PDX), San Francisco International Airport (SFO) and Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA).

You can bring in either your immediate family members (spouse or domestic partner and children under 18 years of age) or up to two guests. They don’t need to be on the same flight as you — just any American or Oneworld flight with a same-day boarding pass.

Related: The best lounge access credit cards to add to your wallet

The offers valuable perks when flying American, including priority check-in at business-class counters (where available) and priority boarding privileges (where available) for you and up to eight travelers on the same reservation.

You also get your first checked bag free on domestic itineraries with American Airlines, saving you at least $45 each time. (Note that this is only for domestic flights; I had to pay out of pocket when I traveled to Mexico, forgetting the restrictions of this perk.)

Additionally, you'll receive a statement credit of up to $120 for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck (once every four years). I suggest maximizing your credit by applying for Global Entry, as it includes TSA PreCheck anyway.

You'll also receive elite status with two partner programs:

Furthermore, the card includes travel protections, such as trip cancellation, trip interruption, trip delay, lost baggage protection and car rental insurance coverage.

And there are no foreign transaction fees, making this card a good option for international purchases.

Related: Which airline is now best if you don't want to pay bag fees?

If chasing AAdvantage elite status is important to you, the will help you achieve it. You’ll earn 1 Loyalty Point for every mile you earn from purchases.

Cardholders also earn 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points after reaching each of the following milestones in the same status qualification year:

Related: 8 methods that earned American AAdvantage Executive Platinum

The inKind dining credit is worth close to face value if you already eat at participating restaurants. Check the map for places you’d actually visit near home or on a trip.

I’ve had issues with the car rental credit, so I wouldn’t rely on it for value. Previously, a Budget rental in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico, was not coded correctly, and Citi wouldn’t manually apply the credit. Later, I completed another Budget rental in Ireland and waited the obligatory 10 weeks. Again, it didn't post, and again, Citi refused to apply a manual credit.

I don’t value the Lyft perk because you don’t get the $15 credit until after you’ve taken three (nondiscounted) rides in a month. Instead, I use my (see rates and fees) to earn 5 points per dollar spent, plus a $10 monthly in-app credit on Lyft purchases (through Sept. 30, 2027).

The inflight (and Admirals Club) credit is useful if you regularly buy onboard refreshments or snacks.

Related: Frequent Uber or Lyft user? These are the best credit cards for you

If you’re looking to supercharge your points earning across several programs, I'd suggest putting your spending on a card that earns transferable points. However, if you want to maximize your AAdvantage mile balance specifically, the will earn you:

AAdvantage miles are more valuable (at 1.45 cents each) than Delta SkyMiles and United MileagePlus miles (both 1.2 cents), according to TPG's November 2026 valuations.

I redeemed part of the welcome bonus I received on this card for a luxurious flight. I used 70,000 miles (plus $174 in taxes and fees) for a one-way business-class flight in Qatar Airways’ fantastic Qsuite from Doha to Houston.

Given that this flight retails for $3,910 one-way, I got a very high 5.3 cents per mile from this redemption, more than triple TPG’s valuation of AAdvantage miles.

Related: How to redeem American Airlines AAdvantage miles for maximum value

Finally, the is a great option if you want to extend Admirals Club access to friends and family affordably.

You can add up to three authorized users for $175 total (about $58 each), with each additional authorized user costing $175.

Every authorized user you add receives Admirals Club access (with a same-day boarding pass for an eligible flight) for themselves and up to two traveling companions. However, authorized users only get Admirals Club access, not a full Admirals Club membership.

Related: Everything you need to know about authorized credit card users

If you’d otherwise pay for a full Admirals Club membership, the card’s $695 annual fee is already less than the cost of joining directly.

The welcome bonus can add substantial value in your first year. At renewal, base your decision on how often you used the lounges and how much the credits and travel perks actually saved you.

If lounge access isn’t important to you, consider one of Citi’s lower-fee AAdvantage cards instead.

#6052. Trump banks on personal relationships moving Putin, Xi toward U.S. interests

Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. (Win McNamee/AFP via Getty Images)

That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.

“It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.

Trump and Putin then posed for the cameras with wide grins, again underscoring the U.S. president’s closeness with a world leader who has been partially shunned by the West since he launched a war with Ukraine in February 2022. Trump on Thursday also appeared several times alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping, who like Putin has been scorned by Republican and Democratic lawmakers for years.

“We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We've known each other for a long time. And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this — or, at least, start,” Trump told reporters as Putin beamed from a few feet away.

They later were joined by Xi for a group photo before sitting down at a round wooden table with a large arrangement of pink flowers in the center.

His interactions with and comments about Putin and Xi reflect Trump’s belief that his personal relationships can bend them toward U.S. interests. But that gambit clashed Thursday with his second term’s expiration date — the White House did not disclose any agreements reached during his various meetings with the two leaders, nor did Trump hold a press conference following the three-way session.

Both Putin and Xi are adept at playing the geopolitical long game. The 26 months left in Trump’s term is a relatively short amount of time compared to the duo that has been in power for a combined 56 years and will remain in place for the foreseeable future.

Indeed, even Trump acknowledged the first-ever meeting might not immediately yield much progress on its ostensible goal: paring each powers’ nuclear weapons arsenals.

“I must say, it's, quite frankly, a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them. It's very hard to give them up as the leader of a country,” Trump said as Putin and Xi looked on. “Something that's very difficult to say, because … it's the way life works.

“You know, you have thousands of weapons and you're supposed to give them up, and yet you have countries in addition to us, in much smaller numbers, but they have nuclear weapons, also,” he added. “So it's not an easy thing to do and give them up.”

Trump, who was convicted by a New York jury in a business records case and who saw a federal election interference case against him dismissed only because of his reelection, also appeared to join Putin’s resistance to international criminal justice entities that have alleged Putin has committed war crimes in Ukraine.

“In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” Trump said, a statement that would be almost unthinkable to hear from any other sitting U.S. president.

Other world leaders, including democratically elected ones, at two Pacific region economic summits in which Trump participated this week did not receive the kind of cordial and personal treatment from the U.S. side that Putin and Xi enjoyed.

And other world leaders and congressional Democrats this week expressed concern with Trump's closeness to the Russian and Chinese strongmen.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., on Thursday called the unprecedented summit a “historic embarrassment.” He criticized Trump for leaving the meeting without any apparent concrete commitments from Moscow or Beijing on a number of issues, including curbing Chinese espionage inside U.S. companies and ending the Ukraine conflict.

“This summit was nothing but a glorified photo op and a gift to Putin and Xi,” Schumer said.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote this Thursday on X, shortly after Trump’s warm greeting for the former KGB officer: “God, protect us from such friends.”

Nicolas Burns, a former senior U.S. diplomatic official under GOP and Democratic presidents, was critical of Trump’s meetings with Xi. He said it was “important” for U.S. and Chinese leaders to hold talks, but added: “We need stability in the relationship with China — but there’s a but.”

“The president seems to be following a detente policy with China, with very little substance. There’s a lot of pomp and circumstance, red carpets, a lot of nice words,” the former ambassador to China, NATO and Greece told “Morning Joe” on MS NOW. “Too friendly with Xi Jinping, who’s not going to be swayed by rosy words from President Trump.”

Even before Trump met with the Russian and Chinese leaders behind closed doors, Republican and Democratic lawmakers said they doubted very much would come from it.

“I want nuclear weapons to be reduced. As you know, China has been unwilling to even have a conversation with the United States about nuclear arms reduction until they reach a certain plateau in the number of weapons that they have,” House Armed Services Committee Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., told reporters Tuesday.

“I'm glad that they're willing to have the conversation. We do need a limit, as you know,” added Wittman, who lost his reelection bid earlier this month. “Right now, neither Russia nor China has a nuclear arms reduction treaty with the United States. It would be nice for us to actually have one.”

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., an Armed Services Committee member, wanted Trump to press Putin over Ukraine.

“Ukraine is defending itself from Putin's aggression, which this president should be opposing as well,” Blumenthal said Tuesday. “We are spending no money on Ukraine. Let's be very clear: Arms to Ukraine are purchased by Ukraine with financial support from Europe, not America. … Let's support Ukraine.”

On spending, Trump and administration officials have been pressing Senate Republicans to quickly pass another budget reconciliation measure with $350 billion more for the Defense Department. However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and other GOP senators have signaled in the last 24 hours that they had shelved the notion of another fast-track spending measure.

“You have to have a path forward. You've got to get on it, and you have to protect it, and that takes 50 in the Senate,” Thune told reporters Thursday. “And then you've got to get it through the House. As you probably saw yesterday, a lot of folks in the House were lobbing grenades at the Senate reconciliation bill and complaints about it not being offset, et cetera. So, you know, in my view at least, you want to have a path forward to success.”

John M. Donnelly and Jackie Wang contributed to this report.

#6051. 82% Of Americans Fly Once A Year Or Less—And Don’t Know The Rules

Last Thanksgiving, if you saw an open aisle seat on Southwest Airlines, you were welcome to take it. Do exactly what you learned a year ago and this Thanksgiving you’re the guy holding up the aisle because the passenger behind you has a boarding pass for your seat, and you’re getting scolded by a flight attendant. Travel rules change! Boarding at Southwest has changed! You might not even know you’re going to have to pay baggage fees if you don’t travel every year. every behavior you see in the airport makes perfect sense when you remember >50% of Americans fly less than once a year— Alexis (@aleozimok) November 25, 2026 The actual number is higher than this. In YouGov’s November 17–19 poll of 1,092 U.S. adult citizens, 34% said they fly less than once a year, 32% said never and 16% said once a year. That’s 66% who fly less than annually (including never) and 82% who fly once a year or less. Just 34% said they’d flown in the past 12 months and 65% said they hadn’t. Who’s Actually In The Seat Next To You? In 2015, then-American Airlines president Scott Kirby said 87% of American’s customers flew them just once in the previous year and generated about half their revenue. Kirby was explaining why American needed basic economy. For every 100 American adults who flew in 2017, 24 took just one trip, and all 100 averaged 5.3 trips apiece. In the 1970s and 1980s, roughly half the air trips Americans took were for business. Personal trips already accounted for about 70% before the pandemic and 74% in 2025. My line when business travel dried up during the pandemic was that “all airline passengers are Spirit Airlines passengers now.” Mask rules drove most of the reported trouble. Of 5,981 unruly passenger reports the Federal Aviation Administration received in 2021, 4,290 involved masks. But losing the regulars sprinkled through coach mattered too. What It Costs To Go See Family In 1977, before deregulation, 25% of U.S. adults flew that year and 63% had ever flown. I’ve written about how much less work it takes to buy a ticket. Between 1995 and 2025, the average domestic fare fell from $618 to $387 in 2025 dollars, a 37% drop excluding bag and seat fees. Fee-inclusive costs are down, too. In a separate YouGov poll earlier in November, 18% of people with family incomes under $50,000 had flown in the past year, compared with 66% at $100,000 or more. Family travel multiplies the cost of tickets across each person while driving costs are constant. AAA expects 72.9 million Americans to drive this Thanksgiving holiday and just under 6 million to fly domestically. Frequent Flyers Share The Same Frustrations With Once A Year Travelers YouGov also asked which things are a major problem with U.S. air travel. Price topped these everyday complaints for both groups. Called this a major problem   Fly less than annually(excludes “never”)   Fly at least annually High fares 64% 66% Delays and cancellations 42% 50% Extra or hidden fees 42% 49% Long security lines 35% 36% But The Travel Experience Is Very Different My status gets me on early enough to find space for my bag. When a flight cancels, I’m looking up alternatives on my phone while I’m in line for an agent. I still have days when I wonder how anybody who does this once a year manages to get where they’re going. A parent buys four tickets and gets a seat map full of prices. Will their eight-year-old sit next to a stranger if they don’t pay? American tells families on one reservation who can’t get seats together that they’re better off skipping seats for everybody than selecting the two they can see. The person who took their laptop out at security on the way there and left it in the bag on the way home may have followed instructions both times. It depends on the scanner in their lane. Say you book a 40 minute connection. You don’t know whether that’s a good idea or not, and may not even know or understand the connecting time, just the departure and arrival times. The airline ends boarding 15 minutes before departure. You’ve got 25 minutes even if you’re on time, some of which you’ll spend getting off the first plane. And if your regional jet on the first segment valet tags your bag, you’re waiting for it on the jet bridge, too. I wound up on Southwest’s first day of assigned seating because American went through three itineraries trying to get me to Washington and I finally bought a ticket to Baltimore. At the gate, Southwest called Group 3 to line up under a sign that still said Group 1. Where, exactly, was the passenger who stopped to read the sign supposed to stand? I’m home this Thanksgiving. I traveled the week before and will travel again the week after. I like to avoid ‘amateur day’. And when I do travel I try to go where other people aren’t. My favorite Thanksgiving trip was Chennai (I wanted to have Thanksgiving dinner with Indians), and I had to explain to CBP on arrival back in the states that we’d done that because it was cheaper booking Lufthansa first class (on points) than going to visit my wife’s family. The basic, occasional flyer should get the most miles, not the rich guy that already has lots of miles. Tax the rich. Tax those miles, like 50% (50% of your annual miles taken by the IRS and given to the poor, then a wealth tax on your balance). AOC must be President in 2028. Pay your fair share.

@KIRK: “I cannot understand why I have to remove my belt, even as a Trusted Traveler, while keeping my watch that contains 10x the metal.”

Kirk, I realized almost two years ago that my belt is best kept on, while I remove my watch, and stuff it with container containing the carry-ons. First of all, it takes less time to put on my watch than my belt. Second, I have yet to confront a screening station in major European airports that catch my belt. OK, the trick is don’t try it with a Texas style belt buckle. I have a web belt, with link that is small amount of metal. Oh, and I never try to go through a European screening station that makes me show my belt is off before going through.

I used to fly alot for business. I dread even getting on planes now.

Between the extra fees for just about everything, FAs for the most part hating their jobs, people dressed liked their headed for the bedroom and not a trip, planes leave and arrive late, FF miles pretty much worth nothing, CEOs complaining they need to add more premium seats to gouge their customers more, its no wonder why people do not fly, I pretty much drive if under 750 miles, for the 12h of driving half that time would be spent getting to the airport, waiting for flight, delays, then if lucky landing on time, costing 5x what it costs to drive to the same location and much less hassle.

Until the customers decide they are not going to put up with these issues they will continue.

Airlines could absolutely care less, they are more concerned pushing their CC ads than operating a airline.

People are oblivious and stupid. Simple as that

Surprised OPM flying is still that much of a percentage. Good to see it going down every year.

We have flown quite a bit (vacations) and want to feel as safe as possible. So, whatever the airlines want to do is fine with me.

We avoid busy times (lThanksgiving, Christmas, New Year’s, etc.). Unless we can fly out a week before the holiday and return a week or so after it, we would not fly during those times.

In general, we avoid international flights from late April – mid-October. The airports major cities around the world can be packed. We do not fly U.S.-based airlines. With the many articles this great site has posted, we agree with every less than positive things that they have shared. There are some great airlines out (that care about their passengers) there, but sadly. we prefer not to fly American, Delta or United. We will do an occasional short flight on Alaska.

This all reminds me of the comedy at Christmas Mass in 1970…

Basically, there was a BIG overhaul in 1970. The regulars knew the new process, but your Christmas/Easter attendees…didn’t. So you had e.g. half of the congregation kneeling at the wrong time.

#6049. Why Entitlement Reform Is Easier Abroad Than in America

Privatization, among other proposals, requires a particular set of conditions that the U.S. seems to lack.

Pedestrians walk along a street in the Old Town of Stockholm, Sweden, October 17, 2024.

Senator Ron Johnson’s proposal to sustain Social Security payouts even after the projected depletion of its funds in 2032 has attracted new interest in entitlement reform. Fifteen years ago, Paul Ryan became the victim of character assassination over his plans for modest entitlement reforms. In 2005, George W. Bush attempted to reform Social Security, yet his efforts were in vain.

Johnson’s proposal is poorly conceived, even by the low standards of populists. It would set the United States on course to default even faster than it currently is.

John Gustavsson is a writer from Sweden and holds a doctorate in economics. He is Senior Editor of Nation & Citizenship at Restoring the West and a former adviser to the Sweden Democrats in the European Parliament.

#6048. Why Austin’s Airport Is Packed While Others Feel Empty—It’s Not Just About Number Of Gates

Austin’s airport can be so crowded that you can barely move through the terminal. Passengers spill out of gate areas into the corridor, where everyone else is trying to get somewhere. Then you visit another airport, walk through an almost empty concourse, and wonder why we’re spending billions building more gates there. Adam Nathan put together an interesting comparison of passengers per airport gate. Austin comes out at 637,000, Seattle at 592,000, and Washington Dulles at just 212,000. There’s a lot to learn from this, but the gates aren’t interchangeable, and neither are the conclusions you can draw from them. For instance, Nathan flags that Austin reduced its gates this year. That’s true – it closed its South Terminal with three gates – but those gates handled just 3.6% of the airport’s passengers last year. And Charlotte’s large number of regional jet gates makes average passengers per gate look much more reasonable – when outside of that E concourse, the place is a dense mess. Adam Nathan’s airport passengers-per-gate comparison Austin Closed Gates, But They Were Largely Immaterial Nathan’s slide specifically refers to the South Terminal closure, and that’s fair. Austin closed the separate Allegiant and Frontier facility on March 31, moving those airlines into the main terminal April 1. The site is needed for new taxiways and the airport’s construction program to grow. However, the airport’s 2025 passenger totals show how lightly those three gates were compared with the main terminal: 2025 traffic South Terminal Main terminal Passengers 771,354 20,895,498 Share of airport passengers 3.6% 96.4% Gates 3 gates 34 gates Annual passengers per gate 257,118 614,573 Frontier carried 553,311 passengers and Allegiant 218,043. Each South Terminal gate handled about 42% as many passengers as a main terminal gate. Moving those flights into an already crowded building wasn’t ideal, but losing three of 37 nominal gates didn’t mean losing 8% of the airport’s passenger capacity. There are actually three different construction stories here: The South Terminal’s three boarding positions went away to make room for work on the airfield. The three new gates at the west end of the main terminal were built to offset gates being taken out for expansion, including the underground connection to the new concourse. Austin is building Concourse M, a separate six-gate facility reached by bus, in addition to the new 26-gate Concourse B. Those six gates will help maintain operations during construction. West Gate Expansion So commenters suggesting “reopen the closed gates” aren’t familiar with the airport. This is space being used to build out the airport. Terminal width matters, too. Boarding lines, arriving passengers and people walking to other gates all compete for the same floor space. Austin’s master plan identified 89,600 square feet of circulation corridors after the 2019 east expansion, compared with a modeled requirement of 125,350 square feet at 16 million annual passengers and 173,650 at 22 million (almost twice the space). Atlanta’s Concourse D project is a good contrast because it widens the building from 60 feet to 99 feet, increases the depth of gate waiting areas from 20 feet to 35 feet, and reduces the gate count from 40 to 34, with all remaining gates accommodating larger aircraft. Hold passenger traffic constant and passengers per gate rises nearly 18% simply because the denominator shrank—even as passengers get more space. An airport can have fewer gates, higher passengers per gate, and a substantially less density for a better experience walking through the terminal. Charlotte Shows Why A Low Passenger Count Doesn’t Mean An Idle Gate Charlotte comes out at about 432,000 passengers per gate, well below Austin. If you’ve tried to get through its piers during a connecting bank, that doesn’t describe the experience very well. The airport has an enormous regional operation. It has 45 gates on Concourse E and that concourse handles more aircraft operations per gate than the others. A gate turning regional jets all day can move fewer passengers than a gate with fewer departures on larger aircraft. Charlotte’s planned expansion adds gates and improves aircraft circulation without widening the existing B and C corridors. The ends of the piers at Washington National has the same problem. Why Bigger Planes Don’t Produce The Highest Numbers Flights per gate is a more direct starting point for judging how hard an airline is using its gates. But passengers per gate adds size of aircraft, carrying more people without adding departures. So the surprising part of this comparison is how dense airports with relatively little widebody flying are. But narrowbody gates tend to turn over more frequently. Long haul aircraft often need longer turns, and their schedules are constrained by overnight flying, arrival times and connections at the other end. An international gate can sit empty for hours. And you can’t just replace every regional jet with an Airbus A321. Some routes can’t support it, some passengers value frequency, and some gates and alleyways can’t accommodate it. Upgauging also puts more people into the waiting area for each departure. Dulles Already Has Room To Grow? Washington Dulles is the most provocative comparison because it looks so lightly used while pursuing a roughly $20 billion reconstruction program. I’ve criticized the economics of that plan. First, the slide labels Dulles as having 137 jetbridge gates, excluding 16 remote stands. The airport authority’s 2025 bond documents tell a different story: 121 aircraft parking positions, including regional hardstands without boarding bridges, and excluding 16 remote hardstands. Adding those remote positions produces 137. Since that inventory Concourse E opening November 10 with 14 new gates. Its flexible layout can accommodate a large widebody in space used by two smaller narrowbodies. The number of usable gates actually depends on which planes park there. The same bond documents show 7.3 scheduled departures per gate per day at National versus 3.4 at Dulles for June 2025. The question is how much of that unused time airlines can profitably use. A quiet international concourse at one hour doesn’t establish spare gates where United needs them at another. Nor does it address the 1980s temporary midfield C/D concourse. Replacing outdated buildings, improving train access and getting passengers out of mobile lounges can be worthwhile even without a shortage of gates, although the proposed cost of the project would drive up expenses so much that Dulles could never support a low cost carrier flight again. Analyzing Additional Airports Seattle is working its gates hard. The Port of Seattle’s master plan includes a second terminal with 19 additional gates. Dallas Love Field Is Noticeably Absent This analysis set a threshold of airports with at least 25 gates, so a 20-gate airport serving around 17 million passengers per year gets excluded. That’s roughly 850,000 passengers per gate. Austin leads this sample, not the country. Congress agreed to remove and legally cap gates at the airport as a way of entrenching incumbent positions of American Airlines (limiting competition to their DFW operation) and Southwest (limiting the ability to compete at Love Field) – gates were actually destroyed, in fact six became a Lincoln dealership. Former hubs naturally have leftover capacity. Cincinnati and Pittsburgh were built to handle connecting operations that shrank. Pittsburgh has a reduced 53-gate footprint, rather than its old 75-gate layout. Detroit is lighter use than Atlanta, but that doesn’t mean flights can be re-routed to a different hub. Local demand, fares, geography and the connections already available determine whether shifting a flight makes more or less money. Similarly, San Antonio isn’t interchangeable with Austin, Ontario with Los Angeles, or San Jose with San Francisco. It’s Time To Build—But Users Have To Pay Gates are only one constraint. Runways, weather and available airspace determine how many planes can arrive and depart. Nearby airports may need the same airspace. Taxiway bottlenecks can keep a landed plane from reaching an empty gate. Security, baggage systems, customs and curbs can each run out of capacity too. Austin needs more room for people. Charlotte needs people and airplanes to move through the airport better, wider concourses (and higher ceilings!). Dulles needs to… not do the thing that was announced. And none of this explains why growing airports with millions of customers should get taxpayer money. Airports can issue revenue bonds, with debt repaid through airline rents and charges, concessions, parking and passenger fees. The recent infrastructure law’s airport money came from the Treasury’s general fund. That’s stupid. I’ve written about using air traffic control failures to sell billions more in terminal subsidies. A new terminal doesn’t fix a failed air traffic control system. And a project justified by strong future passenger demand should be able to borrow against the revenue those passengers will generate. If the resulting airport charges would drive that traffic away, that’s a reason to reconsider the project’s cost not to ask to take moeny away from non-traveling citizens. Analyzing Additional Airports Seattle is working its gates hard. The Port of Seattle’s master plan includes a second terminal with 19 additional gates. Dallas Love Field Is Noticeably Absent This analysis set a threshold of airports with at least 25 gates, so a 20-gate airport serving around 17 million passengers per year gets excluded. That’s roughly 850,000 passengers per gate. Austin leads this sample, not the country. Congress agreed to remove and legally cap gates at the airport as a way of entrenching incumbent positions of American Airlines (limiting competition to their DFW operation) and Southwest (limiting the ability to compete at Love Field) – gates were actually destroyed, in fact six became a Lincoln dealership. Former hubs naturally have leftover capacity. Cincinnati and Pittsburgh were built to handle connecting operations that shrank. Pittsburgh has a reduced 53-gate footprint, rather than its old 75-gate layout. Detroit is lighter use than Atlanta, but that doesn’t mean flights can be re-routed to a different hub. Local demand, fares, geography and the connections already available determine whether shifting a flight makes more or less money. Similarly, San Antonio isn’t interchangeable with Austin, Ontario with Los Angeles, or San Jose with San Francisco. It’s Time To Build—But Users Have To Pay Gates are only one constraint. Runways, weather and available airspace determine how many planes can arrive and depart. Nearby airports may need the same airspace. Taxiway bottlenecks can keep a landed plane from reaching an empty gate. Security, baggage systems, customs and curbs can each run out of capacity too. Austin needs more room for people. Charlotte needs people and airplanes to move through the airport better, wider concourses (and higher ceilings!). Dulles needs to… not do the thing that was announced. And none of this explains why growing airports with millions of customers should get taxpayer money. Airports can issue revenue bonds, with debt repaid through airline rents and charges, concessions, parking and passenger fees. The recent infrastructure law’s airport money came from the Treasury’s general fund. That’s stupid. I’ve written about using air traffic control failures to sell billions more in terminal subsidies. A new terminal doesn’t fix a failed air traffic control system. And a project justified by strong future passenger demand should be able to borrow against the revenue those passengers will generate. If the resulting airport charges would drive that traffic away, that’s a reason to reconsider the project’s cost not to ask to take moeny away from non-traveling citizens. Flights per gate is a more direct starting point for judging how hard an airline is using its gates. But passengers per gate adds size of aircraft, carrying more people without adding departures. So the surprising part of this comparison is how dense airports with relatively little widebody flying are. But narrowbody gates tend to turn over more frequently.

Long haul aircraft often need longer turns, and their schedules are constrained by overnight flying, arrival times and connections at the other end. An international gate can sit empty for hours.

And you can’t just replace every regional jet with an Airbus A321. Some routes can’t support it, some passengers value frequency, and some gates and alleyways can’t accommodate it. Upgauging also puts more people into the waiting area for each departure.

Airports can issue revenue bonds, with debt repaid through airline rents and charges, concessions, parking and passenger fees. The recent infrastructure law’s airport money came from the Treasury’s general fund. That’s stupid.

I’ve written about using air traffic control failures to sell billions more in terminal subsidies. A new terminal doesn’t fix a failed air traffic control system. And a project justified by strong future passenger demand should be able to borrow against the revenue those passengers will generate. If the resulting airport charges would drive that traffic away, that’s a reason to reconsider the project’s cost not to ask to take moeny away from non-traveling citizens.

#6047. The House has a new lame-duck challenge: Attendance

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S. Capitol on Thursday, said attendance is 'a great frustration.' (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a new challenge: Attendance.

Thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break. This, a day after House GOP leadership pulled a procedural rule vote when it was clear the vote might fall short because of GOP no-shows – and then canceled a planned Friday voting session.

The House has just 12 scheduled voting days left in the 119th Congress. And leaders who have at times struggled to ensure sufficient support for their agenda from the narrow majority now say they will work to make sure cases of senioritis don’t compound the problem, as both returning and nonreturning members have been part of the problem.

"Attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told reporters Thursday. “We'll be addressing that with members."

“We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can't do that unless people are present at work, so that's our challenge,” Johnson continued.

Of 13 roll call votes in the House since the midterms, all but one has had a double-digit number of no-shows; for five of the 13, more than 30 members did not vote. The average number of members not voting has more than doubled since the midterm elections, compared to the final 13 roll call votes beforehand.

Johnson has just a few more weeks before he steps out of the spotlight and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, takes over the GOP conference as minority leader. But his members are still counting on him to get them back to Washington.

“I think there's going to be some serious conversations over the phone, behind the scenes over the weekend,” Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas, said. “We all took an oath of office. We have a sworn duty to be here. We're still being paid to be here, and you have to show up and do the job.”

And it's not just leadership that's frustrated with their missing colleagues this week.

“There is, no question,” Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., who narrowly won reelection, responded when asked whether there was frustration in the caucus over members' absences.

“I don't know what you do with people that don't understand the concept of duty,” Harrigan said. “I mean, look, you signed up for a two-year term. You execute your two-year term, no matter what happens along the way politically. You have an obligation both to your constituency and to your country to be here, so the fact that they're not self-motivated to be here, I don't think that there's really much that you can do.”

Attendance has also been a bipartisan problem. A group of House Democrats, including members of leadership, faced harsh criticism from party activists for not returning to the chamber in time for a vote related to a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

While Republican leadership grapples with the fallout from the party’s election losses earlier this month, lawmakers still face a slew of legislative items as Congress looks ahead to the holidays and a government shutdown looms.

Many Republicans want to see a party-line defense spending bill cross the finish line, while the NDAA remains in treacherous territory and Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act has been dark for months.

However, the frustration does not lie solely with absent House members.

“The Senate needs to do their job,” Rep. John McGuire, R-Va., said. “I know we had a hard time in the midterms. History doesn't favor the party in the president's office, but we passed the Save America Act five times here. It goes over there, nothing. We've got a farm bill, nothing. We got an NDAA. We got so many things.”

The Norway-based long-haul budget airline said in a statement early Thursday that all flights were suspended "pending clarification as to whether a viable financing solution can be established."

"There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found," Norse added.

The confirmation followed the cancellation of all Norse flights late on Wednesday, the flight tracking website FlightRadar24 shows.

Pakistan International Airlines, which contracts Norse to operate select flights, said Wednesday evening on X that Norse had suspended operations "without prior notice."

Norse flew just one U.S. route at the time of its shut down: Orlando International Airport (MCO) to London's Gatwick Airport (LGW), schedules from aviation analytics firm Cirium show.

During the prime summer months, Norse also seasonally flew from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Athens International Airport (ATH) in Greece, LGW and Rome's Fiumicino Leonardo da Vinci International Airport (FCO).

At its peak in 2024, Norse served five U.S. destinations, including Las Vegas's Harry Reid International Airport (LAS), Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Miami International Airport (MIA), from gateways in Europe.

The collapse of Norse comes at a challenging time for airlines. Jet fuel is at historic highs, spiking after Iran war and other conflicts. Geopolitical tensions have closed significant swaths of airspace, including Russia and significant portions of the Middle East. And, high interest rates have pushed the cost of capital for any business to the highest levels in years.

Norse warned on Wednesday that its financial situation was "critical" and said its continued operation was "dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs."

Luis Gallego, the CEO of International Airlines Group that owns British Airways and Iberia, told the Financial Times in October that smaller airlines would struggle this winter due to the those financial headwinds.

Norse was one of the last airlines trying to make long-haul, low-cost work between the U.S. and Europe. Play Airlines, which attempted the same strategy via a connecting hub at Iceland's Keflavik International Airport (KEF), shut down in September 2025. And both Norse and Play were formed following the retrenchment and collapse of previous attempts; Norse from Norwegian Air's withdrawal from the market in 2021 and Play from the ashes of WOW Air that shut down in 2019.

Only independent French Bee and the budget arms of the larger European airline groups, including Discover, Level and Edelweiss Air, continue to offer lower-cost transatlantic flights.

Story updated with Norse confirmation of its shut down.

#6045. Why I’m Especially Grateful This Year

Every year on Thanksgiving I offer a reflection on the good fortune I’ve had in travel, mile and points and to be able to interact with so many wonderful readers over the course of the year. And as difficult as the past several years have been for so many (it was in many ways a dumpster fire, and we thought nothing could match 2020 and 2021) – and as tough as the coming year may be, I’m even more thankful than I’ve ever been. I’m thankful for my family’s health. I’m also thankful for the way I’ve been able to grow through challenging times. The growth I’m most pleased with is as a dad. And I’m extremely grateful for my readers. I get to interact with brilliant and thoughtful people through this blog. Sure, the comments on posts often descend into madness (it’s the internet, and I’ve been forced to delete more comments than I used to and still don’t delete nearly enough) but I’ve gotten to know so many people. I’ve been practicing at it since the start of this blog in 2002, and really going back to my BBS days in the mid-1980s. If there’s one thing I think I have to offer writing for nearly 25 years here, it’s a memory. I remember when things have happened before, been promised before, and how they worked out. And I try to offer some of that context to the day’s developments. I remember most of the people I’ve had the good fortune to get to know since I began in miles and points, and it’s sustained me throughout the years and throughout both good times and difficult times. I thought I’d take the Thanksgiving opportunity to express my thankfulness for each of you that reads my blog and interacts with me throughout the year. I’ve said this many times before but I really do consider myself one of the luckiest people, and certainly much more fortunate than I could have ever imagined. I’m deeply shy, which some people can find off-putting when I meet them (thinking that by not being outgoing with them I must not be interested, or somehow aloof). I’ve talked about my being a bit on the spectrum. The written form has allowed me to connect so well with many. And I’m grateful for those connections, although I don’t share nearly as much detail that’s personal many of you know me very well from my writing — certainly my opinions, my quirks, my sense of humor. This hobby has enriched my life in so many ways, including less obvious ones. In many ways this is still the same personal blog I first started, I write and share what is interesting to me. I usually write as though no one is reading, and I’m shocked when I get a call from an airline’s or hotel’s communications shop because a C-level executive is unhappy with something I’ve said. (Or when one of those C-level folks comments here or drops me a note, as happens so often too.) Now there are a whole lot more people reading the blog than when I started and I appreciate each and every one of you. Even the ones that are trying to insult me! I don’t always have as thick a skin as I should, but I try my best, because each and every reader has something to teach me or challenge me. And the positive feedback touches me deeply. So thank you. Thank you. I look forward to continuing to share this journey together, and I appreciate this opportunity to reflect — and to acknowledge. #6043. Your Flight Takes 10 Minutes Longer Than It Used To—And That’s A Luxury Worth Paying For

Flying takes longer than it used to – and, retirement of the Concorde notwithstanding, it’s not because planes aren’t as fast. There are more than twice as many commercial flights as there were at the time of airline deregulation, and air traffic control hasn’t been upgraded very much. There’s congested airspace and also congested airports. We also don’t build major new airports – the last one was Denver, 30 years ago. (Austin’s new 1999 airport was a converted military base, and there were others like that in the 90s.) By one estimate flights have gotten 8% longer. That means a two hour flight is 10 minutes longer than it used to be. And the single biggest factor is often tagged as strategic padding of schedules. Airlines are often chided for ‘schedule padding’ – claiming that flights take longer than they should. Often, this just reflects the reality of telling customers when they can expect to arrive – although there’s greater variance than there used to be, which isn’t great for having a gate available when you land early. Airlines do not like this! Though real airfares (even including fees) are down significantly since deregulation, longer flight times are expensive for staffing, fuel and efficient use of $50 – $100 million planes. And longer travel times historically disadvantaged an airline trying to sell tickets, because it meant their flights were displayed lower on the screen that travel agents and later passengers directly saw – which translates into fewer sales. A new study finds that airlines with more “padding” in their schedules tend to charge higher fares. That sounds like passengers paying more for a slower trip. But those extra minutes can also let United hold your plane with ConnectionSaver and get you home that night, and still arrive on time. It also means fewer delays and missed connections. So that ‘premium’ is actually a more valuable product to many consumers. I’ve argued for years that schedule padding often isn’t really padding. Sometimes an airline is finally admitting how long the trip takes. Customers can plan around an honest arrival time. There’s a new chapter by Embry-Riddle’s Jules Yimga, “The Price of Punctuality,” in The Economics of Airline Pricing. It combines 2019 flight time data with the government’s ticket price survey. It compares schedules against different percentiles of actual flight times, then examines how the resulting measures relate to fares. More padding is associated with higher fares, especially when the comparison uses the faster end of actual flight times. The relationship appears in both competitive and concentrated markets. The abstract itself allows that reliability could be a service customers value. (Interestingly, Yimga’s earlier research on schedule padding attributed higher prices primarily to higher costs rather than higher margins.) Even scheduling to the median arrival time means roughly half of trips take longer than published. It’s often better for a customer if an airline underpromises and overdelivers – or arrives ‘on time’ rather than late. Predictability matters when you’re scheduling connections or trying to arrive in time for a meeting. An airline that leaves little buffer is going to appear less reliable, so customers book earlier flights and longer layovers or even fly in the night before an important meeting. Then the buffer hasn’t disappeared, it just changes who’s scheduling it. That’s why I argued American’s investment in more realistic schedules could pay for itself. Avoiding rebooking, mishandled bags and aircraft and crews getting out of position can justify spending running an on-time schedule even before a customer chooses the airline again because the trip met expectations. American’s Dallas – Fort Worth overhaul that began in April combined longer scheduled flight times with a move from nine daily banks of flights to thirteen. Spreading flights into smaller waves reduced congestion that made some of the extra time unnecessary. One plane waiting for a gate can delay its passengers, its next departure, and other flights whose crews are stuck on board. Giving the operation room to recover can prevent that problem from cascading. In January, I covered American network planning chief Brian Znotins explaining that bookings for 40–54 minute connections at DFW were 4% below what its model predicted. Bookings for 55–84 minute connections were 8% above prediction. Customers have actually started choosing longer connections because they feel more reliable and less likely to leave them stranded. When I covered United’s media day in 2019, Greg Hart explained that 25% of its flights each day were expected to arrive ten minutes early. That gave United room to use ConnectionSaver to hold flights for connecting passengers and still arrive on time. Of course there’s such a thing as too much slack. An airline can improve its reported punctuality by moving the promised arrival later without getting anyone anywhere sooner. Excessively long connections waste customer time. And routinely beating an absurdly generous schedule doesn’t make an operation excellent. Not all padding is something customers will pay a premium for. YimgaUnited AirlinesAirline deregulationAirline IndustryBrian ZnotinsConcordeCustomer experienceDallas Fort Worth International AirportDenver+7 more More From View from the Wing

#6042. Appeals court stands by LaMonica McIver ruling

Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.

The decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark. McIver has challenged the charges, arguing that her visit fell under the “speech or debate” immunity she has as a member of Congress because she was there to inspect detention conditions.

In a statement McIver said she and her attorneys were looking at “every possible option” in response to the appeals court ruling. Her statement invoked the Trump administration’s threats to treat oversight efforts as criminal conduct and said “we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”

“Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver said in her statement.

Following Thursday’s decision on rehearing, McIver could next ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case.

The August majority opinion from Judge Cindy Chung, which Thursday’s decision leaves in place, said that two of the three charges against McIver did not fall under the immunity, which is limited to legislative acts. The majority sent the third charge back to the lower court for another ruling.

“We have considered the ‘nature’ of the charged conduct and concluded it is unambiguously non-legislative,” the judge wrote.

Separately, Judge Thomas Ambro partially dissented to offer a different approach to the case. Ambro would have required the trial judge to more closely examine the exact conduct McIver was charged with, as well as to examine whether the Trump administration targeted her because of her political views.

“I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter — not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote.

Ambro did not vote on whether the full 3rd Circuit should rehear the case. Three judges voted to have the full 3rd Circuit hear McIver’s case, and Judge Emil Bove, a former Trump administration official and former personal attorney for the president, did not participate in the vote.

The criminal case started shortly after the Delaney Hall visit in May 2025, as prosecutors alleged that McIver assaulted federal agents during a scuffle around Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Officials arrested Baraka that day and charged him with trespassing, but later dropped those charges

Court filings in the case alleged that McIver struck agents during the confrontation. McIver has argued that she was effectively being charged for doing her job and federal agents were interfering with her attempts to inspect the facility.

Earlier this year, Judge Jamel K. Semper of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey disagreed and ruled that the case could move forward.
