#5966. Trump signs bill to halt penny production

President Donald Trump conducts a news conference in the White House briefing room on Friday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The penny is officially history under a bill President Donald Trump signed into law Friday that codifies the end of production of the one-cent piece.

The copper-plated coin is mostly composed of zinc and costs far more to produce than it's worth, prompting members of Congress at least since 1989 to consider killing it as an easy cost-saving measure for the federal government.

“Washington has a spending problem, and it shows up in places big and small,” the bill's sponsor, Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., said Friday in a statement released by the office of House Financial Services Chairman French Hill, R-Ark. “If the federal government is spending nearly four cents to make a penny worth one cent, something is broken.”

Hill said in the statement that the bill also provides "clear legislative guidance for retailers, financial institutions, and consumers," referring to the measure's requirements that cash transactions not settled with exact change will be rounded to the nearest nickel.

The U.S. Mint stopped producing pennies a year ago under an executive order. Pennies already in circulation will still be legal tender, and the Mint may still issue special collectors editions. The legislation, named the Common Cents Act, also sets composition specifications for nickels.

Like a well-traveled coin, the bill itself took a winding road to the White House. The House originally passed a similar bill in July and the Senate passed its version by unanimous consent on Aug. 7.

But the Senate added a section that would require the Treasury secretary to notify Congress before discontinuing other coins. That sent the bill back to the House with a Senate number.

As the sponsor of the original measure, McClain insisted that the legislation have a House bill number. So, she reintroduced the revised Senate version, and the House voted on it on Sept. 14. The Senate passed it once again by unanimous consent on Sept. 28, sending it to the president's desk.

Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., said the bill “modernizes our currency system and most importantly gives families and businesses clear rules for everyday cash transactions.”

#5965. Goodbye from Salon

Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

Itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

Foreign airlines are returning to Dubai in stages while Riyadh stays largely cut off, and the two recoveries run on different clocks. Dubai's constraint is regulatory: EASA's conflict-zone bulletins for the Middle East expire Jan. 31, and carriers including British Airways, Air France, Lufthansa's Munich service, and Eurowings from Berlin have already resumed, though Dubai International was served by 57 airlines in mid-November against 108 a year earlier. Riyadh's constraint is Houthi strikes that closed King Khalid International in October, when 86% of scheduled flights were canceled, and that have continued since, including hits on the Aramco tower on Nov. 8 and the Public Investment Fund tower on Nov. 19 and 24. No foreign long-haul carrier plans to fly to Riyadh before January, and Delta and Singapore Airlines have pushed launches to March. The hotel data shows the split: Riyadh occupancy fell to 34.3% in October from 69% a year earlier, while Dubai fell to 68.4% from 84.9%, according to CoStar's STR. Linus Bauer of BAA & Partners said airlines can manage elevated risk but struggle with sustained unpredictability, and that four to six weeks of uninterrupted stability could bring some carriers back in phases, with conservative long-haul operators needing two to three months.

#5962. GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx ousted in rematch

Rep. Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., presides over a House Rules Committee hearing in the Capitol on July 20. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

After more than two decades in office and weeks of ballot counting, North Carolina Republican Virginia Foxx, chair of the powerful House Rules Committee, has conceded defeat in her reelection bid.

Retired journalist Chuck Hubbard bested Foxx in a nail-biter of a race — he was up by about 0.1 percentage point, or 330 votes out of nearly 300,000 ballots cast when the Associated Press called the race on Sunday.

Foxx lost in a rematch against Hubbard, whom she beat by almost 20 points in their 2024 race.

“Earlier today I spoke with Congresswoman Virginia Foxx who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process,” Hubbard wrote in a Facebook post Sunday. “Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices.”

Foxx was swept from office as part of a midterm surge that will put Democrats in charge of the House with the largest majority for either party since 1993 at 258 seats and counting; two other races where the Democrat is currently leading have yet to be called.

A 260-seat majority would be the largest since 1989, according to the House historian's office.

Until recently, Foxx's district was solidly Republican and had not elected a Democrat since 1992.

It took nearly three weeks for the race to be called as provisional and mail-in ballots were added to the total. Three days after the election, as the final votes were tallied, Foxx requested the presence of nonpartisan election observers to monitor the counting process.

“Election integrity is not a mere suggestion — it is the keystone of free and fair elections that have always guided the course of our nation throughout history,” she wrote in a Facebook post at the time. “The counting process for the 5th District election has not halted. The count is ongoing in accordance with North Carolina state law.”

On November 16, with the race still officially uncalled, Foxx requested a full recount; however the recount confirmed that Hubbard had won.

“After a hard-fought and thorough election process, the voters of the Fifth Congressional District exercised their constitutional rights and made their voices heard,” Foxx said in a statement Sunday. “While I am saddened that I did not emerge victorious in this election, I continue to have great faith in our nation, our state and the people of North Carolina.”

As the recount was underway, Foxx filed for reelection in 2028, at which point she will be 85 years old.

In her 11 terms in the House, Foxx built a reputation as a sharp-witted social conservative, unafraid to offer unfiltered views. She has also been a key ally of President Donald Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.

Foxx is the first Republican woman to serve as chair of the Rules Committee. The late Rep. Louise M. Slaughter, D-N.Y., who led the panel from 2007 to 2011, was the only other woman to hold the gavel.

On the Rules panel, Foxx has been a workhorse for House Republicans’ agenda, often working late into the night and amending rules text on the fly in response to the high-stakes intraparty negotiations that have dominated Johnson’s speakership.

Foxx’s acerbic wit is well matched on Rules by the panel’s ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. The two often spar over policy and procedure alike.

Foxx is the only woman chairing a House committee in the 119th Congress. According to the House historian's office, the last time the House had no female committee chairs was from 2005 to 2007, during the 109th Congress.

Next in line in seniority to become the top Rules Republican is Minnesota Rep. Michelle Fischbach, who's expressed interest previously and got some practice sitting in for Foxx during committee hearings and managing rules on the floor when Foxx was away.

Before her Rules role, Foxx was the top Republican on the House Education and Workforce panel from 2017 to the end of 2024.

She has been a vocal supporter of conservative efforts to abolish the Education Department and said she would do so “in a heartbeat." She points to the 10th Amendment, which says that the powers not delegated in the Constitution to the federal government are reserved for the states and individuals. Education, she asserts, is therefore not a federal responsibility.

As a former school board member for 12 years, she says that the government telling school boards how to work is “not the way this country should be operating.”

A devout Catholic, Foxx is well known on Capitol Hill for her religious faith, attending weekly prayer meetings and Bible study sessions. She starts each day “with a prayer for wisdom and strength to do God’s will,” she told CQ Roll Call.

In 2016, she published “God is in the House: Congressional Testimonies of Faith,” a book of essays on faith and legislative work by members of Congress.

The Rules Committee has experienced relatively high turnover in recent years. Foxx’s predecessor, former-Rep. Michael Burgess, R-Texas, succeeded Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., in April 2024 after Cole departed to chair the Appropriations Committee. Cole himself only held the position for just over a year after taking over for McGovern, though he became the panel's top Republican in 2019.

She served in the state Senate from 1995 to 2004, and when Republican Richard M. Burr left his House seat to run for the Senate in 2004, Foxx entered the race to succeed him. She prevailed over seven other Republicans in the primary and went on to defeat her Democratic challenger in November. At 61, she was one of the oldest members of the freshman class of 2005.

North Carolina’s 5th District encompasses much of northwestern North Carolina, including the Blue Ridge Mountains and the foothills of the Piedmont.

#5961. Paying People to Quit Smoking Is a Real Drag

Taxpayers shouldn’t be footing the bill to encourage virtue or healthy behavior in others.

To relieve stress nowadays, modern high school students may fire up a game of Grand Theft Auto VI or bring a puppy dog to class. But in the recent past, American high schools would set aside a patch of blacktop where tense teenagers could fire up a couple of heaters between classes, presumably so nobody would show up to fourth-period algebra in nicotine withdrawal. Understanding that there was nothing they could do to prevent kids from lighting up, schools in the 1970s and 1980s frequently had smoking courts. The calculation was that they might as well keep the students in their line of sight.

In those days, airplane passengers could light up while in flight, swathing 150 strangers inside a metal tube at 30,000 feet in Pall Mall smoke from Milwaukee to Phoenix.

Christian Schneider is a National Review contributor and writes the Anti-Knowledge newsletter. He is a co-host of the podcast Wasn't That Special: 50 Years of SNL.

On “Paying People to Quit Smoking Is a Real Drag”

To relieve stress nowadays, modern high school students may fire up a game of Grand Theft Auto VI or bring a puppy dog to class. But in the recent past, American high schools would set aside a patch of blacktop where tense teenagers could fire up a couple of heaters between classes, presumably so nobody would show up to fourth-period algebra in nicotine withdrawal. Understanding that there was nothing they could do to prevent kids from lighting up, schools in the 1970s and 1980s frequently had smoking courts. The calculation was that they might as well keep the students in their line of sight.

In those days, airplane passengers could light up while in flight, swathing 150 strangers inside a metal tube at 30,000 feet in Pall Mall smoke from Milwaukee to Phoenix.

#5956. Risk and Reward Along Africa’s Red Sea Littoral

Essay: Risk and Reward Along Africa’s Red Sea Littoral

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

The new era of maritime chokepoint disruption has, in many ways, highlighted the importance of Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden states. The Houthis’ ability to hold the Bab el-Mandeb at risk, combined with the deepening rivalry between the Abraham and Mecca blocs of the Middle East, have created powerful incentives for a range of extra-regional actors to further expand their partnerships along the Horn of Africa’s coastline. This is particularly clear in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, where the United Arab Emirates, Israel, and the United States have grown their diplomatic and military engagement in Puntland and Somaliland, and where the United States has pursued a diplomatic rapprochement with Eritrea.

What does this mean for the Horn of Africa’s littoral states? Although their geographic proximity to what Bruno Macaes called “the strait at the center of the world” has emerged as valuable strategic currency, it is not hard to see how the attempt to coopt Africa’s Red Sea states into one alliance or another could go wrong. The concerns are threefold: that the Horn’s littoral states might become entrapped in conflicts that are not their own; that the intra-Horn rivalries the littoral states are already enmeshed in are made more acute; and that internal governance conditions in the Horn’s states further deteriorate.

The new era of maritime chokepoint disruption has, in many ways, highlighted the importance of Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden states. The Houthis’ ability to hold the Bab el-Mandeb at risk, combined with the deepening rivalry between the Abraham and Mecca blocs of the Middle East, have created powerful incentives for a range of extra-regional actors to further expand their partnerships along the Horn of Africa’s coastline. This is particularly clear in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, where the United Arab Emirates, Israel, and the United States have grown their diplomatic and military engagement in Puntland and Somaliland, and where the United States has pursued a diplomatic rapprochement with Eritrea.

What does this mean for the Horn of Africa’s littoral states? Although their geographic proximity to what Bruno Macaes called “the strait at the center of the world” has emerged as valuable strategic currency, it is not hard to see how the attempt to coopt Africa’s Red Sea states into one alliance or another could go wrong. The concerns are threefold: that the Horn’s littoral states might become entrapped in conflicts that are not their own; that the intra-Horn rivalries the littoral states are already enmeshed in are made more acute; and that internal governance conditions in the Horn’s states further deteriorate.

The Horn’s littoral states cannot wish away geography or the incentives that it creates. But they do have room to maneuver. Robust public debate among Horn publics, prudent decision-making from ruling elites, and conscientious engagement from key external partners can ensure that this new chapter of geopolitical centrality does not further destabilize a region that is already at the precipice.

The Horn of Africa has been a critical node since the inauguration of the Suez Canal in 1869. But the intensity with which this fact has been felt has waxed and waned over time. The start of the Yemen War in 2015 initiated another period of growing entanglement between the Horn of Africa and a range of outside powers, each of whom sought a strategic perch near the Red Sea corridor from which to project their security and commercial interests.

But the turmoil in the  Middle East after Oct. 7, 2023, has sharpened this dynamic. Two developments have been particularly consequential. The first is the Houthi campaign to interrupt maritime traffic in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, with a first wave of attacks beginning in November 2023 and a second wave targeting Saudi shipping starting in the summer of 2026. The second dynamic has been the deepening rivalry between the Abraham and Mecca blocs of the Middle East. Although these respective blocs are not entirely coherent, there are clear divisions over Israel’s increasingly muscular security policy; the Iran crisis; and their respective interventions in conflicts between national governments and subnational armed actors across the region.

In the face of new strategic pressures, several extra-regional actors have sought enhanced access and position in this zone, over and above what they had secured in preceding years. A triumvirate of littoral countries/de-facto states have been immediate targets: Somaliland, Puntland, and Eritrea.

The impact is most apparent in Somaliland. Its economic partnership with the UAE, through the latter’s investment in the Berbera corridor, is long-standing. But this relationship has become increasingly securitized since 2024. The clearest evidence is what transpired at Berbera Airport, which has come under the effective security control of the UAE. Satellite imagery suggests the construction of an adjoining dock and the hardening of the airport’s infrastructure, including the development of underground bunkers that are potentially for ammunition and fuel. Many believe the airport has also become a logistical node in the UAE’s broader military supply network across East Africa, enabling the delivery of weapons to Sudan and Ethiopia.

Israel’s expanding role in Somaliland has run in parallel with the growing Emirati military presence. Israel diplomatically recognized Somaliland in December 2025—making it the first country in the world to do so—and some reports suggest an active Israeli intelligence presence in Berbera and the use of the airport for refueling its jets during the Iran war. Somaliland officials generally do not confirm these reports but acknowledge that an Israeli military presence is an eventual possibility.

A Soviet-made MiG-17 fighter jet, formerly belonging to the Somali Air Force, sits atop the Hargeisa War Memorial monument in Hargeisa, Somaliland, on Oct. 16. Mohamed Ahmed/Reuters

Washington has also joined the club. In the last year, Somaliland has hosted the commanding generals of AFRICOM and SOCAFRICA. A number of U.S. military personnel based at the Baledogle Airfield in Somalia have now been redeployed to Somaliland, prompting one senior Somaliland official to privately quip, “Team Mogadishu has now become Team Hargeisa.” U.S. training opportunities for Somaliland’s security forces appear to have also grown. These developments are still nascent and as such do not yet involve the deployment of critical intelligence, security, and reconnaissance capabilities, but the direction of travel is fairly clear.

The Emirati government’s formula in Puntland has largely tracked its approach to Somaliland. Beginning in the 2010s, the Emirati footprint in the statelet had mostly consisted of a commercial port concession in Bosaso and training Puntland’s Maritime Security Forces. But from 2024 onward, the UAE scaled up its activity in Bosaso, turning an airbase next to the civilian airport into another logistical hub through which weapons, ammunition, and personnel flowed to Emirati allies throughout the Horn. The UAE has also supported Puntland’s 2024-2025 offensive against Islamic State contingents in the region through direct drone strikes. The United States has also directly backed counter-Islamic State military operations, and according to Puntland authorities, agreed in August 2026 to establish a military facility at the same Bosaso airbase that houses an Emirati presence.

Eritrea’s incorporation into this picture looks a bit different. Its external alignments sharply diverge from Somaliland and Puntland, and there is currently no evidence that Eritrea is poised to play host to foreign military facilities. Yet if the past is prologue, then Eritrea could soon find itself housing a more significant military presence. There are unconfirmed reports of the potential for an increased Egyptian presence in the southern port of Assab. Assab served as the logistical fulcrum of Emirati military operations in Yemen, and back in the early 2000s, the Eritrean government lobbied the United States to establish a military base in Eritrea. At the time, Washington declined the Eritrean offer and established its premiere African military base in neighboring Djibouti.

People sail past container ships anchored near the Bab el-Mandeb strait on Aug. 6. AFP via Getty Images

Maritime exigencies in and around the Bab el-Mandeb have now pushed Eritrea higher on the Trump administration’s agenda. While U.S.-Eritrea relations have been relatively poor for more than two decades, Washington allowed a Tigray-related sanctions package targeting the Eritrean government to expire in September 2026. This was a clear bid to enhance relations with Asmara and was tied to a broad, if not clearly defined, sense that Eritrea mattered for Red Sea security. This sanctions removal occurred even though some important U.S. policymakers believed that Eritrea had not really done enough to warrant such action.

Somaliland, Puntland, and Eritrea will probably extract clear strategic rewards from their emerging geopolitical centrality and the related expansion of security partnerships. All three face increasingly acute security dilemmas from what they regard as revanchist neighbors and their respective external backers. All of their national political projects are also at critical junctures: Somaliland is attempting to build momentum for wider recognition; Puntland is maneuvering to protect its autonomy within a Somali federation; and Eritrea is working to fully break its political estrangement from much of the international system. Somaliland and Puntland have even leveraged the good offices of Abu Dhabi and Washington to improve a bilateral relationship long riddled with tension.

People participate in a rally to celebrate the Houthis’ takeover of the strategic port city of Mocha and the Bab el-Mandeb strait in Sana’a, Yemen, on Sept. 11. Mohammed Hamoud/Getty Images

The risks, however, are very real. The first is that these small polities quickly find themselves entrapped in conflicts that are not their own. The concern is most relevant to Somaliland, where the intensification of the Emirati, Israeli, and U.S. security presence is clearest. Though Houthi attacks in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden have had negative economic repercussions on Berbera port, Somaliland’s authorities have no interest in getting involved in a regional war against the Houthis. But they might not have a choice. The Houthis themselves have threatened to strike any Israeli military presence in Somaliland and even hacked the website of Somaliland’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs in early July. If a conflict led to missile or drone strikes on Berbera, it would have a catastrophic impact on trade, government revenue, and oil imports.

There is also a risk that Somaliland’s deepening security engagement with the Abraham bloc alienates it from Saudi Arabia, which is clearly unnerved by the growing security presence of the Emiratis and Israelis in the southern Red Sea. Somaliland’s critical livestock export sector, which provides 80 percent of all export earnings, is oriented toward the Saudi market, meaning it can ill afford to antagonize Riyadh.

Somaliland’s authorities are no doubt hoping to manage the scale and conduct of the foreign military element within its borders, so as to not provoke retaliation from actors they otherwise have few differences with. Although not widely known, when it was negotiating a memorandum of understanding for sea access with Ethiopia in late 2023, Somaliland placed real limitations on an Ethiopian naval presence in its Gulf of Aden shores. This included the denial of a land corridor between the Ethiopian border and naval base, as well as limits on the Ethiopian military’s interactions with local communities and third-party military activity. But does Somaliland have the autonomy to fully constrain what Israel, the UAE, and the United States do within its borders?

The second risk is that external actors’ push for new Red Sea-oriented partnerships might inadvertently fuel escalatory dynamics in the region. This is most evident in the growing tensions between Eritrea and Ethiopia. The scramble for positions along the Horn’s Red Sea littoral has provided landlocked Ethiopia a new set of justifications to press its maritime claims, including to the port of Assab in Eritrea. Ethiopian officials have argued that since the Red Sea and its Horn ports are increasingly contested terrain, an Ethiopian naval presence is the only way to ensure the country’s economic and security interests. They also make the point that if it is legitimate for outside powers to establish military bases along the Red Sea littoral, then it is an equally legitimate course of action for Ethiopia.

A view of U.S. military aircraft at Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti on Jan. 21, 2024. Djibouti sits opposite Yemen, across the Bab el-Mandeb strait, and between Eritrea and Somaliland.Getty Images

At the same time, U.S. sanctions removal, and the growing proximity between Cairo and Asmara, has increased Eritrea’s willingness to risk conflict with its southern neighbor. Indeed, the decision by the TPLF and the Alliance for Survival to launch offensives on Sept. 23, likely with the approval of Asmara, came just six days after the U.S. sanctions regime on Eritrea expired.

Meanwhile, Emirati-Israeli involvement in Somaliland and Puntland has further consolidated Mogadishu’s increasing all-weather alliance with Turkey. President Hassan Sheikh has used Somalia’s growing defense partnerships with Turkey, which has deployed F-16s to the region to fight Al-Shabaab, to put pressure on Somaliland and Puntland. Most recently, this has involved an electronic visa scheme managed by Mogadishu to control the movement of foreign passport holders into Somaliland, and a reported agreement with Ankara to build a military base in Laasqoray, which sits in territory that Somaliland considers its own.

Analysts fear that the renewed conflict could quickly draw in other regional actors.

How Washington bargains away its Africa strategy to other regions.

As a result, the risk of conflict between Mogadishu, Garowe, and even Hargeisa has increased considerably. In July and August, for instance, there were military confrontations between Puntland’s government and the Puntland Security Force, a militia that had increasingly come under the sway of Mogadishu, resulting in the PSF bases in Galkayo and Bosaso being seized by Puntland authorities.

A final risk is related to the core governance questions that will shape the regional security landscape of the Horn in the coming years.

Consider Eritrea, which has been mired in a deep human rights crisis for decades. This has driven hundreds of thousands of its young people abroad and produced deep, if still suppressed, social fissures. The country has no functioning constitution or electoral system, and thus no mechanism for peacefully navigating succession or adjudicating domestic political differences. Its political elite, in power since 1991, is unwilling to cultivate younger leaders or embrace basic economic and political reforms, offering little more than time-worn cliches about the need to defend against sabotage by external enemies.  Unsurprisingly, U.S. sanctions relief engages none of these issues.

In Somaliland and Puntland, the problem is one of political polarization, as deepening external partnerships have widened disagreements between contending political factions. Somaliland’s recognition deal with Israel has drawn internal criticism, including from religious actors, on both moral and strategic grounds. This was particularly true after Hargeisa made the controversial decision to place its embassy in Jerusalem rather than Tel Aviv in July. In Puntland, some opponents of President Saeed Deni believe he is using Emirati patronage to further consolidate his power. In all of these debates and more, fairly explosive clan rivalries lurk just beneath the surface.

Members of the Somaliland Coast Guard participate in a parade in Hargeisa on May 18. Kang-Chun Cheng/AFP via Getty Images

The Horn’s littoral states can navigate the risks associated with their emerging geopolitical centrality. But it will require more than business as usual. The first step is robust public debate about the risks and rewards of external security entanglements, so that all relevant considerations are surfaced. In many ways, Somaliland is ahead of the curve in this regard, a reflection of its relatively strong—although far from perfect—democratic system.

Ruling elites must also prudently assess the costs and benefits of foreign basing and military cooperation. The challenge here is that the democratic deficit in some of these states means that regime security often prevails over public interest. There are also separate questions of state capacity in some of these polities and the fundamental ability of the government to recognize substantive problems and devise responses. Finally, external partners, particularly the United States, must recognize that the transactionalism of the moment will not deliver stability in one of the world’s most essential maritime corridors. The only solution is to encourage better and more accountable governance along Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden littoral.

This work is supported by the Cross-Border Conflict Evidence, Policy and Trends (XCEPT) research program, funded by UK International Development. The views and opinions expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent those of the U.K. government.

Michael Woldemariam is an associate professor and the Ph.D. program director in the University of Maryland’s School of Public Policy.

Biruk Terrefe is a lecturer in African politics at the University of Bayreuth and a research associate at Oxford’s African Studies Centre.

#5952. Europe Steps Into the Breach on Ukraine

Analysis: Europe Steps Into the Breach on Ukraine

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Understanding the conflict four years in.

Now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival. This week will be crucial, with the European Council meeting on Nov. 26-27 to decide on an additional loan of 45 billion euros (about $49.5 billion) to tide Ukraine over next year as it wrestles with nonstop missile strikes, jet-powered drones, and a gaping hole in its budget.

The Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities. That hostility, like the war, has only escalated, with U.S. President Donald Trump suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports (in a bid to lower fuel prices) and neutering the latest legislation meant to economically punish Moscow.

Now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival. This week will be crucial, with the European Council meeting on Nov. 26-27 to decide on an additional loan of 45 billion euros (about $49.5 billion) to tide Ukraine over next year as it wrestles with nonstop missile strikes, jet-powered drones, and a gaping hole in its budget.

The Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities. That hostility, like the war, has only escalated, with U.S. President Donald Trump suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports (in a bid to lower fuel prices) and neutering the latest legislation meant to economically punish Moscow.

“It began with the diesel deal. This is the longest sustained effort by Team Trump” to put its thumb on the scales, said John Herbst, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine. “It annoys me even more that they are helping [Russian President Vladimir] Putin do this. Putin wants to undermine NATO, and that is why it is so frustrating.”

Trump had previously adumbrated his approach to Ukraine by delaying approval of the bipartisan legislation, championed by former Sen. Lindsey Graham, that would have levied stiff tariffs on Russia’s trading partners and put additional sanctions on top Russian officials. When the legislation finally did pass, Trump watered it down, waiving the sanctions and for once forgetting about tariffs.

“I found U.S. policy over the last six weeks depressing,” said Steven Pifer, another former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine. “I think Trump is lost to the cause, even if the American people are not.”

Now it falls to Europe to fill the gap, both in terms of Kyiv’s budget and its defense needs. About half of the new loan is earmarked for Ukraine’s administration and the other half for defense procurement.

The European loan is not a done deal. There are four holdouts among the usual suspects—Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria, and the Czech Republic—that are leery of signing onto more blocwide debt to support a country they view askance. But by Friday, informed observers say, the European Union will probably be able to hammer through a fresh 45 billion on top of the 90 billion euro loan for Ukraine that it is still doling out.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has said the latest loan would be backed by frozen Russian assets held in Europe. Those central bank assets total about $300 billion worldwide, with just over $200 billion in Belgium. Despite years of posturing, four years into the war, neither Europe nor the United States nor the United Kingdom has moved from freezing to seizing, fearful of the potential legal, financial, and other consequences of grabbing illicit Russian money. That makes the ultimate collateral for this new European loan something of a question mark.

“Europe has no choice but to fund Ukraine’s defense. The question is how you do it,” said Timothy Ash, a Russia expert at Chatham House. “I find it incredible, when you put it across like this, which taxpayers should pay for this: Europe’s or Russia’s?” (He has some thoughts.)

The bigger question is broader. Europe knows that enabling Ukraine to survive the war, or at least avoid a dishonorable peace, is critical to the country’s survival as well as its own. The problem, which has been apparent since January 2025, is that Ukraine and Europe are on their own. The United States has not provided any fresh financial support for Kyiv since Trump came back to office, has at times interrupted intelligence-sharing and satellite links, and continues to block the sale of much-need missile interceptors held in European inventories.

U.S. Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby scolded Ukraine last week for striking Russian oil facilities, arguing that such attacks were ineffective. (Ukraine’s long-range strikes have taken offline about half of Russia’s refinery capacity in recent months, cratered its energy exports, and are leading to lines at gas stations in Russia.) Meanwhile, Russian missiles and drones continue to rain down on Kyiv, Kharkiv, and other major cities.

“Trump is just defending Putin and making it harder for Ukraine to defend itself,” Herbst said.

Germany’s vocal support for mobilizing hundreds of billions of Moscow’s reserves could be a game-changer for Ukraine.

For all the talk of a new world order, the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting produced little of substance.

One question that looms now is whether Europe’s determination to support Ukraine—Europe has already provided nearly 240 billion euros (about $260 billion), far more than the United States or any other country—will push Trump into reprisal mode. He has in the past slapped tariffs on Europe while waiving penalties on Russia. Over the weekend, Trump posted a photo of himself with Putin titled, simply, “My Friend.”

“If Trump wants to go down that route, it might get ugly in Europe, but I don’t think Europe can afford to let Ukraine lose. There is a real understanding in Europe about how high the stakes are for them,” Ash said.

“It will be interesting to see where this goes in terms of the U.S.-EU relationship. This could be a huge crisis. We have to see how far he is willing to take this.”

#5951. Hail Mary effort on college sports bill could boost power conferences

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, pictured talking with reporters Nov. 17, has expressed confidence the Protect College Sports Act can clear Congress before the end of session. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump and GOP leaders are mounting a late push for a sweeping college sports bill that has stalled in the House, with new revisions that appear designed to appeal to several large state delegations by making it easier for high-profile schools to jump to the most lucrative conferences.

The Senate’s version of the bill known as the Protect College Sports Act, which passed in September, would cap collegiate athletic conference sizes at 20 schools. But a revised House version released Friday evening would raise that conference roster cap to 22 institutions after several Atlantic Coast Conference schools went public with their collective desire for the change.

The change could clear the way for another round of conference realignment, including the Southeastern Conference and Big Ten expanding again after both did so in 2024.

College sports insiders have reported for some time that SEC and Big Ten officials have been eying a number of ACC schools to join their ranks — a list that includes the University of Florida, Florida State, the University of North Carolina and South Carolina’s Clemson University. All four recently sent letters to House lawmakers requesting the conference size change, according to the Charlotte Business Journal.

The SEC and Big Ten currently have 16 members for revenue-generating sports.

To reach the revised House bill’s 22-team ceiling, there has been speculation about other ACC schools also jumping ship, including North Carolina State University, Duke University, Wake Forest University, the University of Virginia and Virginia Tech. Because the bill, even with changes made by House Republican leaders, faces an uphill battle in the chamber, the 22-team cap change could assist its proponents.

That’s because of factions that have opposed college sports legislation. The nearly 60-member Congressional Black Caucus still opposes the measure over GOP efforts to terminate majority-minority House districts and an assessment it would not do enough to help historically Black colleges and universities. And some House conservatives have raised concerns that it might hurt colleges and conferences by allowing student athletes to do things like unionize.

The Sunshine, Tar Heel and Old Dominion states have 53 total House seats, making the conference cap change a potentially tactical weapon, should the amended measure hit the House floor. The House Rules Committee, in a Friday evening announcement, signaled the revised bill could get floor votes next week, after the chamber returns from a Thanksgiving recess.

The same Rules announcement informed members they have until midday Wednesday to submit further amendments ahead of a likely committee session on the legislation next week. If the panel signs off on a rule for the revised measure and some amendments, the next stop would be the chamber floor.

The bill got a big boost from Trump during a Friday press conference at the White House.

“If we don't pass that bill, you're not only going to not have sports, but you're going to have every college in the country go bankrupt,” Trump said.

A White House official signaled the president was not concerned about the proposed House changes. “The president wants NIL reform to get done and for Congress to send him a bill that can reach his desk quickly,” the official said in an email.

House Republicans did not make any changes to the Senate-passed measure’s provisions meant to help safeguard women’s sports.

House GOP leaders have proposed dropping the Senate’s threshold for when any conference merger would trigger antitrust violations. The House is proposing a breach of those laws if a conference that makes $600 million attempts to merge with or acquire another conference, down from the Senate’s $700 million level.

Along with the proposed conference size and antitrust changes, the chamber’s revised bill would make a handful of targeted changes, including new rules for how colleges and universities count name, image and likeness (NIL) agreements against a revenue-share cap.

It also proposes changing schools’ disclosure requirements for student athletic fees and a lower threshold for certain conference mergers. And it proposes changes to what would be a new congressional commission to oversee the college athletics landscape.

The House has proposed altering the Senate-passed bill’s NIL accounting language with a provision stating that any institution with annual average media rights revenue of at least $50 million could no longer use student fees to help finance their sports teams. The change appears geared toward lawmakers hailing from districts with HBCUs, smaller “Group of Six” FBS conference members and schools that compete in Football Championship Subdivision.

The revised measure would stipulate that all NIL agreements between a student athlete and an institution, an institution employee or volunteer, a conference, a conference employee or an associated entity would count against that institution’s revenue-share cap and player-retention funds.

In another proposed alteration, institutions of higher learning would be required to report certain student athlete compensation data “individually by program and in the aggregate.” The Senate-approved bill would have required reporting “for personnel of each intercollegiate sports program.”

Instead of allowing “a person” to bring a civil action, as would the Senate-approved language, the rewritten House provision would grant such rights only to a “current or former student athlete.”

The House version also would make several changes to the Senate’s proposed 24-member Congressional Commission on the Future of College Athletics by shaking up which congressional committees would get to select its members. The changes also include adding representation from midsized conferences and would give one seat to “a student athlete or former student athlete.”

In a brief interview last week, Senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz said he was confident the House would pass the bill “the week after Thanksgiving.”

“There’s plenty of time,” the Texas Republican, a co-author of the Senate bill, said when asked if the lame-duck session’s remaining planned three weeks would allow the House to finish its work on the measure and then give the Senate time to vote on an amended version. The House is slated to leave for a holiday season recess on Dec. 17; the Senate is scheduled to exit the next day.

“I believe the House is going to take it up and pass the bill,” Cruz said, adding that he had talked to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., about his plans. “I believe we will see in the House what we saw in the Senate: an overwhelming bipartisan vote.”

Criticism is mounting among experts concerned with the U.S. Army's "risky" plan to resume helicopter training flights near Washington National Airport following a deadly midair collision in 2025.

Rep. Don Beyer Jr., D-Va., attends a protest in Washington. (Tom Williams/Getty Images)

A U.S. Army Black Hawk helicopter collided with American Airlines Flight 5342 in January 2025, killing all 67 people aboard both aircrafts. #5948. The Case for a Trump-Xi-Putin Summit

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

CHARLES KUPCHAN is Professor of International Affairs at Georgetown University and a Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. He is the author of Bringing Order to Anarchy: Governing the World to Come.

In just a few days’ time, U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin could be holding a three-way summit on the sidelines of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, China. According to The Wall Street Journal, Putin floated the idea of a trialogue last month as an opportunity to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. No firm plan has yet been announced, but even the prospect of this meeting has provoked widespread consternation. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned against a repeat of the Yalta Conference of 1945, when U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill capitulated to Soviet leader Joseph Stalin’s push for the Soviet Union to dominate Eastern Europe. U.S. Senator Chris Coons posted on X that “there can be no talks about Ukraine’s future without Ukraine at the table, and there can be no real negotiations as long as Trump signals weakness and servitude to Xi and Putin at every opportunity.”

These worries are entirely justified; Trump has a track record of cozying up to autocrats and turning his back on democratic allies. Should he sit down with Xi and Putin, he must avoid selling out European and Asian partners who will not be at the table. And given the three leaders’ headstrong personalities and competing national interests that pit the United States against what Xi calls a “no limits” partnership between China and Russia, the meeting might ultimately yield little progress on major issues.

Nevertheless, Trump would be right to join a summit with Xi and Putin. No U.S. president has ever held a trilateral meeting with the leaders of China and Russia, and the proposed talks would break the ice and begin to normalize much-needed dialogue. Authoritarianism is not going away, so autocracies and democracies must learn not only to live comfortably alongside one another but also to work together to tame geopolitical rivalry and tackle global challenges in an interdependent world. Americans will not find it easy to get along with the likes of Russia and China, whose political systems threaten the U.S. commitment to spreading democracy. But Trump is taking a bold step in the right direction by engaging with the heads of the world’s leading autocracies.

If he meets with Xi and Putin, Trump should aim low and focus on making meaningful, if limited, progress on a small number of core issues that could benefit from a three-way conversation: the flash points of the Korean Peninsula, Ukraine, and Iran, as well as arms control and strategic stability. But even if the summit yields no concrete results, it will nonetheless have been worthwhile. Trump, Xi, and Putin are paving the way for their successors to advance great-power cooperation across ideological lines and stabilize a fragmented world.

I have argued previously, including in a 2021 Foreign Affairs essay with Richard Haass, that a global concert—an informal steering group of great powers modeled on the nineteenth-century Concert of Europe—offers the best hope of curbing geopolitical competition and enabling collective action in a multipolar world. In addition to the United States, China, and Russia, a new concert would include India, Japan, the European Union, and representatives from Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Concerts sacrifice representation for efficacy and give only the geopolitically influential states that must be there a seat at the table. They set aside ideological differences and bring democracies and autocracies together to focus on international cooperation. Because concerts eschew binding, enforceable procedures in favor of informal consensus building, they can succeed when formal institutions such as the UN Security Council are paralyzed and when the United States wavers in its commitment to rules-based multilateralism.

But the time has not come for a global concert. Concerts function effectively only when their members are committed to the territorial status quo, are willing to exercise strategic restraint and pursue mutual benefits, and are ready to settle disputes diplomatically. Putin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and Xi’s decision to back Russia have, for now, scuttled hopes that the great powers will normalize restraint and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Meanwhile, Trump’s “America first” statecraft shuns joint action and mutual gain in favor of unilateralism.

Yet even though Trump, Xi, and Putin are the wrong leaders at the wrong time to establish a great-power steering group that other major players would eventually join, Trump’s iconoclastic diplomacy sets a useful precedent. His Alaska summit with Putin last year and two summits with Xi this year were admittedly long on pageantry and short on substance. But by taking the controversial step of pursuing joint talks with the two leaders, Trump is widening the diplomatic Overton window and expanding what is politically possible for future U.S. presidents. Avoiding great-power conflict and taming a world in increasing disarray requires the United States to build constructive relations with both China and Russia. Trump deserves credit for starting a trialogue that his successors can carry forward.

If they meet in Shenzhen, Trump, Xi, and Putin should focus on easing tensions at key geopolitical flash points. The Korean Peninsula presents the best opportunity for the three leaders to collaborate. At the UN General Assembly in September, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung laid out an ambitious plan for normalizing relations with Pyongyang, including a proposal to replace the peninsula’s 1953 armistice with a “peace regime” that promotes “respect for each other’s systems and acknowledgement of our differences.” As part of that plan, Lee has advocated a phased approach to North Korean denuclearization, with an initial freeze on weapons development followed by gradual reductions in Pyongyang’s arsenal of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles until the peninsula is denuclearized.

Lee’s bold proposal could bring U.S., Chinese, and Russian interests into alignment. Trump has made it clear that he wants to de-escalate tensions on the Korean Peninsula and is already seeking a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Beijing and Moscow are competing for influence over Kim, but both want a stable relationship between North and South Korea, so they might be willing to cooperate on proposals to halt nuclear weapons production and encourage talks between Pyongyang and Seoul. Trump, Xi, and Putin should aim to emerge from their meeting with a plan for advancing Lee’s peace agenda; jointly supporting a freeze on North Korean nuclear weapons development is a good place to start.

The prospects for progress toward ending the war in Ukraine are much dimmer but not nonexistent. Trump should be striving to weaken Russia’s ability to sustain the war, but he has long resisted tightening sanctions on Moscow. He talks up potential business ventures with Russia and, in recent weeks, even struck a deal with Putin to get more Russian diesel into global markets and waived a new round of congressional sanctions against Moscow. Trump evidently cares more about trying to bring down fuel prices than about curbing Russia’s ability to fund its war against Ukraine.

A summit offers Trump the opportunity to change course and try to convince Xi to restrain Putin. Trump has vowed to bring the war in Ukraine to an end, and the Chinese leader can help him achieve that goal. Xi has enormous leverage over Putin: China backs the Kremlin diplomatically, is the largest buyer of Russian oil and gas, and is the main supplier of dual-use items such as semiconductors and machine tools that are critical to Russian weapons manufacturing.

Xi has played along with Putin’s war against Ukraine so far, presumably because the conflict diverts U.S. attention and resources away from Asia, divides NATO, and allows Xi and Putin to cast themselves as leading a global resistance to Western hegemony. But when Xi and Trump met this May, the leaders agreed to pursue “a constructive relationship of strategic stability” between China and the United States, which Xi could advance by pressing Putin to de-escalate. As more Russians feel the effects of the war, the Kremlin may be newly receptive to such pressure. Ukrainian drone strikes are taking a significant toll on Russia’s oil sector and logistics networks, which means Russian citizens face mounting gas and commodities shortages. Meanwhile, some 35,000 Russian soldiers per month are losing their lives or sustaining severe injuries in eastern Ukraine, forcing Putin to consider the unpopular move of ramping up military mobilization. With no battlefield victory in sight, Putin has reasons to entertain a diplomatic off-ramp.

Trump and Xi could press Putin to accept a set of limited but consequential steps to de-escalate the conflict. These could include an agreement between Russia and Ukraine—brokered and monitored by Washington and Beijing—to end attacks on energy installations and infrastructure, civilian targets, and commercial shipping. Trump and Xi could also jointly press Putin to refrain from actions that could broaden the war, such as penetrating NATO airspace with Russian drones, sabotaging European infrastructure, and threatening to use nuclear weapons. This pressure, combined with the allure of improving diplomatic and commercial ties to the United States, might convince Putin to relent on at least some of these issues.

Trump could also use a trilateral summit to seek help extricating the United States from its war in Iran—a quagmire that has produced regional mayhem and soaring oil prices. As Tehran continues to issue maximalist demands and the war disrupts shipping through the straits of Hormuz and Bab el Mandeb, Trump needs an out.

Neither Xi nor Putin has yet been inclined to lend a hand. China is still buying Iranian oil and providing Tehran with military intelligence and dual-use items that end up in Iranian drones and missiles, and Russia is providing satellite targeting data, munitions, advanced drone technology, and logistical support. Both Beijing and Moscow are happy to see the United States mired in a conflict that is exacerbating divisions within the American electorate and fracturing NATO.

As a major energy exporter, Russia benefits from the spike in oil prices that the conflict has triggered, so pressing Putin to cease supporting Iran is likely a lost cause. But China is the world’s largest oil importer, and Beijing has a vested interest in lowering energy prices by stabilizing exports from the Middle East. Although China’s large oil reserves have buffered its economy from rising oil prices so far, those reserves have been significantly depleted. China’s crude oil imports have begun to climb again, leaving its economy exposed to high energy prices if the conflict drags on. And as the world’s largest exporter of goods, China suffers from the dampening effect high energy prices have on global growth.

Xi might therefore be amenable to helping Trump end the war. Trump should ask Xi to stop or at least slow the flow of Chinese dual-use items to Iran. Washington’s naval blockade and financial and commercial sanctions on Tehran have already taken a toll on Iran’s economy and military supply chains. By cutting off Chinese technology shipments to Iran, Beijing could deepen this economic isolation and help convince Tehran to negotiate an end to the conflict.

Xi could also press Iran to drop its unrealistic demands for ending the war, including that the United States withdraw its forces from the Gulf, release frozen Iranian assets, and remove economic sanctions. Washington might well be willing to offer economic relief, but only as part of postwar negotiations toward a deal that reins in Iran’s nuclear ambitions. Xi could help clear the way for those talks by urging Iran to accept credible terms for ending the immediate conflict.

Beyond working to resolve current conflicts, Trump should promote future strategic stability by pursuing arms control negotiations with Xi and Putin. Every arms control agreement negotiated between Washington and Moscow has expired; their final nuclear pact, New START, ended in February. There are currently no caps on the American and Russian strategic arsenals and no regular inspections, data exchanges, or notifications of nuclear exercises. This nuclear free-for-all is particularly dangerous given Russia’s nuclear saber rattling amid the war in Ukraine and the Kremlin’s fondness for provocations such as sending explosive-laden drones into NATO airspace.

In October, Trump appropriately proposed that a trilateral summit include a discussion of nuclear arms control. China has long resisted engaging in arms control talks, arguing that it should not have to limit its nuclear program when its arsenal is much smaller than that of the United States and Russia. But Beijing is rapidly expanding and modernizing its nuclear arsenal. The Pentagon has projected that China will possess more than 1,000 operational warheads by 2030, putting it in nearly the same league as the United States and Russia, which have stockpiles of roughly 1,800 operational warheads each. With the uncertain trajectory of U.S.-Chinese relations, instability on the Korean Peninsula, and China’s tense relationship with Taiwan heightening the risk of conflict in East Asia, Beijing must be part of high-level nuclear arms control discussions.

Realistically, Trump can do little more than start this conversation and invite Xi and Putin to continue it in future trilateral negotiations led by teams of diplomats and arms control experts. In future talks, the three countries should discuss not only caps on nuclear weapons stockpiles but also military-to-military contacts, crisis management protocols, notifications of military exercises, counterproliferation, and other measures that can contribute to strategic stability.

Trump could add a host of other topics to the summit’s agenda, including trade, energy security, and AI regulation, but he should avoid a wide-ranging conversation that goes nowhere. He might, however, notch an easy win by proposing a three-way initiative in an area in which cooperation is relatively straightforward—for example, a joint medical mission to the Democratic Republic of the Congo to help fight Ebola or a joint aid operation to deliver humanitarian relief to Gaza or Yemen. A concrete, public effort along these lines would show that trilateral dialogue can yield viable cooperation.

Yet Trump should guard against being so eager for a win that he lets Xi and Putin take advantage of him. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit takes place only two weeks after American voters dealt Trump and his party a historic rebuke in the U.S. midterm elections. The notoriously thin-skinned president could be tempted to make concessions to Beijing and Moscow to score a foreign policy breakthrough. He must avoid making a behind-closed-doors compromise on Ukraine that he then tries to force on Kyiv and its European supporters. Similarly, he must hold the line on Taiwan even as he seeks Xi’s help on North Korea, Ukraine, and Iran. Otherwise, Trump will leave the trilateral meeting confirming the worst fears of those who foresaw a new Yalta in the making. Capitulating to Xi and Putin would alienate Washington’s allies, project American weakness, and erode global deterrence.

Trump must also carefully manage the optics of a trilateral summit. Putin is an indicted war criminal who continues to prosecute a ruthless war of aggression against Ukraine. It is far too soon to let him out of the penalty box. And although Washington is right to seek a good working relationship with Beijing, it is time for Trump’s “truly great friendship” with Xi to bear fruit. Trump must approach talks with sobriety and pragmatism, seeking to demonstrate that Washington, Beijing, and Moscow can work together to help promote global peace and stability.

A summit next week will not usher in a new era of great-power collaboration anytime soon. It might not even yield concrete deliverables. Still, the meeting would set a valuable precedent. Simply by sitting down with Xi and Putin, Trump would begin a much-needed trilateral conversation.

How to Prevent Catastrophe and Promote Stability in a Multipolar World

Stephen E. Biegun and Emma Chanlett-Avery

And the Coming Crisis in Strategic Stability

#5947. What Did Xi Jinping Get From the Shenzhen Summit?

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: What Did Xi Jinping Get From the Shenzhen Summit?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

A brief summit between the leaders of China, the United States, and Russia was held in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19. Critics saw little substantive achievement, arguing that the three had merely taken advantage of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum to meet for a photo opportunity. Some American observers faulted U.S. President Donald Trump in particular for yielding to China and Russia rather than showing leadership.

In my view, the summit, short as it was, did matter. In great-power politics, the format can sometimes matter more than the concrete results. The leaders of the three countries had never sat down together in this format; that they managed to do so says something about the kind of era that we are entering.

A brief summit between the leaders of China, the United States, and Russia was held in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19. Critics saw little substantive achievement, arguing that the three had merely taken advantage of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum to meet for a photo opportunity. Some American observers faulted U.S. President Donald Trump in particular for yielding to China and Russia rather than showing leadership.

In my view, the summit, short as it was, did matter. In great-power politics, the format can sometimes matter more than the concrete results. The leaders of the three countries had never sat down together in this format; that they managed to do so says something about the kind of era that we are entering.

In an era of great-power politics, one of the keys to avoiding military conflict is for the powers to hear one another out. They did so in Shenzhen. They also exceeded expectations by issuing a joint peace declaration with four points of agreement. And for Chinese President Xi Jinping in particular, the summit offered a first chance to try out an approach to great-power relations that he had originally proposed to Washington, this time with both the United States and Russia at the table.

Yet while Xi hosted, the biggest winner was clearly Russian President Vladimir Putin. The war in Ukraine has left Russia diplomatically isolated from much of the West. Shenzhen could not end that isolation, but it showed that Russia could not simply be shut out of great-power diplomacy. Russia is a major military power and rich in natural resources, but its overall strength still falls well short of that of the United States or China. By sitting down with Putin as an equal, the Chinese and American leaders acknowledged that Russia remains a power that they cannot bypass on questions of global strategic security.

Xi was a winner, too. Beijing showed that it could bring two adversaries, the United States and Russia, together on Chinese soil and secure a joint declaration. The format itself put China back at the center of the international stage. A decade ago, it would have been hard to imagine China convening such a meeting. That also helped Xi’s standing at home.

Trump had just suffered a crushing defeat in the midterm elections. Yet both China and Russia accorded him the respect due an American president with whom they could still discuss strategic matters. China, in particular, gave him a lavish welcome rather than treating him as a lame duck.

But the three leaders did not sit around a table simply for the sake of appearances, and Xi in particular made some meaningful gains here. The Chinese president raised the question of how the three powers should deal with one another from here on. His answer: with mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, mutually beneficial cooperation, and dialogue and consultation.

These are principles that Beijing has long pressed in its dealings with Washington, rooted in Xi’s proposal for a “new type of great-power relations” between China and the United States. As host, Xi set the tone by extending that framework to all three countries. The summit was a chance for Beijing to put it into practice. In effect, Xi brought Putin into the room to press Trump on an approach that he had long advocated for U.S.-China relations.

That, from Beijing’s perspective, was the summit’s most important achievement. Rivalry between Washington and Beijing, and outright hostility between Washington and Moscow, did not prevent the three countries from coordinating on strategic stability.

This takes a minimum of trust. None of the three countries has to believe that its rivals will give up competing. Each has to believe that the others also want to prevent a miscalculation from triggering a conflict, that they are willing to explain their intentions, and that they will listen when another country spells out its red lines. Sitting down together, rather than meeting only in pairs, means letting down their guard enough to acknowledge that some risks involve all three and cannot necessarily be managed through bilateral talks alone.

If regular coordination takes hold, then Shenzhen will matter even more to Beijing. After the summit, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said that China would stay in touch with Russia and the United States at the working level. That is a start. Whether the leaders’ dialogue lasts will depend on whether they meet a second or third time, and whether communication holds up when relations come under strain.

Those gains stem largely from the format. The declaration itself offers further clues to what Beijing wanted to accomplish. The first, third, and fourth points are particularly revealing.

The first concerns U.N. reform. The three countries agreed to work toward reforming the United Nations so it could respond more effectively to global challenges and better fulfill its basic mission of maintaining international peace and security.

My reading is that Beijing pushed for this language to reassure the global south. Beijing knows that some countries in the global south are uneasy about China sitting down with the United States and Russia at a summit of its own making. Putting the U.N. reform first sent a related message: The three powers had met to help the United Nations fulfill its peace and security mandate and had no intention of making new rules over the heads of the global south. Wang’s insistence after the summit that countries large and small are equal was meant to convey the same point.

The third point in the declaration names the International Criminal Court. The leaders emphasized the importance of state consent and respect for the immunity of state officials, and they said the court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction. Moscow likely pushed for this provision in response to the court’s arrest warrant for Putin, backed by Trump due to the U.S. far right’s hostility toward the court. But the words “and other similar bodies” were most likely added at Beijing’s insistence. They give China a joint statement that it can cite in future disputes over jurisdiction, such as the South China Sea arbitration.

Those words also have implications for Taiwan. If mainland China were to attack Taiwan and Washington were to push for Chinese leaders to be held criminally accountable for alleged war crimes, Beijing could point to a declaration the United States helped issue and ask: What did you say in Shenzhen about state consent and the immunity of officials?

The fourth point can be read as a gain for Beijing on nuclear issues. The three countries reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought—language that originated with U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, but that has been taken up by China. They also agreed to hold talks on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation.

Trump wanted trilateral nuclear disarmament talks. What made it into the declaration was language on risk reduction and nonproliferation. Beijing succeeded in redirecting U.S. pressure to join disarmament talks toward issues that all three countries might be willing to keep discussing.

China also gained a basis for putting diplomatic pressure on Japan, where changes to—or even the abandonment of—the three non-nuclear principles are under consideration. If Tokyo goes down that path, particularly if the debate turns to Japan acquiring nuclear weapons of its own, Beijing can cite the trilateral agreement and press Washington to say where it stands on those risks.

Xi showed at Shenzhen that China could convene two adversaries, set a framework for discussing strategic stability, and get them to agree on some common positions. As much criticism as the meeting drew, it also raised hopes that trilateral talks might become a regular fixture. Xi’s remarks suggest that he would like to see that happen. The real test will come when the three countries face a crisis and their interests collide. Will they still be willing to talk the way that they did in Shenzhen?

Deng Yuwen is a Chinese writer and scholar.

#5945. Appeals court rules lack of quorum invalidated House proxy voting

Rep. Rich McCormick, R-Ga., runs up the House steps with his skateboard to the Capitol for the final vote of the week on Sept. 3. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

A federal appeals court found the proxy voting rules the House adopted during the COVID-19 pandemic violated the constitutional requirement for a quorum in a case challenging a 2022 omnibus spending package.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit, based in New Orleans, issued its ruling Friday.

The case hinges on a clause in the Constitution requiring a majority of the House, or quorum, be present for the chamber to do business. Friday’s ruling by the full court held that not enough members voted to pass the 2022 law because they were not actually in the chamber.

Judge Cory Wilson, writing for the 9-8 majority, said that while the Constitution provides broad discretion for Congress to pass its own rules, the legislature cannot get around the requirement that its members be present. The ruling focused on a series of provisions called the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act within the broader spending law and prohibited its enforcement against Texas.

“While the chambers of the legislature have much discretion regarding their rules of procedure, the Quorum Clause’s constraints on congressional power cannot be circumvented by congressional fiat,” the opinion says. The Democrat-led House adopted proxy voting as part of a broader social-distancing program during the pandemic.

The ruling opens up additional challenges to the spending law, and could be appealed to the Supreme Court. The final House vote on the law in 2022 saw low attendance, with only 201 members voting, short of the 218 majority.

Eight judges on the 5th Circuit dissented from the decision Friday, in two separate opinions. Judge James Graves Jr., writing for himself and six colleagues, chided the majority for being selective in its application.

“There is no explanation offered to explain why, if the entirety of the statute was unconstitutionally passed, this court’s judgment should be limited only to one small sliver of the multitrillion dollar bill,” Graves writes.

Graves criticizes the majority for looking too deeply into congressional procedures, and points out that both chambers have used unanimous consent, which does not include establishing a quorum, to pass measures for more than two centuries.

House Democrats adopted the proxy voting rules in 2020 but Republicans scaled them back when they took over the chamber. Throughout the current Congress, Democrats have pushed to reinstate at least some proxy voting rules.

Republicans and others filed legal challenges to the proxy voting rules in 2020, including then-Minority Leader Kevin McCarthy, but those cases were ultimately unsuccessful.

Texas officials first brought the lawsuit that resulted in Friday’s ruling in 2023, arguing the law is unconstitutional. Initially a federal judge agreed with the state, but was reversed by a three-judge panel of the 5th Circuit.

Texas then asked the full appeals court to weigh in, resulting in Friday’s ruling.

There are at least two active investigations underway, according to sources: One into allegations of immigration fraud and another into Omar's finances.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is seen on Capitol Hill in Washington D.C., on Tuesday for the first time since two federal investigations were opened against her, looking into her immigration status and financial filings. (Reuters/Tim Evans)

Omar has repeatedly denied wrongdoing to Fox News Digital in connection with the investigations, but the investigations remain ongoing, and no official charges have been filed to date. The Justice Department’s Oct. 7 brief identifies her as Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, also known as Ilhan Abdullahi Omar. Both names appear together twice in the unredacted portions of the recently released documents.

Boasberg of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia after news organizations sought access. Prosecutors described the matter as seeking evidence of violations occurring between 1980 and the present. That timeframe extends well before Omar entered Congress and aligns with public reporting on her arrival in the United States in the mid-1990s, sources and court filings indicate.

A 1981 birth year would have made her 18 by then, while a 1982 birth year would have made her 17.

The Justice Department agreed to that protocol but later pushed back, arguing that the court had applied a different standard in another recent search warrant approved by the same judge involving an unnamed individual who appears similarly situated.
